\emph{The number.}  At $\xi = 1$ the mirror is a full Standard-Model copy at the photon temperature. Its energy density is that of a photon, worth $\tfrac{8}{7}(\tfrac{11}{4})^{4/3}$ neutrino species, plus three neutrinos:
\[
\Delta\Neff \;=\; \underbrace{\tfrac{8}{7}\bigl(\tfrac{11}{4}\bigr)^{4/3}}_{\text{mirror photon}} \;+\; \underbrace{3.044}_{\text{mirror neutrinos}} \;=\; 4.40 + 3.044 \;=\; 7.45 \qquad \text{(K2)}.
\]

dark-tower-matter.pairs.technical: The conformal space $\hatV$ of a causal tower has signature $(p+1, q+1)$ with $\min(p,q) = 1$, so its real Witt index is $2$, while its complex Witt index is $\lfloor \dim\hatV/2 \rfloor$. In the three-dimensional towers both are $2$: two real ladder pairs, and no unit is needed. In this tower, the mirror and the five-dimensional towers the real index is $2$ and the complex one $3$, so the third pair needs a complex unit; in this tower and the mirror the field is $\C$ and the unit is fixed up to sign.
dark-tower-matter.pairs.lay: Each constituent carries internal ladder pairs, pairs of creation and annihilation operations built from the directions of its conformal algebra. In the three-dimensional towers there are two, built from real numbers alone. In the four- and five-dimensional towers there are three, and the third can only be built with a square root of minus one; in our tower and the mirror that root is fixed up to sign.

proofs.main:
In a causal tower $\min(p,q) = 1$, and $\hatV$ has signature $(p+1, q+1)$. Its Witt indices are
\[
\text{real: } \min(p+1, q+1) = 2, \qquad
\text{complex: } \Bigl\lfloor \frac{\dim\hatV}{2} \Bigr\rfloor =
\begin{cases} 2, & \dim\hatV = 5, \\ 3, & \dim\hatV = 6, 7. \end{cases}
\]
Check D1 builds the two real pairs of $\Cl(3,2)$ and $\Cl(2,3)$ on their modules and verifies the relations. In this tower and the mirror the field of (ii) is $\C$ by Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}.

dark-tower-matter.r1-has-no-mechanism-od.formal: In this tower and the mirror a quantum's mass is a confinement scale, $m = c\Lambda$ \cite[Prop.~4.7]{ButlerT14}. In the three-dimensional towers the gauge algebra is abelian and the coupling dimensionful, so there is no dimensional transmutation and the cells' masses are bare parameters; the viable phase needs $m/e^{2} \lesssim 1.4 \times 10^{-8}$, which nothing in the content protects (no chirality; parity broken by the forced Chern-Simons level). In the five-dimensional towers nothing confines (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.five-dimensional-towers}(ii)) and the quanta are elementary with bare masses. So T14's R1, equal mass per quantum, has no mechanism for about $81$ percent of the dark matter and is a premise about bare masses there. Assembly level.

dark-tower-matter.residue-seven-unit.technical:
Along the residue-seven tower ($\Cl(2,3)$, $\Cl(3,4)$, $\Cl(4,5)$, and so on) the pseudoscalar $\omega$ is central with $Q(\omega) = -1$ at every rung, and along the residue-one tower it is central with $Q(\omega) = +1$. At $r = 7$, $\omega$ is odd: it carries the even ideal into the odd one, so it does not act on the constituent ideal, and the grade involution reverses it.

On the Clifford module $\Cl(\hatV)\hf = T \oplus \omega T$, left multiplication by $c + s\omega$ with $c^2 + s^2 = 1$ commutes with the whole Clifford action and sends $X + \omega Y$ to $(cX - sY) + \omega(sX + cY)$: on a pair of real constituents it is the slot rotation, supplied by the algebra itself, and every cell has charge $\pm 1$ under it. At assembly level, if the tower's action is built from operations commuting with the Clifford action, a Majorana-type mass (charge $2$) is forbidden at $r = 7$, gauged or not.
dark-tower-matter.residue-seven-unit.lay: In the residue-seven tower the algebra itself contains a square root of minus one that commutes with everything, at every step of the tower. It cannot act on a single constituent, but it rotates a pair of real constituents into each other and gives them a conserved charge. If the tower's dynamics respects the algebra, an assumption at assembly level, this charge forbids the kind of mass that would turn a particle into its own antiparticle.

proofs.main:
\textit{(i)}\enspace By the formula of the section “Setting, imports and premises” (\claimref{primer.sign}), $Q(\omega) = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^{q}$. Each rung adds $(1,1)$ to the signature, so $n$ rises by two and $q$ by one, and the first exponent changes by
\[
\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}{2} - \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \;=\; 2n + 1,
\]
which is odd. The two sign changes cancel, so $Q(\omega)$ is constant along each tower and equal to its value at the first rung:
\[
Q(\omega_{2,3}) = (-1)^{10}(-1)^{3} = -1, \qquad Q(\omega_{3,2}) = (-1)^{10}(-1)^{2} = +1.
\]
Every rung has odd dimension, so $\omega$ is central (H1, H2; \claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}).



\emph{(ii)}  $\omega$ is a product of five vectors (H3), so it is odd, left multiplication by it exchanges the even and odd parts, and $\hat{\omega} = (-1)^{5}\omega = -\omega$ (\claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}).



\emph{(iii)}  $\omega$ is central with $\omega^{2} = -1$ (H4), so $c + s\omega$ commutes with the Clifford action, and for $X, Y \in T$
\[
(c + s\omega)(X + \omega Y) \;=\; cX + s\omega^{2}Y + \omega(sX + cY) \;=\; (cX - sY) + \omega(sX + cY).
\]

dark-tower-matter.same-kind-matter.technical:
Under H2 and Premise U the two towers of each odd dimension have the same constituent field, the same mass onset, the same gauge algebra and the same content, and differ only in discrete structure. At $r = 1$ the slot rotation rotates two modules of the same type, the slot reflection is internal, there are two module types ($\omega = \pm 1$), and number-violating masses are forbidden once the slot rotation is gauged; at $r = 7$ the rotation is the algebra's central unit, exact at every rung, the reflection exists only fused with orientation reversal, there is one module type, and such masses are forbidden by the unit, gauged or not.

At $r = 3$ the pair unit is $I_7$, fixed by the algebra, with one reversion-type invariant form, Hermitian for $I_7$, and one module type; at $r = 5$ the unit is a point of $S^2$, not fixed, with no such form and two module types.
dark-tower-matter.same-kind-matter.lay: Under the two premises that carry the Standard-Model construction to other towers, the two three-dimensional towers hold the same kind of matter as each other, and so do the two five-dimensional ones. What distinguishes the partners is only discrete structure, such as whether a needed square root of minus one is fixed by the algebra or freely chosen.

dark-tower-matter.sterile-kinematics.technical: In $\R^{2,2}$ the orthogonal complement of every non-null vector is nondegenerate and indefinite, so every vector of either sign of $Q$ is a sum of two null vectors, $v = (\tfrac12 v + w) + (\tfrac12 v - w)$ with $w \perp v$ and $Q(w) = -Q(v)/4$; and the null cone minus the origin, $S^1 \times S^1 \times \R_{>0}$, is connected, so it has no invariant future half. In $\R^{4,0}$ and $\R^{0,4}$ the only null vector is zero: there is no massless constituent, no time and no evolution.
dark-tower-matter.sterile-kinematics.lay: The two sterile towers cannot hold ordinary matter. In the one with two time and two space directions, massless pieces can add up to anything, and there is no consistent distinction between future and past. In the one with no time direction at all, nothing can be massless and nothing evolves.

Levels pass: levels written from scratch, keeping every condition and level qualifier of the formal statement.

proofs.main:
\textit{(i) Sums of null vectors.}\enspace For non-null $v$, $v^{\perp}$ is three-dimensional, of signature $(1,2)$ if $Q(v) > 0$ and $(2,1)$ if $Q(v) < 0$, since the counts of \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii) add over $V = \R v \perp v^{\perp}$. Either way $Q$ is indefinite on it, so it takes the value $-Q(v)/4$ at some $w \perp v$, and then
\[
Q\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}v \pm w\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4}Q(v) + Q(w) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{4}Q(v) - \tfrac{1}{4}Q(v) \;=\; 0
\]
(J1, which also checks nondegeneracy and indefiniteness on random vectors, and J2, which exhibits sums of both signs).



\emph{(i) The cone is connected.}  In coordinates $(t_{1}, t_{2}; x_{1}, x_{2})$ with $Q = t_{1}^{2} + t_{2}^{2} - x_{1}^{2} - x_{2}^{2}$, the null cone minus the origin is
\[
\bigl\{\, |t| = |x| > 0 \,\bigr\} \;\cong\; S^{1} \times S^{1} \times \R_{>0},
\]
which is connected. In signature $(1,3)$ the same set has the two components $t_{0} > 0$ and $t_{0} < 0$. T16 proves the corresponding statement for the timelike sets \cite[Lem.~4.4]{ButlerT16}.



\emph{(ii)}  $Q$ is a sum of four squares, so $Q(v) = 0$ only at $v = 0$ (J3).

dark-tower-matter.survival-sheets.formal: Decimal. On a sheet the comoving number per unit area and the expansion rate both fall as $a^{-2}$ in radiation domination, so two-dimensional s-wave annihilation with $\sigma_{1}v = 2P/m$ ($P$ the absorption probability per encounter) depletes a symmetric population logarithmically, $1/N_{f} = 1/N_{0} + (2P/m)\ln(a_{f}/a_{i})/(a^{2}H)$. At R2's density a symmetric sheet relic keeps $99$ percent of its number only for $P \lesssim 2 \times 10^{-16}$; at $P = 1$ about $10^{-14}$ survives (K3). In phase (T) this needs $e^{2}/m > 7 \times 10^{7}$, which also makes the relic collisionless in clusters (threshold $5.9 \times 10^{6}$, from the in-sheet phase-shift bound $1.7 \times 10^{-7}$ of T14b's cluster computation \cite[Comp.~3.3, Prem.~2.12]{ButlerT14b}) (K4). Phase (C) fails R2 by itself.

dark-tower-matter.third-pairs-unit-five-.technical:
On the sixteen-dimensional irreducible module of the conformal algebra, the constituent ideal, with spin commutant $\HH$. At $r = 3$ the pseudoscalar $I_7$ of $\Cl(5,2)$ lies in $\HH$, squares to $-1$ and commutes with every vector, and the third pair $\tfrac12(e_a \pm I_7e_b)$ joins the two real pairs to give three pairs obeying the canonical relations, whose bilinears span a $\uu(3)$ with centraliser $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_7\}$ in $\HH$. Every unit $J \in \HH$ anticommuting with $I_7$ acts as the grade involution, sends $w_3$ to $-\bar w_3$, and with $\uu(3)$ generates a Lie algebra of dimension $30$, not the twelve-dimensional $\su(2) \oplus \uu(3)$.

At $r = 5$ the algebra supplies no canonical unit: no element of $\HH$ outside $\R$ is central, and $Q(\omega) = +1$. Every unit $u \in \HH$ builds a third pair, $w_3 = \tfrac12(e_a + ue_b)$, $v_3 = -\tfrac12(e_a - ue_b)$ with $Q(e_a) = Q(e_b) = -1$, giving $\uu(3)_u$ with centraliser $\mathrm{span}\{1, u\}$; any two units are conjugate in $\HH$, and the choices form the sphere $Sp(1)/U(1) = S^2$.
dark-tower-matter.third-pairs-unit-five-.lay: The five-dimensional towers need a square root of minus one to build their third internal pair. In one of them the algebra itself provides exactly one such root, and every other candidate spoils the pair structure. In the other the algebra provides none, so any of a whole sphere of quaternionic roots will do, all equivalent to one another.

proofs.main:
\textit{(i) The unit $I_{7}$.}\enspace $I_{7}$ is central in $\Cl(5,2)$ (odd dimension) with $Q(I_{7}) = -1$ (the section “Setting, imports and premises”). Central elements commute with the spin action, so $I_{7} \in \HH$, the spin commutant of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}. Take $Q(e_{a}) = Q(e_{b}) = +1$ and
\[
w = \tfrac{1}{2}(e_{a} + I_{7}e_{b}), \qquad \bar{w} = \tfrac{1}{2}(e_{a} - I_{7}e_{b}).
\]
Since $I_{7}$ commutes with vectors and $e_{a}e_{b} = -e_{b}e_{a}$,
\begin{align*}
w^{2} &= \tfrac{1}{4}\bigl(Q(e_{a}) + I_{7}^{2}\,Q(e_{b})\bigr) = \tfrac{1}{4}(1 - 1) = 0, \\
w\bar{w} + \bar{w}w &= \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(Q(e_{a}) - I_{7}^{2}\,Q(e_{b})\bigr) = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + 1) = 1.
\end{align*}
The cross relations with the real pairs hold because distinct basis vectors anticommute and $I_{7}$ commutes with them (D3). Closure and the centraliser are computed (D4, D5).



\emph{(ii) A unit anticommuting with $I_{7}$.}  $J$ commutes with the even algebra (it lies in the spin commutant) and anticommutes with $I_{7}$. Every vector factors as $e = (eI_{7}^{-1})\,I_{7}$ with $eI_{7}^{-1}$ even, so
\[
JeJ^{-1} \;=\; (eI_{7}^{-1})\,\bigl(JI_{7}J^{-1}\bigr) \;=\; (eI_{7}^{-1})(-I_{7}) \;=\; -e \qquad \text{(D6)}.
\]
Hence $J(I_{7}e_{b})J^{-1} = I_{7}e_{b}$ and
\[
Jw_{3}J^{-1} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}(e_{a} - I_{7}e_{b}) \;=\; -\bar{w}_{3},
\]
and the closure has dimension $30$ (D7).



\emph{(iii) The residue-five tower.}  The centre of $\HH$ is $\R$ and $Q(\omega) = +1$ (A4), so the algebra names no unit. The spin and Clifford commutants coincide on this module (D8), so every unit $u \in \HH$ commutes with the vectors. With $Q(e_{a}) = Q(e_{b}) = -1$ and $u^{2} = -1$,
\[
w_{3}v_{3} + v_{3}w_{3} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(Q(e_{a}) - u^{2}\,Q(e_{b})\bigr) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}(-1 - 1) \;=\; 1 \qquad \text{(D9 to D11)}.
\]
For the conjugacy, with $u^{2} = u'^{2} = -1$,
\begin{align*}
(1 - u'u)\,u &= u - u'u^{2} = u + u', \\
u'\,(1 - u'u) &= u' - u'^{2}u = u' + u,
\end{align*}
so the two sides agree, and $1 - u'u = 0$ only at $u' = -u$ (D12).

dark-tower-matter.three-dimensional-cont.formal:
In the towers $r = 1, 7$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The generators are the four cells of $\R^{2} \otimes \R^{2}$, of weights $(s, p) \in \{\pm 1\}^{2}$; as complex two-component fermions they are $A$, with $(q_{+}, q_{-}) = (1, 0)$, and $B$, with $(0, 1)$, and their conjugates. Each is charged under one factor only: the tower is two copies of single-flavour electrodynamics in $2+1$ dimensions, exchanged by the pair reflection $p \mapsto -p$.
\item[(ii)] Every weight of the exterior algebra of the cells has $s + p$ even; no state of the tensor state space has weight $(\pm 1, 0)$ or $(0, \pm 1)$.
\item[(iii)] Under (S) the constituent-level states have weight $(\pm 1, 0)$, off the lattice $s + p$ even: (S) and the global form of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.gauge-algebras}(i) are incompatible. Of the directions the transport adds, the rung directions carry $(\pm 1, 0)$ and the pair directions $(0, \pm 1)$, and both are excluded; the one neutral direction (the leftover generator of the odd conformal algebra) is allowed, and its value is a bare mass. The tower has no charged Higgs analogue.
\item[(iv)] There is no chirality: the odd-dimensional modules carry no Lorentz-invariant grading \cite[Prop.~3.9]{ButlerT14}. Gauge-invariant Dirac masses exist for $A$ and $B$ without any condensate, and there is no baryon-like composite: every gauge-neutral state has zero net number of each cell.
\end{enumerate}

Assuming the slot hypothesis would add states that do not fit the towers' symmetry, so here the hypothesis and the symmetry are incompatible. The particles can have masses without a Higgs-like field, and there are no proton-like bound states.

proofs.main:
\textit{(i)}\enspace The cells are single-occupation states. The charges $q_{\pm} = (s \pm p)/2$ of the $U(1)_{+} \times U(1)_{-}$ of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.gauge-algebras}(i) send
\[
(s, p) = (1, 1) \;\mapsto\; (q_{+}, q_{-}) = (1, 0), \qquad (1, -1) \;\mapsto\; (0, 1) \qquad \text{(F2)},
\]
and the pair reflection $p \mapsto -p$ exchanges them.



\emph{(ii)}  A product of cells adds weights, and each cell has $s + p \in \{-2, 0, 2\}$ (F1).



\emph{(iii)}  A constituent-level state occupies one slot mode and no pair mode, so its weight is $(\pm 1, 0)$, off the lattice $s + p$ even (Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.why-s-fails-three-dimensions-not}). The weights of the transported directions are computed in the supplementary script \file{D3R} (checks H5 to H9): rung directions $(\pm 1, 0)$, pair directions $(0, \pm 1)$, the leftover generator $(0,0)$.



\emph{(iv)}  This is the odd case of T14's Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chiralities}. A mass term $\bar{A}A$ has weight zero, and a neutral product of cells pairs each cell with its conjugate.

dark-tower-matter.three-dimensional-phas.technical:
At assembly level, with imported Polyakov confinement, topological mass and flux attachment. With the minimal bare Chern-Simons level $|k| = \tfrac12$ forced by the parity anomaly, each abelian factor is in one of two phases, set by whether the cell's mass sign is aligned with its bare level: (C) effective level $0$, Polyakov-confining, the cells binding into neutral onia that annihilate at full strength into a lighter channel; or (T) effective level $\pm 1$, topologically massive with the photon gapped at $e^2/2\pi$, the unit-charge lines transparent and the cells effectively neutral and, interpretively, of spin $0$. In phase (T) with $e^2 \gg m$ the cells are stable by their gauge charges (at $r = 7$ also by the central unit), and contact processes scale as $(m/e^2)^2$.

The dark-matter paper's statement that every compact $U(1)$ in three dimensions confines holds in phase (C) only. Both phases close its radiation channel: even two massless $2+1$ dimensional photons at the photon temperature would give $\Delta\Neff$ of about $4 \times 10^{-3}$ on sheets.
dark-tower-matter.three-dimensional-phas.lay: At assembly level, and relying on established results about forces in two space dimensions, each three-dimensional tower's force can sit in one of two phases. In one it confines, binding particles into neutral pairs that annihilate; in the other the force carrier gains a mass, and with strong coupling the particles become effectively neutral and stable. Either way the towers add almost no radiation to the early universe.

dark-tower-matter.u-transposition-rule.formal:
(U1) A constituent is an element of the spin-irreducible even ideal of the conformal algebra, as T12 defines this tower's, and its field is the commutant of the spin action on it. (U2) The hierarchy's first factor counts constituents at mass onset, and its slot group is the momentum-preserving group of that many constituents; the pair group is the group of mixings of the ladder pairs that preserves their canonical relations and the field's positive norm, the unitary group over the pairs' scalars ($\R$, or $\C$ where a complex unit builds the pairs), as T12 takes $U(m) \times U(k)$ \cite[Thm.~4.1]{ButlerT12}. (U3) Every complex unit used to build a ladder pair is an element of the constituent's field that the real algebra supplies; no external imaginary unit is adjoined.

\emph{Type: a definition.} The three clauses define what the series calls a constituent in another tower, its field, the slot and pair groups, and which complex units are admitted; they assert nothing about nature that could be derived or refuted, and can only be replaced by another definition (Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.branches-break-u-what-they-give} lists what other choices give). The definition has consequences through what it excludes: with it, the lowest-causal choice of Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives} at residues $1$ and $7$ follows. Results stated under Premise U hold for the objects so defined; the entity keeps the status of a premise so that those results show the choice among their conditions.
dark-tower-matter.u-transposition-rule.technical:
Premise U carries the Standard-Model construction to other towers in three clauses. (U1) A constituent is an element of the spin-irreducible even ideal of the conformal algebra, and its field is the commutant of the spin action on it. (U2) The hierarchy's first factor counts constituents at mass onset, with the momentum-preserving group of that many constituents as its slot group; the pair group is the group of mixings of the ladder pairs that preserve their canonical relations and the field's positive norm, the unitary group over the pairs' scalars ($\R$, or $\C$ where a complex unit builds the pairs). (U3) Every complex unit used to build a ladder pair is an element of the constituent's field that the real algebra supplies; no external imaginary unit is adjoined.

Type: a definition. The clauses define the constituent, its field, the two groups and the admitted units in the other towers; they can be replaced by another definition, with other results, but not derived or refuted. The entity stays among the premises so that results stated under it show the choice.
dark-tower-matter.u-transposition-rule.lay: This is an assumption, not a result: it fixes how the steps that give our own particle physics are repeated in the other towers. It says what a constituent is, which mixings of constituents and of their internal pairs count as symmetries, and that any square root of minus one must come from the tower's own algebra rather than being added from outside. It is best read as a definition: it says what the words mean in the other towers, and a different definition would give different results; nothing in nature could prove it wrong.

dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins.formal:
Let $\psi, \psi_{1}, \psi_{2} \in S$ in a causal tower of dimension $n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For $n = 3$ and $n = 4$ the reversion pairing is alternating, $\rev{\psi}\psi = 0$, every single constituent's momentum is null, and
\[
m^{2}\bigl(j(\psi_{1}) + j(\psi_{2})\bigr) \;=\; 2\,\ip{xx^{\dagger}}_{0}, \qquad x = \rev{\psi}_{1}\psi_{2}.
\]
Mass begins at two constituents; it vanishes exactly when $\rev{\psi}_{1}\psi_{2} = 0$.
\item[(ii)] For $n = 5$ the reversion pairing is not alternating, and
\[
m^{2}\bigl(j(\psi)\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\ip{xx^{\dagger}}_{0}, \qquad x = \rev{\psi}\psi,
\]
which vanishes on a nonzero proper cone in $S$. Mass begins at one constituent.
\end{enumerate}
In every causal tower the total momentum of any number of constituents is timelike or null, never spacelike.
dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins.technical:
For constituents $\psi, \psi_1, \psi_2$ in the spinor ideal $S$ of a causal tower of dimension $n$: when $n = 3$ or $4$ the reversion pairing is alternating, $\rev{\psi}\psi = 0$, every single constituent's momentum is null, and $m^2(j(\psi_1) + j(\psi_2)) = 2\langle xx^\dagger\rangle_0$ with $x = \rev{\psi}_1\psi_2$, so mass begins at two constituents and vanishes exactly when $\rev{\psi}_1\psi_2 = 0$. When $n = 5$ the pairing is not alternating, and $m^2(j(\psi)) = \tfrac12\langle xx^\dagger\rangle_0$ with $x = \rev{\psi}\psi$, which vanishes on a nonzero proper cone in $S$: mass begins at one constituent.

In every causal tower the total momentum of any number of constituents is timelike or null, never spacelike.
dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins.lay: A single constituent in a three- or four-dimensional tower always moves like light; mass appears only when two combine, and then only if they are not aligned in a particular way. In five dimensions a single constituent can already be massive. In every tower with a time direction, collections of constituents never move faster than light.

proofs.main:
\textit{The pairing as a sandwich.}\enspace Write $\psi = \phi f$ with $\phi \in \Cl^{0}(V)$ and $f = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + b)$, $b$ a bivector of square $+1$. Then $\rev{b} = -b$, so $\rev{f} = 1 - f$ and
\[
\rev{\psi}\psi \;=\; (1 - f)\;\rev{\phi}\phi\;f.
\]
The element $\rev{\phi}\phi$ is even and reversion-invariant, so it has grades $0$ and $4$ only:
\[
\rev{\phi}\phi = s + F, \qquad s = \ip{\rev{\phi}\phi}_{0}, \quad F = \ip{\rev{\phi}\phi}_{4}.
\]
Since $(1 - f)f = 0$, every part of $\rev{\phi}\phi$ that commutes with $b$ drops out of the sandwich:
\[
(1 - f)\,c\,f \;=\; c\,(1 - f)f \;=\; 0 \qquad \text{whenever } cb = bc.
\]



\emph{Dimensions three and four.}  In dimension three $F = 0$. In dimension four $F = uI$ is a multiple of the pseudoscalar, which commutes with every even element and in particular with $b$. In both cases all of $\rev{\phi}\phi$ commutes with $b$, so $\rev{\psi}\psi = 0$. This is the alternation in (i).



\emph{Dimension five.}  Here $F$ is a general four-vector, which need not commute with $b$, and $(1 - f)\,F f \neq 0$ for suitable $\phi$, so the pairing is not alternating.



\emph{The mass laws.}  The two displayed laws are identities between polynomials of degree four in the coordinates of $\psi_{1}, \psi_{2}$ (respectively $\psi$) on a basis of $S$. The script verifies them as polynomial identities over $\mathbb{Q}$, not on samples, in all six causal towers (checks B4, B5), together with the nullity of $j(\psi)$ in dimensions three and four (B4); it exhibits a nonzero $\psi$ with $\rev{\psi}\psi = 0$ in each five-dimensional tower (B6). The right-hand sides are nonnegative by Lemma \claimref{dark-tower-matter.adjoint-norm}(i), so each single momentum (and in dimensions three and four each pair sum) is timelike or null.



\emph{Any number of constituents.}  For every $\psi \in S$,
\begin{align*}
Q(e_{t})\,\bigl(j(\psi)\cdot e_{t}\bigr) &= Q(e_{t})\,\ip{\psi e_{t}\rev{\psi}\,e_{t}}_{0} \\
&= \ip{\psi\,e_{t}\rev{\psi}e_{t}^{-1}}_{0} \\
&= \ip{\psi\psi^{\dagger}}_{0} \;\geq\; 0 \qquad \text{(B7)}.
\end{align*}
So every constituent's momentum is causal and lies in the same closed half-space bounded by $e_{t}^{\perp}$, hence in the same half of the causal cone, and that half is closed under addition.

obj.dark-matter.frozen-phase-operators.formal: Two things are fixed, and they are different. The one gravitational metric is shared by every tower (Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p1-single-frozen-point}); each tower $r$ has its own soldering $V_{r}$, the generating subspace of its own algebra $(A_{r}, V_{r})$, with $V_{6}$ the one metric's tangent space and the others the other towers' (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-not-algebraic-one}). The \emph{frozen-phase sector decomposition} is the hypothesis that the frozen phase's state space is the direct sum over residues of sectors, the $r$-th a module over the soldered algebra $(A_{r}, V_{r})$, and that a \emph{frozen-phase local operator} is a section of one tower's soldered Clifford bundle: built, fibrewise, from that tower's soldering by Clifford multiplication and the connection it defines, with gravity entering every sector only through the shared metric's stress-energy coupling. This is the operational reading of Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p1-single-frozen-point}, stated as a hypothesis and carried as one.
obj.dark-matter.frozen-phase-operators.technical: Two structures are distinguished. The one gravitational metric is shared by every tower (premise P1), while each tower $r$ has its own soldering $V_{r}$, the generating subspace of its algebra $(A_{r}, V_{r})$, with $V_{6}$ the metric's tangent space. The frozen-phase sector decomposition is the hypothesis that the frozen phase's state space is a direct sum over residues of sectors, the $r$-th a module over $(A_{r}, V_{r})$. A frozen-phase local operator is a section of one tower's soldered Clifford bundle, built fibrewise from that tower's soldering by Clifford multiplication and the connection it defines, with gravity entering every sector only through the shared metric's stress-energy coupling. The definition is the operational reading of P1 and is carried as a hypothesis.
obj.dark-matter.frozen-phase-operators.lay: This definition says what counts as a physical operation in the universe's present, frozen phase. All towers share one gravitational geometry, but each has its own algebraic structure, and an allowed local operation is built from a single tower's structure. Towers then affect one another only through gravity. The paper states this as a hypothesis rather than deriving it.

obj.dark-matter.null-blades-fock-ideal-c.formal: Let $V_{\C}$ be the complexified ambient of a representative, of dimension $2m$ or $2m + 1$, and let $V_{\C} = W \oplus W'$ ($\oplus\, \C\ell$ in odd dimension) be a Witt decomposition into a maximal isotropic subspace $W$ and a dual isotropic complement $W'$, with null bases $w_{1}, \ldots, w_{m}$ of $W$ and $v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m}$ of $W'$ normalised so that $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$, and, in odd dimension, an extra unit generator $\ell$ orthogonal to both. The \emph{null blade} of $W$ is $f = w_{1}w_{2}\cdots w_{m}$, and it is annihilated by $W$ from the left: $wf = 0$ for every $w \in W$. The \emph{pseudoscalar} is $I = e_{1}\cdots e_{\dim V}$ for an orthonormal basis, normalised by a fourth root of unity so that $I^{2} = 1$ (the sign of $I$ is a convention; only ratios of its eigenvalues are used below); in even dimension it anticommutes with every vector, in odd dimension it is central. The \emph{Fock ideal} is, in even dimension, the left ideal $S = \Cl(V_{\C})\,f$, spanned by the $2^{m}$ states $v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}f$ ($i_{1} < \cdots < i_{k}$), the \emph{Fock grade}-$k$ states (counting creation operators, not the Clifford grade); it is the spinor module. In odd dimension the left ideal $\Cl(V_{\C})\,f$ has dimension $2^{m+1}$ and is the sum of the two irreducible modules; the Fock ideal is then either chirality-projected half, $S_{\pm} = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 \pm I)\,\Cl(V_{\C})\,f$, of dimension $2^{m}$, graded by the Fock grade of the projected states $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 \pm I)\,v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}f$, on which $I$ acts as $\pm 1$ and the extra generator $\ell$ acts as that grade's parity up to a fixed scalar. A state $\psi \in S$ with $I\psi = \pm\psi$ has \emph{chirality} $\pm 1$. For a maximal isotropic subspace $U \subset V_{\C}$, a \emph{pure spinor of $U$} is a nonzero $\psi_{U} \in S$ with $U\psi_{U} = 0$.
obj.dark-matter.null-blades-fock-ideal-c.technical: Take a Witt decomposition $V_{\C} = W \oplus W'$ (with an extra $\C\ell$ in odd dimension) of the complexified ambient, with null bases $w_{i}$ of $W$ and $v_{i}$ of $W'$ normalised so that $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$. The null blade $f = w_{1}\cdots w_{m}$ satisfies $wf = 0$ for every $w \in W$. In even dimension the Fock ideal $S = \Cl(V_{\C})\,f$ is spanned by the $2^{m}$ states $v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}f$, graded by the number $k$ of creation operators, and is the spinor module. In odd dimension $\Cl(V_{\C})\,f$ has dimension $2^{m+1}$, and the Fock ideal is either half $S_{\pm} = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 \pm I)\,\Cl(V_{\C})\,f$, with $I$ the pseudoscalar normalised so that $I^{2} = 1$. Chirality is the eigenvalue $\pm 1$ of $I$ on a state, and a pure spinor of a maximal isotropic $U$ is a nonzero $\psi_{U} \in S$ with $U\psi_{U} = 0$.
obj.dark-matter.null-blades-fock-ideal-c.lay: These definitions build spinors, the objects that describe matter particles, out of a geometric algebra. The directions are split into null pairs, one member of each acting as an annihilator and the other as a creator. The product of the annihilators gives a vacuum state, and applying creators to it produces a basis of states, counted by how many creators were used. Chirality, a state's handedness, is read off from how the algebra's top element acts on it.

obj.dark-matter.spinor-module-type.formal: For a representative $\Cl(p,q)$ let $S$ be an irreducible real module (a real spinor space), and let $D = \End_{\Cl(p,q)}(S)$ be its commutant, a real division algebra by Schur's lemma. Its \emph{type} is $D \in \{\R, \C, \mathbb{H}\}$ together with the number of inequivalent irreducible modules (one or two). The \emph{intrinsic group} of $S$ is the group of $D$-unitary automorphisms of $S$ commuting with the Clifford action, $U(1, D) = \{d \in D : d\bar{d} = 1\}$: $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$, $U(1)$ or $Sp(1)$.
obj.dark-matter.spinor-module-type.technical: For a representative $\Cl(p,q)$ take an irreducible real module $S$, a real spinor space. By Schur's lemma its commutant $D = \End_{\Cl(p,q)}(S)$ is a real division algebra, so $D \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$. The type of $S$ is $D$ together with the number, one or two, of inequivalent irreducible modules. The intrinsic group is the group of $D$-unitary automorphisms of $S$ commuting with the Clifford action, $U(1,D) = \{d \in D : d\bar{d} = 1\}$, which is $\Z_{2}$, $U(1)$ or $Sp(1)$.
obj.dark-matter.spinor-module-type.lay: A spinor space of a geometric algebra comes with symmetries that commute with everything the algebra does. Those symmetries form one of three number systems: the real numbers, the complex numbers or the quaternions. The type records which one it is and how many distinct spinor spaces there are, and the intrinsic group is the set of such symmetries of unit size.

obj.dark-matter.witt-flag.formal: On a rung's hyperbolic plane $H_k$ with null pair $(v_k, w_k)$, a \emph{flag} chooses one null line as the annihilated half; $v_k \leftrightarrow w_k$ exchanges the two. The \emph{descent's flag} chooses for every pair at once: a maximal isotropic $W$ of the complexified conformal ambient, the Fock vacuum's annihilator (Definition \claimref{obj.dark-matter.null-blades-fock-ideal-chirality}), on the three-pair structure of Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-derived-generation-flag}. Its conjugate exchanges all three halves, an odd number, which puts it in the other family (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chiralities}(iii)) and makes the flag a bit (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.flag-bit-exists-exactly-tower-dimension}). A flag is an orientation datum, not a plane.
obj.dark-matter.witt-flag.technical: On a rung's hyperbolic plane $H_{k}$ with null pair $(v_{k}, w_{k})$, a flag chooses one null line as the annihilated half, and $v_{k} \leftrightarrow w_{k}$ exchanges the two. The descent's flag chooses for every pair at once: a maximal isotropic subspace $W$ of the complexified conformal ambient, the annihilator of the Fock vacuum, on the imported three-pair structure. Its conjugate exchanges all three halves, an odd number, which puts it in the other family and makes the flag a bit. A flag is an orientation datum, not a plane.
obj.dark-matter.witt-flag.lay: Each pair of null directions in the theory can be split in two ways, according to which member is taken to annihilate the vacuum. The Witt flag is the single choice made for all pairs at once by the descent that set up the present universe. Flipping it swaps three halves, an odd number, so the flipped choice is genuinely different, and the choice amounts to one bit of orientation.

obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-mome.formal:
Let $\hf$ be a primitive idempotent of $\Cl^{0}(\hatV)$, and in a causal tower let $f = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + e_{t}e_{a})$ for a space direction $e_{a}$, which is a primitive idempotent of $\Cl^{0}(V)$ in dimensions three to five (Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}); in the sterile towers $f$ is any primitive idempotent of $\Cl^{0}(V)$. The \emph{constituent ideal} is $T = \Cl^{0}(\hatV)\hf$ and the \emph{spinor ideal} is $S = \Cl^{0}(V)f$. Their \emph{fields} are the commutants $\F(T) = \mathrm{End}_{\Cl^{0}(\hatV)}(T)$ and $\F(S) = \mathrm{End}_{\Cl^{0}(V)}(S)$, the latter realised as right multiplication by the corner algebra $f\Cl^{0}(V)f$. In a causal tower the \emph{adjoint} is $x^{\dagger} = e_{t}\rev{x}e_{t}^{-1}$, and the \emph{momentum} of $\psi \in S$ is
\[
j(\psi) \;=\; \ip{\psi e_{t} \rev{\psi}}_{1}.
\]
The total momentum of constituents $\psi_{1}, \ldots, \psi_{n}$ is $P = \sum_{i} j(\psi_{i})$, and its \emph{squared mass} is $m^{2} = Q(e_{t})\,Q(P)$.
obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-mome.technical:
With $\hf$ a primitive idempotent of $\Cl^0(\hatV)$ and, in a causal tower, $f = \tfrac12(1 + e_te_a)$ for a space direction $e_a$ (any primitive idempotent of $\Cl^0(V)$ in the sterile towers), the constituent ideal is $T = \Cl^0(\hatV)\hf$ and the spinor ideal is $S = \Cl^0(V)f$. Their fields are the commutants $\F(T)$ and $\F(S)$, the latter realised as right multiplication by the corner algebra $f\Cl^0(V)f$.

In a causal tower the adjoint is $x^\dagger = e_t\rev{x}e_t^{-1}$, the momentum of $\psi \in S$ is $j(\psi) = \langle \psi e_t\rev{\psi}\rangle_1$, and constituents $\psi_1, \ldots, \psi_n$ have total momentum $P = \sum_i j(\psi_i)$ and squared mass $m^2 = Q(e_t)\,Q(P)$.
obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-mome.lay: This definition fixes the basic objects of the dark-tower note. A constituent lives in a minimal piece of an even Clifford algebra, of the tower's conformal algebra or of the tower itself, and its numbers are the operations that commute with the algebra's action there. Its momentum is a vector built from the spinor and the time direction, and the mass of a collection comes from the length of its total momentum.

odd-extensions.copy-theorems-blind-spot.formal: The copy theorem identifies this world and its mirror by working in an algebra, $\Cl^{0}(2,4) \cong \Cl(2,3)$, that contains both real forms and is the complexification of each, its complex unit being the conformal pseudoscalar $I_6$ that spans its centre with $1$. It is therefore exactly blind to the distinction that a single extension sees: the two oriented towers have isomorphic conformal spin groups, isomorphic conformal spinor modules (twistor modules) and one complexified ambient, but odd extensions that signature reversal does not identify (Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.twistor-algebra}(iv)), whose centres differ. The shadows themselves are non-isomorphic (Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types}); every object the copy theorem is built from, the even subalgebra of the rung, the conformal spin group and the conformal spinor module $\CS$ (Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.twistor-algebra}(iii)), identifies the two towers, while the rungs themselves, $\Cl(2,4)$ and $\Cl(4,2)$, do not, being of the two towers' types by Facts \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-towers-clock} and \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types}; the odd extension is the first construction above the shadow, by dimension, that keeps them apart, and it does so through an element, the bare fifth generator, that no derived quantity of the series uses (Proposition \claimref{odd-extensions.two-towers-one-curved-universe}).
odd-extensions.copy-theorems-blind-spot.technical: The copy theorem identifies this world $(1,3)$ with its mirror $(3,1)$ by working in $\Cl^{0}(2,4) \cong \Cl(2,3)$, an algebra that contains both real forms and is the complexification of each. Every object it is built from (the rung's even subalgebra, the conformal spin group and the conformal spinor module) therefore identifies the two towers. The shadows themselves are not isomorphic, and the rungs $\Cl(2,4)$ and $\Cl(4,2)$ are not identified either, being of the two towers' types. Nor are the odd extensions: $\Cl(2,3) \not\cong \Cl(3,2)$, with centres $\C$ against $\R \oplus \R$, and $\Cl(1,4) \not\cong \Cl(4,1)$, with centres $\R \oplus \R$ against $\C$. So the odd extension is the first construction above the shadow, by dimension, that keeps the towers apart, and it does so through the bare fifth generator, which no derived quantity of the series uses.
odd-extensions.copy-theorems-blind-spot.lay: The series proves that the mirror tower is a copy of ours by working in an algebra in which the two look identical. This result points out that the method is therefore blind to where they do differ: a five-dimensional extension of each, which reversing the signature does not match up. The difference sits in a single element that none of the series' derived quantities uses.

odd-extensions.imported-representatives-.formal: At the dimension nearest four the residues are represented by the shadows $(1,3)$ at $r = 6$, $(3,1)$ at $r = 2$, $(2,2)$ at $r = 0$, $(0,4)$ and $(4,0)$ at $r = 4$, $(2,1)$ at $r = 1$, $(1,2)$ at $r = 7$, $(4,1)$ at $r = 3$ and $(1,4)$ at $r = 5$; the residues $0$ and $4$ are sterile and the other six admit matter. The real spinor type is a function of the residue alone: $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat(2,\HH)$ (quaternionic, one module) and $\Cl(3,1) \cong \Mat(4,\R)$ (real, one module); in particular the two are not isomorphic as real algebras. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Prop.~3.1, Thm.~3.4]{ButlerT14}.
odd-extensions.imported-representatives-.technical: Imported from earlier in the series. At the dimension nearest four the residues are represented by the shadows $(1,3)$ at $r = 6$, $(3,1)$ at $r = 2$, $(2,2)$ at $r = 0$, $(0,4)$ and $(4,0)$ at $r = 4$, $(2,1)$ at $r = 1$, $(1,2)$ at $r = 7$, $(4,1)$ at $r = 3$ and $(1,4)$ at $r = 5$; the residues $0$ and $4$ are sterile and the other six admit matter; which of them the descent populated is a further question, answered for the mirror by Premise P2 and for the odd towers only by the record. The real spinor type is a function of the residue alone; in particular $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat(2,\HH)$ is quaternionic and $\Cl(3,1) \cong \Mat(4,\R)$ is real, each with one module, so the two are not isomorphic as real algebras.
odd-extensions.imported-representatives-.lay: This collects, for the odd-extensions note, which signature stands for each of the eight towers when the dimension is kept as close to four as possible. Two of the eight have no single time direction and are ruled out; the other six can hold matter, though whether the odd ones actually do is a further question, which only observation can answer. It also records that our world's algebra and the mirror's differ as real algebras, one built on quaternions and the other on real numbers.

pred.dark-matter-direct-detection-null.formal: Permanent direct-detection nulls: dark matter couples through gravity alone, at first order.
pred.dark-matter-direct-detection-null.technical: In the framework dark matter sits in neighbouring towers that couple to this one only through the shared gravitational metric, with no portal interaction to ordinary matter. Direct-detection experiments, which look for non-gravitational scattering of dark matter off ordinary nuclei or electrons, should therefore return nulls permanently. This is registered as a conditional stance: its basis, the superselection and exact-stability result, rests on the single-frozen-point premise P1 and on the wall-sequence theorem's hypotheses, and its gravity-only clause, a first-order coupling statement, on the series' acoustic no-go, which holds within the s-wave current algebra and is conditional on the Indifference premise and premise (Q).
pred.dark-matter-direct-detection-null.lay: Experiments that try to catch dark-matter particles bumping into ordinary atoms should never see anything. In this framework dark matter lives in separate towers that touch ours only through gravity, which is far too weak to register in such detectors. This expectation is conditional: it rests on the framework's premise of a single frozen point, and on a result carried over from earlier work that holds in a spherically averaged description and under two further assumptions of that work.

pred.dimmed-evaporation-bursts.formal: Dimmed final evaporation bursts: the hole radiates into every populated tower, so it loses mass faster than the standard expectation (this tower plus gravitons) by the factor $D = \Psi_{\mathrm{tot}}/\Psi_{0}$ of total to standard emission, and the visible burst of its last $\tau$ is the standard burst of its last $D\tau$ divided by $D$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.dimmed-burst-time-rescaled-copy}). Dimming by the full ratio holds for the primary high-energy tail and for the visible fraction of the power at fixed mass; the visible energy in a fixed final window is dimmed by $D^{2/3}$, and the temperature at a fixed time before the end is lowered by $D^{1/3}$. The populated towers are this one and, under P2, the mirror, whose light content copies ours (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}), so $D = (2 + g + o)/(1 + g)$, with $g$ and $o$ the gravitational and odd-tower emission relative to this tower's: $D \ge 2$ if and only if $o \ge g$, and $D = 2 - g/(1 + g)$ if the odd towers emit nothing. If the four odd towers hold matter, which Premise \claimref{dark-matter.odd-towers-populated} now postulates on the inference of Observation \claimref{dark-matter.which-towers-are-populated} from the observed dark remainder, then $o > 0$ and the dimming is larger. \emph{Scope note.} The time-rescaled copy assumes constant emission coefficients; if a five-dimensional tower is populated, its Kaluza-Klein levels are emission channels under the interface premise and the copy holds only for holes well above the crossover mass $M_{\times}$ of \claimref{synthesis.five-dimensional-tower-kaluza-klein-channels-steepen-burst}(ii): below it $M^{4} = 4B\tau$ and the primary high-energy tail steepens from $E^{-3}$ to $E^{-4}$, so a search for the final burst then tests that law, not the rescaled copy. The baseline ``this tower plus gravitons'' counts emission into the helicity-2 channels of the gravitational field as standard physics does, through the term $g$; the series holds no quantum of that field (conventions, section ``Gravity and the graviton''), and whether $g$ is kept is part of open problem op.graviton-rate-as-classical-field-process ($g = 0$ gives $D = 2 + o$), the prediction being unchanged until that is settled.
pred.dimmed-evaporation-bursts.technical:
An evaporating black hole radiates into every populated tower, in proportion to each tower's light degrees of freedom once its temperature exceeds their gaps, because barriers and greybody factors belong to the shared exterior metric. The hole therefore passes through the same masses, with the same visible spectrum at each, as in the standard case (this tower plus gravitons), but faster by the ratio $D$ of total to standard emission: the visible burst of its last $\tau$ is the standard burst of its last $D\tau$ divided by $D$. At a fixed time before the end, the primary high-energy tail is dimmed by the full $D$, the visible energy only by $D^{2/3}$, and the temperature is lower by $D^{1/3}$.

The series populates two towers by its own results, this one by observation and the mirror under P2, whose light content copies ours, so $D = (2 + g + o)/(1 + g)$ with $g$ the gravitational and $o$ the odd towers' emission relative to this tower's. $D$ is at least two only if the odd towers emit at least as much as the gravitational sector; with no odd-tower emission it is $2 - g/(1 + g)$, just below two. The towers' degree-of-freedom counts are not derived, so $o$, and with it the size of the dimming above the mirror's share, is not fixed. If a five-dimensional tower is populated, these laws hold only for holes well above the crossover mass of \claimref{synthesis.five-dimensional-tower-kaluza-klein-channels-steepen-burst}; below it the burst follows $M^{4} = 4B\tau$, with a steeper high-energy tail. The baseline ``this tower plus gravitons'' counts emission into the helicity-2 channels of the gravitational field as standard physics does, through the term $g$; the series holds no quantum of that field (conventions, section ``Gravity and the graviton''), and whether $g$ is kept is part of open problem op.graviton-rate-as-classical-field-process ($g = 0$ gives $D = 2 + o$), the prediction being unchanged until that is settled.
pred.dimmed-evaporation-bursts.lay: A small black hole ends its life in a final flash of radiation. In this framework the hole radiates into the dark towers as well as into ours, so it loses mass faster and runs through its final stages in less time than standard physics expects. The mirror world alone, whose particles copy ours, roughly doubles the rate. The very high energy light emitted directly by the hole is then dimmed by the full factor, about two, while the total light seen in the last seconds is dimmed less, by that factor to the power two thirds, and the burst looks cooler at a given time before its end. If the other dark towers also hold matter, every one of these effects is larger.

pred.no-dark-radiation.formal: No dark radiation: $\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 0$, conditionally on the dark towers\' open channels closing, which holds if the descent\'s deposit is no hotter than the dark-matter paper\'s estimate, and only with the mirror\'s seeded temperature taken as a free datum: applied with the reach of the copy theorem, P2 gives the mirror $\xi = 1$ and $\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 7.45$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-temperature-p2}), so the stance rests on an exception to P2 for the mirror. This is an exception to P2 at its version-1 reach; P2 as scoped leaves $\xi$ free (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-charge-sector-label-temperature-not}), and the cold mirror then needs a non-equilibrium descent (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.cold-mirror-needs-non-equilibrium-descent}). The seeding floor behind the radiation audit imports a rate computed with a quantised gravitational field (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-massless-graviton-production-rate}, flagged), which the series does not hold; whether the classical gauge field gives that rate, another or none is open problem op.graviton-rate-as-classical-field-process, and the prediction is unchanged until that is settled.
pred.no-dark-radiation.technical: The prediction is $\Delta\Neff \approx 0$: the dark towers add no relativistic species to the radiation content measured in the cosmic microwave background. It is conditional on the dark towers' open channels closing, which holds if the descent's deposit is no hotter than the dark-matter paper's estimate. It also needs the mirror to be cold, which the T14c note shows is an exception to indifference (P2): applied with the copy theorem's reach, P2 makes the mirror as hot as our tower, $\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 7.45$, which would meet the kill condition. That is an exception to indifference at its version-1 reach; indifference as scoped (labels, not states) leaves $\xi$ free (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-charge-sector-label-temperature-not}), and the cold mirror then needs a non-equilibrium descent (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.cold-mirror-needs-non-equilibrium-descent}). The seeding floor behind the radiation audit imports a rate computed with a quantised gravitational field (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-massless-graviton-production-rate}, flagged), which the series does not hold; whether the classical gauge field gives that rate, another or none is open problem op.graviton-rate-as-classical-field-process, and the prediction is unchanged until that is settled.
pred.no-dark-radiation.lay: The afterglow of the early universe records how many kinds of light, fast-moving particles existed at the time. The framework predicts that the dark towers add none, provided the remaining ways of heating them stay closed, which holds if the descent left them no hotter than the paper estimates. It also needs the mirror world to have started cold, which a later note (T14c) shows is an unstated exception to the framework's own indifference principle; applied evenly, that principle would make the mirror as hot as our world and the prediction would fail. As the principle is now scoped, it applies to labels such as charges and not to temperatures, so it leaves the mirror's temperature free; a cold mirror then needs the descent to have left the towers out of equilibrium.

pred.no-indirect-dark-signals.formal: No indirect dark-sector signals: no decay products, since the tower charge is superselected, and annihilation products only at the rate of graviton exchange, suppressed by powers of $E/M_{P}$, and for the mirror, a charge-asymmetric relic, further by its negligible anti-mirror density. The words ``graviton exchange'' import a process of a quantised gravitational field, which the series does not hold (conventions, section ``Gravity and the graviton''); whether the classical gauge field sourced by matter gives an annihilation channel at that rate, at another or at none is open problem op.graviton-rate-as-classical-field-process, and the prediction is unchanged until that is settled.
pred.no-indirect-dark-signals.technical: In the framework dark matter couples to ordinary matter through gravity alone at first order. It cannot decay into ordinary particles, because its tower charge is superselected, and its only annihilation channel into them is graviton exchange, suppressed by powers of $E/M_{P}$; for the mirror it acts on a charge-asymmetric relic with negligible anti-mirror density (the mirror's stored asymmetry is a charge fixed by the descent, Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.stored-asymmetry-charge-not-number}), while the odd towers' matter, if any, is a symmetric relic (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.population-count-one-share-half-percent}(ii)) whose annihilation into this tower is held down by the graviton suppression alone. Indirect-detection surveys, which look for such annihilation or decay products, should see no dark-sector signal. This is registered as a conditional stance: its basis, the superselection and exact-stability result, rests on the single-frozen-point premise P1 and on the wall-sequence theorem's hypotheses, and its gravity-only clause, a first-order coupling statement, on the series' acoustic no-go, which holds within the s-wave current algebra and is conditional on the Indifference premise and premise (Q). The words ``graviton exchange'' import a process of a quantised gravitational field, which the series does not hold (conventions, section ``Gravity and the graviton''); whether the classical gauge field sourced by matter gives an annihilation channel at that rate, at another or at none is open problem op.graviton-rate-as-classical-field-process, and the prediction is unchanged until that is settled.
pred.no-indirect-dark-signals.lay: Some searches look for the leftovers of dark-matter particles destroying each other or breaking down, such as unexpected gamma rays. This framework says dark matter can turn into ordinary particles only through gravity, far too weakly to be seen (and that in the mirror world there is almost no anti-matter for its matter to meet), so those searches should find nothing. This expectation is conditional: it rests on the framework's premise of a single frozen point, from which exact stability follows, and on a result carried over from earlier work for the gravity-only coupling, which holds in a spherically averaged description and under two further assumptions of that work.

refuted.a-pre-descent-term-sources-the-m.formal: A pre-descent $\theta$-term sources the matter asymmetry
refuted.a-pre-descent-term-sources-the-m.technical: The refuted claim is that a $\theta$-term present before the descent sources the matter asymmetry through the topology of gauge bundles. A $\theta$-term integrates a characteristic class of even degree, so the odd-dimensional towers carry no continuous $\theta$. In this tower a non-relaxing angle of order one at the descent is excluded by the neutron electric dipole bound, which gives $|\theta| \lesssim 10^{-10}$ today; an angle that relaxes or rolls is not excluded. The framework instead inherits its asymmetry as initial data, the Witt flag being the one mechanism it supplies itself.
refuted.a-pre-descent-term-sources-the-m.lay: One proposed explanation for why the universe has more matter than antimatter is a special angle in the laws of particle physics, set before the universe took its present form. The paper rules out the simplest version: such an angle cannot exist in the odd towers, and in our world measurements of the neutron show the angle is far too small, unless it changed over time. The framework instead treats the imbalance as part of the universe's starting conditions.
refuted.a-pre-descent-term-sources-the-m.typing_note: Refuted claim; levels follow the refuting proposition's clause (ii), including its scope limit that a relaxing or rolling angle is not excluded.

refuted.the-particle-antiparticle-orient.formal: The particle-antiparticle orientation is determined by the charge-zero condition
refuted.the-particle-antiparticle-orient.technical: The refuted expectation is that the charge-zero condition fixes the one absolute bit the Standard-Model derivation left open, the particle-antiparticle orientation. A $\Z_{2}$ covariance argument on three premises (CPT conjugation is an isomorphism of every kinematic structure and leaves every action invariant, Hypothesis (S), and the premise that the flag is a datum of each solution; no exhaustiveness of the trichotomy is used) shows that whatever the structures determine is conjugation-invariant, while the orientation is not. The charge-zero condition fixes all relative structure; the absolute bit is initial data, and it is the Witt flag, the same choice as the arrow of time.
refuted.the-particle-antiparticle-orient.lay: The series' derivation of the Standard Model left one yes-or-no choice open: which member of each pair counts as the particle and which as the antiparticle. It had been expected that a neutrality condition would settle it. The paper shows that it cannot, because the relevant laws treat both choices alike, so the choice is part of the universe's starting conditions and is the same choice as the direction of time's arrow.

simulations.averaged-pair-operator.technical: In the simulations the sheet fluid's pair forces are contracted with $P_{ij}(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v} - \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl((\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i})\mathbf{n}_{i} + (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{j})\mathbf{n}_{j}\bigr)$, the mean of the two particles' in-plane projectors. Since $P_{ij} = P_{ji}$ and the kernel gradient is antisymmetric, the contracted pair forces conserve momentum exactly and, in the equations before time integration and with the smoothing lengths held fixed within a step, total energy. For parallel normals with $Q(\mathbf{n}) = 1$, $P_{ij}$ is the rejection $\mathbf{v} \mapsto (\mathbf{v}\wedge\mathbf{n})\,\mathbf{n}$, the projection onto the sheet, and annihilates $\mathbf{n}$. For orthogonal normals its eigenvalues are $1, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}$, keeping half of each normal component, and it is idempotent only when $\mathbf{n}_{i} = \pm\mathbf{n}_{j}$.
simulations.averaged-pair-operator.lay: The simulations model three-dimensional dark matter as sheets that can only push along their own surface. Forces between two such particles are filtered through an averaged projection that keeps the part lying in the sheets. This result checks that the filter still conserves momentum and, within each step, energy, that it is an exact projection when the sheets are parallel, and that it is only a partial one when they are not.
simulations.averaged-pair-operator.typing_note: Self-contained algebraic lemma; no edges, and the paper's citation of the standard symmetric SPH form is for the equations, not a statement that the lemma is recovered classically.

proofs.main: (i) $P_{ij}$ is symmetric in $i$ and $j$ and $\mathbf{g}_{ij} = -\mathbf{g}_{ji}$, so the force of $j$ on $i$, $-m_{i}m_{j}F_{ij}P_{ij}\mathbf{g}_{ij}$ with $F_{ij}$ the symmetric bracket, is minus the force of $i$ on $j$. The kinetic power of the pair is $-m_{i}m_{j}F_{ij}\,\mathbf{v}_{ij}\cdot P_{ij}\mathbf{g}_{ij}$, and the two internal-energy terms sum to $+m_{i}m_{j}F_{ij}\,\mathbf{v}_{ij}\cdot P_{ij}\mathbf{g}_{ij}$, since $\mathbf{v}_{ji}\cdot P_{ji}\mathbf{g}_{ji} = \mathbf{v}_{ij}\cdot P_{ij}\mathbf{g}_{ij}$ and the viscous term is split equally. (ii) With $Q(\mathbf{n}) = \mathbf{n}\mathbf{n} = 1$ (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}) and $\mathbf{v}\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} + \mathbf{v}\wedge\mathbf{n}$ (\claimref{std-algebra.product-decomposition}), $(\mathbf{v}\wedge\mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{v}\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{v} - (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n})\mathbf{n}$, which is $P_{ij}(\mathbf{v})$ for $\mathbf{n}_{i} = \mathbf{n}_{j} = \mathbf{n}$. (iii) For $\mathbf{n}_{i}\perp\mathbf{n}_{j}$, $P_{ij}\mathbf{n}_{i} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{n}_{i}$, $P_{ij}\mathbf{n}_{j} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{n}_{j}$ and $P_{ij}$ fixes the direction dual to $\mathbf{n}_{i}\wedge\mathbf{n}_{j}$, $(\mathbf{n}_{i}\wedge\mathbf{n}_{j})I_{3}$ with $I_{3}$ the pseudoscalar of $\Cl(3,0)$, so $P_{ij}^{2} \ne P_{ij}$; in general $P_{ij}$ is idempotent only when $(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i})\mathbf{n}_{i} = (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{j})\mathbf{n}_{j}$ for every $\mathbf{v}$, that is $\mathbf{n}_{i} = \pm\mathbf{n}_{j}$. Not covered by (i): variable smoothing lengths without correction terms, and what acts after these equations (the integrator, the energy floor and cooling). The script checks (i) on a rational instance with distinct normals and viscosity, (ii) exactly in the blade engine, and (iii) in exact rationals.

simulations.c-odd-towers-collisionless.formal:
The matter of the four odd towers (the two three-dimensional and the two five-dimensional towers) has no self-interaction of order one. For the three-dimensional towers this means an in-sheet s-wave phase shift below about $2 \times 10^{-7}$ at cluster speeds for isotropic compression, $4 \times 10^{-6}$ for compression normal to the sheets (Corollary \claimref{simulations.confinement-scale-does-not-matter}).

\emph{Type: model specification.} This is a clause of the specification of the numerical model of the cluster simulations (Premises S1 to S5 and C), not a hypothesis of the series about nature; it is kept with the premises so that the two simulation results show it among their conditions. Premises C and S2 belong to two exclusive readings of the three-dimensional towers' matter in the simulations: reading (C), collisionless, under Premise \claimref{simulations.c-odd-towers-collisionless}, and reading (W), a sheet fluid at composite strength, under Premise \claimref{simulations.s2-sheet-fluid}. The two simulation results (\claimref{simulations.halo-shapes}, \claimref{simulations.merger}) list both among their conditions because each reports both readings; no result holds the two together. C is not a statement about the series' structure: it is the condition the cluster bound requires (Corollary \claimref{simulations.confinement-scale-does-not-matter}), adopted as the premise of reading (C). Whether it holds is not decided by anything stored: the radiation audit leaves the three-dimensional towers' self-interaction at composite strength if their matter is the confined charged matter its closure leaves, which the series does not establish (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.radiation-audit-what-theorem-closes-what}).

simulations.cluster-bound-two-dimensions.technical:
Take quanta of the nucleon mass colliding at a relative speed of $3000$ km/s, so that $k = 0.0238\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}}$ in the centre-of-mass frame. In two dimensions the cross-section is a length, $\lambda = (4/k)\sum_{m}\sin^{2}\delta_{m}$. For a hard disk of radius $0.21$ fm it is $13$ fm from the partial-wave sum ($14$ fm from the logarithmic form), and even a disk of radius $10^{-11}$ fm gives $\lambda = 0.49$ fm, because at small $ka$ the radius enters only through $\lambda \approx \pi^{2}/\bigl(k(\ln(ka/2) + \gamma_{E})^{2}\bigr)$.

With $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} = \lambda s$ at the isotropic spacing of a cluster core, the bound $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/m < 1\ \cmg$ requires $\lambda < 4.8 \times 10^{-12}$ fm. By size alone this needs $a < 10^{-4.0 \times 10^{6}}$ fm; through the interaction strength it needs an s-wave phase shift $\delta_{0} < 1.7 \times 10^{-7}$. These are numerical evaluations, with the spacing fixed by premises R1 to R3.
simulations.cluster-bound-two-dimensions.lay: Matter confined to thin sheets scatters as if it lived in two dimensions, where a particle's target size is a length rather than an area. At the speeds of colliding galaxy clusters even an absurdly small particle presents a sizeable target, because its size enters only through a logarithm. Taking the quanta to have the nucleon's mass, with the spacing in a cluster core fixed by the paper's counting premises R1 to R3, to meet the observed limit on dark-matter collisions there the particles would have to be smaller than any physical scale, or barely interact at all.
simulations.cluster-bound-two-dimensions.typing_note: No proof environment: the paper's 'How it is computed' paragraph says (i) is the two-dimensional scattering fact evaluated and (ii) is the effective cross-section proposition solved for lambda, so those are the uses; R1 and R2 are assumed because the 3.5 cm core spacing is computed from them (R3 enters through the proposition); the cluster bound value itself is treated as a hypothesis of the statement, not a premise. Levels pass: the lay level and one-liner now name premises R1 and R2, which fix the core spacing, and the lay level keeps the nucleon-mass assumption.

simulations.confinement-scale-does-not-m.formal: Any self-interaction of composite strength makes the three-dimensional towers' matter a fluid in clusters, whatever the size of a composite. The cluster bound is met only if the quanta barely interact: an in-sheet phase shift below about $2 \times 10^{-7}$ (isotropic compression in a core; about $4 \times 10^{-6}$ for compression normal to the sheets), which is Premise C.
simulations.confinement-scale-does-not-m.technical:
Sheet matter with an in-sheet cross-section of composite size, $\lambda \ge 0.21$ fm, has $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/m \ge 9.5 \times 10^{7}\ \cmg$ in every cluster region and compression, far above the cluster bounds, so on cluster scales it is a fluid. Shrinking the composite does not help: the radius enters only through $\lambda \approx \pi^{2}/\{k[\ln(ka/2) + \gamma_{E}]^{2}\}$, so even $a = 10^{-30}$ fm leaves $\lambda \approx 0.08$ fm and $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/m \ge 3 \times 10^{7}\ \cmg$.

The bound can be met only if the quanta barely interact: an in-sheet s-wave phase shift below about $2 \times 10^{-7}$ for isotropic compression in a core, or about $4 \times 10^{-6}$ for compression normal to the sheets, since $\lambda \propto \sin^{2}\delta_{0}$ and the allowed $\lambda$ scales as $1/s$. That condition is Premise C.
simulations.confinement-scale-does-not-m.lay: However small the composite particles of the sheet-bound dark sectors are, if they interact with the strength typical of composite particles they collide so often in galaxy clusters that they behave as a fluid. Cluster observations rule that out. The only way out is for the particles to barely interact at all, which is a separate assumption that the particles' size cannot supply.

proofs.main: For $\lambda \ge 0.21$ fm, the table accompanying \claimref{simulations.effective-cross-section-sheet-matter} gives $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/m \ge 9.5 \times 10^{7}\ \cmg$ in every cluster region and compression. Smaller composites barely lower this: a hard disk of radius $a = 10^{-30}$ fm still has $\lambda \approx \pi^{2}/\{k\,[\ln(ka/2) + \gamma_{E}]^{2}\} \approx 0.08$ fm (with $\ln(ka/2) = -73.5$; by \claimref{simulations.imported-low-energy-scattering-two-dimensions}), so $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/m \ge 3 \times 10^{7}\ \cmg$ (by \claimref{simulations.effective-cross-section-sheet-matter}), and the matter remains a fluid on cluster scales. The size of a composite enters $\lambda$ only through the logarithm (Computation \claimref{simulations.cluster-bound-two-dimensions}(i) and (iii)), so no physical confinement scale reaches the bound. The phase-shift limits are Computation \claimref{simulations.cluster-bound-two-dimensions}(iii) at the isotropic spacing and, since $\lambda \propto \sin^{2}\delta_{0}$ and the bound on $\lambda$ scales as $1/s$, a factor $(4.4 \times 10^{10}/9.5 \times 10^{7})^{1/2} \approx 22$ larger at the normal-compression spacing.

simulations.effective-cross-section-shee.formal:
Let the sheets carry $n_{2}$ quanta per unit area, be stacked a distance $s$ apart, and let each quantum have in-sheet cross-section $\lambda$. Then the collision rate of a quantum moving at speed $v$ equals that of a three-dimensional gas of number density $n_{3} = n_{2}/s$ with cross-section
\[
\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} \;=\; \lambda\, s ,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}}{m} \;=\; \frac{\lambda s}{m}.
\]
In a halo region of overdensity $\Delta$ at redshift $z$ the spacing lies between $d_{b}\Delta^{-1}/(1+z)$ (all compression along the normal) and $d_{b}/(1+z)$ (all compression in the plane), and is $s = d_{b}\Delta^{-1/3}/(1+z)$ for isotropic compression.
simulations.effective-cross-section-shee.technical:
A quantum of a three-dimensional tower moves in a two-dimensional sheet and collides only with quanta of its own sheet, so its cross-section is a length $\lambda$. If the sheets carry $n_{2}$ quanta per unit area and are stacked a distance $s$ apart, the in-sheet collision rate is $n_{2}\lambda v = (n_{2}/s)(\lambda s)v$, the rate in a three-dimensional gas of density $n_{3} = n_{2}/s$ with $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} = \lambda s$, so $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}/m = \lambda s/m$.

Under premise R3 the sheets are a cell radius $d_{b}$ apart in the mean, comoving. In a region of overdensity $\Delta$ at redshift $z$ the spacing is $d_{b}\Delta^{-1}/(1+z)$ if all the compression is along the normal, $d_{b}/(1+z)$ if it is all in the plane, and $d_{b}\Delta^{-1/3}/(1+z)$ for isotropic compression.
simulations.effective-cross-section-shee.lay: Matter that lives on stacked sheets collides only within its own sheet. Seen from three dimensions, its collisions look like those of an ordinary gas whose effective target area is the in-sheet target length multiplied by the spacing between sheets. Under premise R3, that the sheets lie on average one cell radius apart, how far apart they are in a galaxy cluster depends on how the cluster has squeezed them.
simulations.effective-cross-section-shee.typing_note: Kept the R3 assumption, which the proof invokes for the mean sheet spacing; the result is a direct rate identity with no standard-route claim in the paper. Levels pass: the lay level now names premise R3 for the sheet spacing.

proofs.main: The in-sheet collision rate is $n_{2}\lambda v$, and $n_{2}\lambda v = (n_{2}/s)(\lambda s)v = n_{3}\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}v$. By R3 (\claimref{dark-matter.r3-one-cell-per-unshared-direction}) the sheets are $d_{b}$ apart in the mean, comoving \cite[Prem.~7.4]{ButlerT14}. A region compressed by $\Delta$ in volume has its comoving lengths reduced by $\Delta$ along one direction, by $\Delta^{1/3}$ along each for isotropic compression, or not at all along the normal if the compression is in the plane; the physical spacing carries the further factor $1/(1+z)$.

simulations.halo-shapes.formal: Isolated assembly from eight progenitors makes rounder halos than infall along filaments, so the measure is the ratio to the CDM run (the table accompanying \claimref{simulations.merger}), and with two seeds the criterion is whether both seeds of a composition lie below both of CDM's. In reading (W) they do: the ellipticity is $0.43$ of CDM's (seed ratios $0.56$ and $0.35$), and the sheet fluid, supported by its pressure, is cored (its density is flat within the noise inside about $75$ kpc) and rounder than the collisionless dark matter (inside $300$ kpc, $c/a$ of $0.78$ and $0.85$ against $0.59$ and $0.44$ in the two seeds). It is also less concentrated: $38$ percent of the mass within $300$ kpc, near its measured share of $0.41$ within $r_{200}$, but only $10$ to $12$ percent inside $50$ kpc, where settled mirror matter is $39$ to $43$ percent. In reading (C) the ratio is $0.77$ ($0.63$ and $0.85$), and the second seed overlaps CDM's range: rounder, not excluded. Inside $300$ kpc in seed $11$ its $c/a$ matches CDM's ($0.62$ against $0.64$) and its $b/a$ is larger ($0.93$ against $0.71$), so the halo is closer to oblate symmetry than CDM's. In reading (C), $39$ and $29$ percent of the mass inside $50$ kpc (seeds $11$ and $23$) is settled mirror matter: the over-cooling of a dissipative gas simulated without feedback (Premise S3), which also makes the inner profiles unreliable. The compositions with the mirror settled from the start sit at $0.75$ to $0.78$ of CDM; at equal sheet fluid, the mixed count with its mirror gas gives $0.49$ and without it $0.75$, and the mirror gas without sheet fluid, reading (C), gives $0.77$: the mirror gas and the sheet fluid together round the halo more than either alone. Computed; observation level.
simulations.halo-shapes.technical:
In simulations of a cluster assembled in isolation from eight progenitors, with two seeds, the projected ellipticity is compared with the cold dark matter (CDM) run of the same seed, since isolated assembly makes even CDM halos rounder than real clusters. In reading (W) both seeds lie below both of CDM's: the ellipticity is $0.43$ of CDM's, and the sheet fluid is cored inside about $75$ kpc, rounder than the collisionless dark matter and less centrally concentrated.

In reading (C) the ratio is $0.77$ and one seed overlaps CDM's range, so the halo is rounder but not excluded; there the over-cooling of mirror gas simulated without feedback (premise S3) settles much of the inner mass and makes the inner profiles unreliable. The mirror gas and the sheet fluid together round the halo more than either alone. These are computed results at observation level.

If it does not, the cluster is only somewhat rounder and one of its two versions falls within the spread of the standard runs, so it is not ruled out by this test; there the inner profiles are unreliable, because the simulated mirror gas over-cools without feedback (premise S3). These are computed results at observation level.

simulations.imported-bullet-cluster.formal: In 1E0657-558 the two galaxy concentrations are $0.72$ Mpc apart on the sky; the lensing peaks lie $9.6''$ ($42$ kpc, subcluster) and $11.8''$ ($52$ kpc, main cluster) from the brightest cluster galaxies, within $1\sigma$ of the galaxy luminosity centroids, and the centres of total mass are offset from the plasma at $8\sigma$ \cite{Clowe2006}. The mass-to-light ratios give $(M/L)_{\mathrm{sub}}/(M/L)_{\mathrm{main}} = 0.84 \pm 0.07$, from which the subcluster has lost no more than about $23$ percent of its mass (a bound on mass loss inferred from the ratio, not on the mass inside a fixed aperture). The self-interaction cross-section per mass is below $1.25\ \cmg$ ($68$ percent) from the absence of an offset between mass and galaxies, whose centroids are known to about $5''$ ($22$ kpc), and below $0.7\ \cmg$ from the mass-to-light ratios \cite{Randall2008}. From $72$ cluster collisions $\sigma/m < 0.47\ \cmg$ at $95$ percent \cite{Harvey2015}, relaxed to about $2\ \cmg$ when that sample's offsets are corrected \cite{Wittman2018}.
simulations.imported-bullet-cluster.technical:
In the merging cluster 1E0657-558 the two galaxy concentrations are $0.72$ Mpc apart, the lensing mass peaks lie within $1\sigma$ of the galaxy luminosity centroids ($42$ and $52$ kpc from the brightest cluster galaxies), and the centres of total mass are offset from the hot plasma at $8\sigma$. The subcluster's mass-to-light ratio relative to the main cluster's, $0.84 \pm 0.07$, implies it has lost no more than about $23$ percent of its mass; this bounds lost mass, not the mass inside a fixed aperture.

The resulting limits on the self-interaction cross-section per mass are $\sigma/m < 1.25\ \cmg$ ($68$ percent) from the absence of a mass-galaxy offset and $\sigma/m < 0.7\ \cmg$ from the mass-to-light ratios. A sample of $72$ cluster collisions gives $\sigma/m < 0.47\ \cmg$ at $95$ percent, relaxed to about $2\ \cmg$ once that sample's offsets are corrected.
simulations.imported-bullet-cluster.lay: The Bullet Cluster is a pair of galaxy clusters that have passed through each other. Gravitational lensing shows that most of the mass travelled with the galaxies while the hot gas lagged behind. That would not happen if dark matter collided strongly with itself, so the observation caps how much dark-matter particles can scatter off one another.

simulations.imported-cluster-shapes.formal: The mean projected ellipticity $\langle 1 - b/a\rangle$ of massive clusters from weak-lensing shear maps is $0.46 \pm 0.04$, in agreement with cold dark matter \cite{Oguri2010}.
simulations.imported-cluster-shapes.technical: Weak-lensing shear maps of massive clusters measure the projected shape of their mass distribution directly. The mean projected ellipticity is $\langle 1 - b/a\rangle = 0.46 \pm 0.04$, with $b/a$ the projected axis ratio, in agreement with cold dark matter.
simulations.imported-cluster-shapes.lay: Massive galaxy clusters are not round: their mass is noticeably elongated, as measured from the way they distort the images of background galaxies. The average elongation matches what standard cold dark matter predicts. This gives a shape test that any alternative form of dark matter has to pass.

simulations.imported-low-energy-scatteri.formal: For elastic scattering in two dimensions by a hard disk of radius $a$, the partial-wave phase shifts are $\tan\delta_{m} = J_{m}(ka)/Y_{m}(ka)$ and the total cross-section is the length $\lambda = (4/k)\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\sin^{2}\delta_{m}$. As $ka \to 0$ only $m = 0$ survives, with $\delta_{0} \to \pi/\bigl(2(\ln(ka/2) + \gamma_{E})\bigr)$; the same logarithmic form holds for any short-range interaction with two-dimensional scattering length of order $a$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Adhikari1986}.
simulations.imported-low-energy-scatteri.technical: For elastic scattering in two dimensions by a hard disk of radius $a$, the partial-wave phase shifts satisfy $\tan\delta_{m} = J_{m}(ka)/Y_{m}(ka)$, and the total cross-section is a length, $\lambda = (4/k)\sum_{m}\sin^{2}\delta_{m}$. As $ka \to 0$ only the s-wave survives, with $\delta_{0} \to \pi/\bigl(2(\ln(ka/2) + \gamma_{E})\bigr)$, so the radius enters only logarithmically. The same logarithmic form holds for any short-range interaction whose two-dimensional scattering length is of order $a$.
simulations.imported-low-energy-scatteri.lay: In a flat, two-dimensional world a particle's target size for collisions is a length rather than an area. At low energies this length depends on the particle's actual size only through a logarithm, so even a very tiny particle remains a surprisingly large target. This is a standard result of quantum scattering theory.

imported_from.citation: S. K. Adhikari, Quantum scattering in two dimensions, Am. J. Phys. 54 (1986) 362.
