simulations.imported-milky-ways-mass-bud.formal: At the Sun the total surface density within $1.1$ kpc of the plane is $68 \pm 4\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$, of which stars and stellar remnants contribute $38 \pm 4$ dynamically \cite{BovyRix2013}; counted, stars and remnants are $33.4 \pm 3$ and gas $13.7 \pm 1.6$, a total of $47.1 \pm 3.4$ \cite{McKee2015}. A thin dark disk is bounded at $95$ percent by $4.56$ ($h \le 50$ pc) and $5.59\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ ($h = 100$ pc), with $68$ percent bounds $2.17$ and $2.71$ \cite{Widmark2021}. The bulge region holds a dynamical mass of $(1.85 \pm 0.05) \times 10^{10}\ \Msun$ with a dark fraction of $17 \pm 2$ percent \cite{Portail2017}. A mirror analysis bounds the excess bulge mass, dynamical minus photometric, by $0.83 \times 10^{10}\ \Msun$ at $2\sigma$, and finds $\Omega_{b'} \lesssim 0.8\,\Omega_{b}$ at low mirror temperature \cite{RouxCline2020}.
simulations.imported-milky-ways-mass-bud.technical:
At the Sun the total surface density within $1.1$ kpc of the Galactic plane is $68 \pm 4\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$, of which stars and stellar remnants contribute $38 \pm 4$ dynamically; direct counts give $33.4 \pm 3$ in stars and remnants and $13.7 \pm 1.6$ in gas, a total of $47.1 \pm 3.4$. A thin dark disk is bounded at $95$ percent by $4.56\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ for scale height $h \le 50$ pc and $5.59$ for $h = 100$ pc.

The bulge region has a dynamical mass of $(1.85 \pm 0.05) \times 10^{10}\ \Msun$, $17 \pm 2$ percent of it dark. A mirror-matter analysis bounds the excess of dynamical over photometric bulge mass by $0.83 \times 10^{10}\ \Msun$ at $2\sigma$ and finds $\Omega_{b'} \lesssim 0.8\,\Omega_{b}$ at low mirror temperature.
simulations.imported-milky-ways-mass-bud.lay: The Milky Way's disk near the Sun and its central bulge can be weighed both from the motions of stars and by counting stars and gas. The two methods leave little room for extra hidden matter concentrated in a thin disk or in the bulge. Any form of dark matter that cools and settles like ordinary gas must fit inside that small margin.

simulations.imported-mirror.formal: The mirror tower is a copy of ours, populated at $\Omega_{b'} = 0.995$ to $1$ times $\Omega_{b}$ where its matter is helium or protons. Its temperature ratio $\xi = T'/T$ lies between the gravitational floor, $2.8$ to $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$, and the hot-deposit estimate, about $4 \times 10^{-3}$, a free datum of the descent that is an exception to P2 at its version-1 reach (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-temperature-p2}; P2 as scoped leaves $\xi$ free, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-charge-sector-label-temperature-not}, and the cold mirror then needs a non-equilibrium descent, Proposition \claimref{synthesis.cold-mirror-needs-non-equilibrium-descent}); its baryon-to-photon ratio is $\eta' = \eta/\xi^{3}$. T14 takes it to be helium on the expected (burning) branch and protons on the alternative; T14c finds it helium for $\xi$ between about $3 \times 10^{-3}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$, an interval containing the hot-deposit estimate, and at the floor degenerate and, for a copied lepton number $L \leq 0$, $96$ to $100$ percent neutrons (Computation \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-composition}). As neutral atoms its elastic cross-section per mass is of order $2 \times 10^{8}$ (hydrogen) or $5 \times 10^{7}$ (helium) $\cmg$, and inside a halo it is a plasma, collisional and dissipative like our gas. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thm.~4.3, Props.~4.6 and 4.7, Prop.~6.2]{ButlerT14}.
simulations.imported-mirror.technical:
The mirror tower carries a copy of our matter content, populated at $\Omega_{b'} = 0.995$ to $1$ times $\Omega_{b}$ where its matter is helium or protons. Its temperature ratio $\xi = T'/T$ lies between a gravitational floor of $2.8$ to $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$ and a hot-deposit estimate of about $4 \times 10^{-3}$, a free datum that the T14c note shows to be an exception to indifference (P2) at its version-1 reach (as scoped, indifference leaves it free and the cold mirror then needs a non-equilibrium descent), and its baryon-to-photon ratio is $\eta' = \eta/\xi^{3}$. The dark-matter paper takes it to be helium on the expected (burning) branch and protons on the alternative; T14c finds it helium for $\xi$ between about $3 \times 10^{-3}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$, which contains the hot-deposit estimate, but degenerate and neutron-rich at the floor.

As neutral atoms it has an elastic cross-section per mass of order $2 \times 10^{8}\ \cmg$ (hydrogen) or $5 \times 10^{7}\ \cmg$ (helium); inside a halo it is a plasma, collisional and dissipative like our gas. These are results of the series' dark-matter paper restated for the simulations.
simulations.imported-mirror.lay: One of the hidden sectors is a mirror copy of ordinary matter with almost exactly as much matter as ours, but much colder. The series' dark-matter paper expected its early-universe chemistry to leave it mostly helium; a later note (T14c) finds that true only if it is moderately warm, and at its coldest it would end mostly as neutrons. That note also shows that keeping it cold is an unstated exception to the paper's indifference principle as first stated. As the principle is now scoped, it applies to labels such as charges and not to temperatures, so it leaves the mirror's temperature free; a cold mirror then needs the descent to have left the towers out of equilibrium. Inside galaxies it is a plasma that, like our own gas, collides and radiates energy away.

simulations.imported-unit-ball-rule-fami.formal:
Under Premises R1 (equal mass per quantum), R2 (one quantum per unit ball of each tower's space, with a common Wigner-Seitz radius $d_{b}$) and R3 (one cell radius per unshared direction), the share of a tower whose space has $D$ dimensions is $V_{3}/V_{D}$, and
\[
\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{dark}}}{\Omega_{b}} \;=\; 1 + 2\cdot\frac{4}{3} + 2\cdot\frac{8}{3\pi} \;=\; \frac{11\pi + 16}{3\pi} \;=\; 5.364 .
\]
With the thickness of the unshared direction left as $c\,d_{b}$ the total is
\[
T(c) \;=\; 1 + \frac{8}{3c} + \frac{16c}{3\pi},
\]
which equals $5.364$ at $c = 1$ and $c = \pi/2$ and has its floor $5.255$ at $c = \sqrt{\pi/2}$. The three-dimensional towers' sheets are stacked one cell radius apart along the direction they lack, and they move with the matter. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Prems.~7.2 to 7.4, Props.~7.6, 7.15 and 7.28]{ButlerT14}.
simulations.imported-unit-ball-rule-fami.technical:
Under premises R1 (equal mass per quantum), R2 (one quantum per unit ball of each tower's space, with a common Wigner-Seitz radius $d_{b}$) and R3 (one cell radius per unshared direction), a tower whose space has $D$ dimensions has share $V_{3}/V_{D}$, and summing over the populated towers gives $\Omega_{\mathrm{dark}}/\Omega_{b} = 1 + 2\cdot\tfrac{4}{3} + 2\cdot\tfrac{8}{3\pi} = (11\pi + 16)/(3\pi) = 5.364$.

Leaving the thickness of the unshared direction as $c\,d_{b}$, the total is $T(c) = 1 + 8/(3c) + 16c/(3\pi)$, equal to $5.364$ at $c = 1$ and $c = \pi/2$, with its floor $5.255$ at $c = \sqrt{\pi/2}$. The three-dimensional towers' sheets are stacked one cell radius apart along the direction they lack, and move with the matter.
simulations.imported-unit-ball-rule-fami.lay: Assuming three premises, that every particle has the same mass (R1), that one particle fills one unit ball of its sector's space (R2) and that each direction a sector lacks counts one cell radius (R3), a counting rule gives each hidden sector a share of matter according to how much room one particle takes up in that sector's space. Added up over the sectors, it gives about $5.36$ times as much dark matter as ordinary matter. If the thickness of the missing direction is left free instead, the totals form a family whose smallest value is about $5.26$, with $5.36$ reached at two different thicknesses.

simulations.merger.formal:
In reading (W) the subcluster's sheet fluid and mirror gas are held back with its gas, $71$ percent of its mass ($56$ percent in the mixed count). Its potential collapses, its galaxies spread, and by the end of the runs it has not separated beyond $500$ to $630$ kpc. With random normals, or with the normals along the line of sight so that the merger axis lies in the sheets, it has no separate lensing peak (contrast $0.81$ to $0.95$). With every normal along this merger's axis (\texttt{rule\_par}) the fluid slides through along the axis; the subcluster then has a lensing peak (contrast $3.24$, $15$ kpc from its galaxies) but keeps half its mass. The mixed count fails in the same way. With the mirror collisionless from the start, so that only the sheet fluid collides, the subcluster keeps a weaker peak (contrast $2.69$ in the mixed count, $3.78$ with one three-dimensional tower colliding) and $0.44$ to $0.55$ of CDM's own mass: with a quarter to a third of the dark matter as sheet fluid, the sheet fluid alone costs about half the subcluster's central mass.

In reading (C) the subcluster reaches the observed separation with its mass peak on its galaxies and its gas $355$ kpc behind. Its own mass inside $150$ kpc of its galaxies is $0.57$ of CDM's, a deficit larger than the $23$ percent bound, because its halo puffs more than it strips. Its galaxies spread with it: the galaxy mass within $150$ kpc of the galaxy peak is $0.83$ of its start, where CDM's is compressed to $1.31$. Mass and light leave the aperture together, so the ratio inside it is kept while the mass inside it falls. Per unit of its collisionless content, the subcluster's collisionless matter inside the aperture is $0.683$ as concentrated as CDM's, and $0.683 \times 0.814$ (the collisionless share of the dark matter in reading (C), $1 - 0.186$) gives $0.556$, its collisionless matter against CDM's dark matter in the aperture; with stars and settled mirror matter the own mass is $0.57$. The mass-to-light ratio, from which the bound is derived, is therefore the test: its change is $0.82$ (the ratio itself $0.89$) against the observed $0.84 \pm 0.07$; CDM's is $0.87$ (ratio $1.00$). With a sampling error of $15$ to $21$ percent this measure does not separate reading (C) from CDM; the lensing peak and the gas offset separate both from reading (W). Its contrast, $4.7$ against CDM's $7.5$, is lower, and it has lost its mirror gas and part of its outer halo (a figure of the original). Each composition is one realisation of one geometry. Computed; observation level.
simulations.merger.technical:
In simulations of a Bullet-like merger, reading (W), with the sheet fluid and mirror gas colliding, holds back $71$ percent of the subcluster's mass with its gas ($56$ percent in the mixed count): its potential collapses, it separates no further than $500$ to $630$ kpc, and with random or line-of-sight normals it has no separate lensing peak. With every sheet normal along the merger axis the fluid slides through and a peak survives, but half the mass is lost; with only the sheet fluid colliding the subcluster keeps a weaker peak and $0.44$ to $0.55$ of CDM's mass.

In reading (C) the subcluster reaches the observed separation with its mass peak on its galaxies and its gas $355$ kpc behind. Its own mass in a $150$ kpc aperture is $0.57$ of CDM's, but its galaxies spread with it, so its mass-to-light change of $0.82$ sits near the observed $0.84 \pm 0.07$ and, with a sampling error of $15$ to $21$ percent, does not separate it from CDM's $0.87$; the lensing peak and gas offset separate both from reading (W). Each composition is one realisation of one geometry; observation level.
simulations.merger.lay: Simulated collisions of two galaxy clusters were run with the proposed dark-matter mixture. If that matter does not collide, the simulation reaches the observed separation with the mass on the galaxies, and the measured mass-to-light change cannot tell it apart from standard dark matter. Each run is one realisation of one geometry, and the result is recorded at observation level.

simulations.mirror-galaxy.formal:
Over the $24$ set-ups:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The proton-only branch, at the feedback a hydrogen population has ($F = 1$), puts $47$ to $56\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ of gas and stars at the Sun and $(15$ to $18) \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$ in the bulge volume. It fails every combination of bounds and normalisations.
\item[(ii)] The helium branch without star formation settles $48$ to $117\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$. It fails.
\item[(iii)] The helium branch with stars at $F = 1$ gives $23$ to $42\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ and $(7$ to $13) \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$. It fails. At equal feedback it settles $49$ to $85$ percent as much as our sector, because it cools more slowly.
\item[(iv)] The helium branch at the helium-star feedback, $F = 3.6$ to $7.3$ with yield $yF$, gives $5.6$ to $20\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ of gas and stars, $1$ to $8$ of gas, and $(1.8$ to $6.2) \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$ in the bulge volume; with yield $y$, $4.2$ to $14$, $1$ to $7$ and $(1.3$ to $4.2) \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$. Whether it passes depends on choices the data and the model do not fix. The first is how much of the bulge's dark mass, $3.1 \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$ (Fact \claimref{simulations.imported-milky-ways-mass-budget}), may be mirror: $0.6 \times 10^{9}$ if it is shared in proportion to the composition, $3.1 \times 10^{9}$ if the collisionless towers contribute nothing there, up to $8.3 \times 10^{9}$ if a mirror bar can hide within the stellar mass-to-light uncertainty. Every floor computed here exceeds $0.6 \times 10^{9}$, so on the proportional reading the bulge excludes the helium branch at every $F$ and yield; it survives in the bulge only on the other two, which require over twice the proportional share ($1.33/0.6 = 2.2$ times with yield $y$, $1.78/0.6 = 3.0$ with $yF$): held as dark mass, over $43$ percent of the bulge's dark mass with yield $y$ and $57$ percent with $yF$; otherwise hidden within the stellar mass-to-light uncertainty. The others are the normalisation of the mirror's gas, the bounds at the Sun, the yield and the IMF.

With yield $yF$, the numbers of converged set-ups that pass the lenient bounds at the Sun (thin gas below $5.59$, gas and stars below $15\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$) and each reading of the bulge room are as follows, given as ranges over the two black-hole cuts and the two disk scales (\file{verdict\_output.txt} has every count):
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
IMF shape & normalisation & room $8.3$ & room $3.1$ & room $0.6$ \\
\midrule
ours & total & $8$ to $9$ of $11$ or $12$ & $0$ to $4$ & $0$ \\
ours & component & $0$ to $2$ & $0$ to $1$ & $0$ \\
best shift & total & all ($9$ or $10$) & $5$ to $8$ & $0$ \\
best shift & component & $2$ to $8$ & $0$ to $7$ & $0$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\item[(v)] With yield $yF$ even the most favourable case leaves at least $5.6\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ at the Sun and $1.78 \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$ in the bulge volume; with yield $y$, at least $4.2$ and $1.33 \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$.
\end{enumerate}
Computed; observation level.
simulations.mirror-galaxy.technical:
A model of the Galaxy with a mirror sector, over $24$ set-ups, compares the mirror gas and stars settled at the Sun and in the bulge with the observed mass budget. The proton-only branch, the helium branch without star formation, and the helium branch with stars at hydrogen-like feedback ($F = 1$) all fail; at equal feedback the helium branch settles $49$ to $85$ percent as much as our sector, because it cools more slowly.

At helium-star feedback, $F = 3.6$ to $7.3$, the helium branch leaves $5.6$ to $20\ \Msun\,\mathrm{pc^{-2}}$ of gas and stars at the Sun with yield $yF$ ($4.2$ to $14$ with yield $y$) and $(1.3$ to $6.2) \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$ in the bulge volume. Whether it passes depends on choices the data and the model do not fix, first how much of the bulge's dark mass may be mirror: on the proportional share, $0.6 \times 10^{9}\ \Msun$, it is excluded at every $F$ and yield, and it survives only if the mirror holds over twice that share. Computed; observation level.
simulations.mirror-galaxy.lay: A model of our Galaxy including the mirror sector asks how much mirror gas would cool and settle into the disk and the central bulge. In most versions far too much settles, contradicting measurements of the Galaxy's mass. Only a helium mirror with strong stellar feedback comes close, and it can survive only if the bulge can hide more mirror matter than a proportional share allows; even then the verdict turns on choices the data and the model do not fix. These are computed model results, at observation level.

simulations.s1-one-species-per-tower.formal:
The matter of each populated tower is one species. Within its tower it is either collisionless or a fluid; across towers species interact only through gravity (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.superselected-hence-dark-exactly-stable}). Our matter is two species: galaxies, collisionless, and our gas.

\emph{Type: model specification.} This is a clause of the specification of the numerical model of the cluster simulations (Premises S1 to S5 and C), not a hypothesis of the series about nature; it is kept with the premises so that the two simulation results show it among their conditions. Its second clause, that species of different towers interact only through gravity, is not a premise: it is the stored Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.superselected-hence-dark-exactly-stable}, under that theorem's own conditions. Its first clause is a simplification of the model: for the five-dimensional towers the stored content under (S) is four Dirac species (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.five-dimensional-content}), treated here as one fluid component.
simulations.s1-one-species-per-tower.technical:
A modelling premise for the simulations: the matter of each populated tower is a single species, either collisionless or a fluid within its tower, and species in different towers interact only through gravity, as superselection of the tower charge implies. Our own matter is modelled as two species, collisionless galaxies and our gas.

Type: model specification. The second clause (towers interact only through gravity) is a stored theorem, under its own conditions, and not a premise; the first (one species per tower) is a simplification of the model, the five-dimensional towers' stored content under (S) being four Dirac species.
simulations.s1-one-species-per-tower.lay: For the simulations, each hidden sector's matter is treated as one kind of stuff, which either passes through itself or flows like a fluid. Different sectors feel each other only through gravity. Ordinary matter is split into galaxies, which pass through each other, and gas, which does not. It is part of the set-up of a computer model, not a claim of the theory about nature. That different sectors feel each other only through gravity is a result proved elsewhere in the series, not an assumption made here.

simulations.s2-sheet-fluid.formal:
At composite strength the three-dimensional towers' matter is an ideal gas with two degrees of freedom ($\gamma = 2$) whose pressure and viscosity act only within its sheet. Along the sheet's normal it moves without pressure, since sheets cross freely \cite[Rem.~7.30]{ButlerT14}. The sheets of a given orientation form one family shared by all the matter of the tower \cite[Lem.~6.1, Prem.~7.4]{ButlerT14}, so parcels of different halos on the same sheet collide. T14 does not say how quanta on differently oriented sheets interact; between two such parcels the force and separation are contracted with the mean of the two in-plane projectors, $(P_{i} + P_{j})/2$, which is the projection onto the sheet when the normals are parallel and otherwise keeps a fraction of each normal component (Lemma \claimref{simulations.averaged-pair-operator}).

\emph{Type: model specification.} This is a clause of the specification of the numerical model of the cluster simulations (Premises S1 to S5 and C), not a hypothesis of the series about nature; it is kept with the premises so that the two simulation results show it among their conditions. Premises C and S2 belong to two exclusive readings of the three-dimensional towers' matter in the simulations: reading (C), collisionless, under Premise \claimref{simulations.c-odd-towers-collisionless}, and reading (W), a sheet fluid at composite strength, under Premise \claimref{simulations.s2-sheet-fluid}. The two simulation results (\claimref{simulations.halo-shapes}, \claimref{simulations.merger}) list both among their conditions because each reports both readings; no result holds the two together. S2 is conditional on the three-dimensional towers' matter interacting at composite strength, the negation of C for those towers; under C it is vacuous for them. In the merger result reading (W) holds the subcluster's sheet fluid back with its gas and, with random or line-of-sight normals, gives no separate lensing peak (\claimref{simulations.merger}).
simulations.s2-sheet-fluid.technical:
A modelling premise: at composite interaction strength the three-dimensional towers' matter is an ideal gas with two degrees of freedom, $\gamma = 2$, whose pressure and viscosity act only within its sheet; along the sheet normal it moves without pressure, since sheets cross freely. Sheets of a given orientation form one family shared by all the tower's matter, so parcels of different halos on the same sheet collide.

For parcels on differently oriented sheets, which the dark-matter paper leaves open, force and separation are contracted with the averaged projector $(P_{i} + P_{j})/2$, which is the in-sheet projection when the normals are parallel and otherwise keeps a fraction of each normal component.

Type: model specification, the premise of reading (W) of the simulations, exclusive with reading (C) (Premise C); under C it is vacuous for the three-dimensional towers. The two simulation results list both premises because each reports both readings.
simulations.s2-sheet-fluid.lay: The sheet-bound dark matter is modelled as a gas that pushes and resists only within its own sheet and moves freely across sheets. Matter from different halos on the same sheet can collide. Where sheets of different orientations meet, a simple averaging rule is adopted, because the underlying theory does not say what happens there. It is part of the set-up of a computer model, not a claim of the theory about nature. It belongs to one of two alternative versions of the model, the one in which this matter collides with itself; the other version (C) treats it as collisionless, and the two are never assumed together.
simulations.s2-sheet-fluid.typing_note: Postulate; no edges. The averaged pair operator lemma in context_refs describes a property of the adopted rule, not a premise of a postulate.

simulations.s3-mirror-cluster.formal:
Mirror matter in a cluster is a fully ionised helium plasma, $\gamma = 5/3$, cooling by bremsstrahlung alone (below about $10^{6}$ K He$^{+}$ line cooling would in reality dominate, so settling would come sooner; Cost K3). Gas that cools below about $7 \times 10^{4}$ K becomes collisionless (the settled phase). There is no mirror star formation and no feedback.

\emph{Type: model specification.} This is a clause of the specification of the numerical model of the cluster simulations (Premises S1 to S5 and C), not a hypothesis of the series about nature; it is kept with the premises so that the two simulation results show it among their conditions. Its window: the helium composition is the stored decimal estimate's only for a mirror temperature ratio $\xi = T'/T$ between about $3 \times 10^{-3}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$ (Computation \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-composition}); at the gravitational floor that estimate gives a neutron-rich mirror and towards the $\Neff$ cap a hydrogen-rich one, and outside the window S3 is not the stored composition. Nothing stored fixes $\xi$.
simulations.s3-mirror-cluster.technical:
A modelling premise: mirror matter in a cluster is a fully ionised helium plasma with $\gamma = 5/3$, cooling by bremsstrahlung alone. Gas that cools below about $7 \times 10^{4}$ K becomes collisionless (the settled phase), and there is no mirror star formation and no feedback. Below about $10^{6}$ K, He$^{+}$ line cooling would in reality dominate and bring settling sooner, a cost the model records.

Type: model specification. S3 holds on the window of the mirror's temperature ratio where the stored estimate gives a helium mirror, $\xi$ between about $3 \times 10^{-3}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$; outside it the stored composition is neutron-rich (at the floor) or hydrogen-rich (towards the cap), and nothing stored fixes $\xi$.
simulations.s3-mirror-cluster.lay: In the cluster simulations the mirror matter is a hot, fully ionised helium gas that loses heat only through the simplest radiation process. Gas that cools enough is treated as settled and no longer collides. The model has no mirror stars, so nothing heats the gas back up. It is part of the set-up of a computer model, not a claim of the theory about nature. The helium composition is what the series' own estimate gives only if the mirror world's temperature lies in a certain range, which nothing in the series fixes.

standard-model.imported-sectors-supersel.formal: The eight towers are the residues of the shadow dimension mod $8$ \cite[Prop.~3.1]{ButlerT14}, this world's tower one of them and the mirror tower another. Under the sector decomposition of \cite[Def.~3.6]{ButlerT14}, every frozen-phase local operator is a section of one tower's soldered bundle and acts within that tower's sector; the tower charge is superselected, the shadow walls separating residues are unreachable, and matter in another tower gravitates on the shared metric and does nothing else: the only inter-tower coupling is gravitational, and the only inter-tower event is the descent \cite[Prop.~4.1]{ButlerT14}. The mirror tower's derived content is a copy of this one's, with the same gauge algebra, global form, generation, hypercharges and chirality halves, hence the same $\beta$-functions at every scale \cite[Thm.~4.3(i),(iii)]{ButlerT14}. \emph{Provenance:} T14, at the levels declared there; Proposition 4.1 rests on the single-frozen-point premise P1 and the sector decomposition, and everything below that uses it is conditional on the same.

The mirror tower's derived content is a copy of ours, with the same gauge algebra, global form, generation, hypercharges and chirality halves, hence the same $\beta$-functions at every scale. The fact is imported from the dark-matter paper at the levels declared there, and is conditional on the single-frozen-point premise P1 and the sector decomposition.

One of them is ours, and another is a mirror copy with the same particles and forces. Because the forces are the same, their strengths change with energy in exactly the same way in both sectors. All of this is carried over from that paper at the levels it declares there.

standard-model.under-s-mirror-inherits-d.formal: Under Hypothesis (S), the mirror tower's one-loop coefficients are $(\tfrac{41}{10}, -\tfrac{19}{6}, -7)$ with one mirror Higgs doublet, its ratio is $r_{0} = 218/115$, and its one-loop equations \claimref{obj.standard-model.one-threshold-spectrum-admissible} are this tower's: from any boundary values at which this tower's couplings fail to meet, the mirror's fail to meet in the same way. Without (S) the mirror copy has no lepton doublet; its coefficients in the normalisation of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-one-loop-running-trace-ratio}(a) are $(\tfrac72, -\tfrac{25}{6}, -7)$, with ratio $46/17$, but that normalisation is the one (S) supplies through $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$. The content's own trace normalisation, that of the ratio $9/26$ of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.weak-angle-over-derived-generation}, gives the ratio $740/289$ instead, and without the lepton doublet the content is anomalous, its $[SU(2)]^{2}U(1)_{Y}$ sum being $\tfrac12$ per generation; so without (S) the content poses no meeting question. Whatever content resolves the desert in this tower, the mirror carries a copy of it by Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-sectors-superselection-mirror-copy}, so the resolution is duplicated, never shared: no content of this tower enters the mirror's run and none of the mirror's enters this one's.
standard-model.under-s-mirror-inherits-d.technical:

The statement concerns the equations, not the values of the mirror's couplings.

synthesis.adiabatic-deposit-modulation-i.formal:
Assume Premise (R) through Proposition \claimref{synthesis.mirror-temperature-measures-deposit-under-r}, whose deposit law gives the mirror an energy $\varepsilon T_{\mathrm{desc}}$ per unit of its charge ($\varepsilon$ is that proposition's deposit per unit charge, not the asymmetry $\epsilon$ of $Q = \epsilon N$), thermalised at once, with $\xi^{4} = \tfrac43 Y_{B}\varepsilon$ up to a floor below $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ in $\xi$; and the charge reading of Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.stored-asymmetry-charge-not-number}, under which the deposited charge is fixed by the descent's data independently of the tower's temperature and the mirror carries the same baryon charge as this tower. Read a classical modulation of the deposit on scales outside the descent's Hubble length in the separate-universe sense: each patch is an unperturbed descended universe with local data on a slice of uniform time at the deposit, namely the visible bath's temperature $T_{d}$, the charge density $n_{Q}$ (the same in this tower and the mirror) and $\varepsilon$, and the towers do not exchange energy afterwards. Write $v = (\delta\ln T_{d}, \delta\ln n_{Q}, \delta\ln\varepsilon)$. Each decoupled population keeps its curvature perturbation outside the Hubble length: $\zeta_{\gamma} = \delta\ln T_{d}$ for the visible radiation, $\zeta_{Q} = \tfrac13\delta\ln n_{Q}$ for every population whose number is fixed by the deposited charge (baryons, the mirror's baryons), $\zeta_{m} = \tfrac14\delta\ln(\varepsilon T_{d}n_{Q})$ for the mirror's radiation; write $S_{Q} = 3(\zeta_{Q} - \zeta_{\gamma})$ and $S_{m} = 3(\zeta_{m} - \zeta_{\gamma})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The adiabatic direction, for the three local data listed; further deposited populations not fixed by the charge would add entropy directions.)} $S_{Q} = \delta\ln n_{Q} - 3\,\delta\ln T_{d} = \delta\ln Y_{B}$ and $S_{m} = \tfrac34(\delta\ln\varepsilon + S_{Q}) = \tfrac34\,\delta\ln\xi^{4}$. The map $v \mapsto (S_{Q}, S_{m})$ has rank $2$ and kernel spanned by $(1, 3, 0)$: a modulation is adiabatic exactly when the charge per unit entropy and the deposit per unit charge are uniform and only $T_{d}$ varies with $n_{Q} \propto T_{d}^{3}$, which is a local shift of the time of the descent; then $\zeta_{\gamma} = \zeta_{Q} = \zeta_{m} = \delta\ln T_{d}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The three parameters one at a time.)} (a) $T_{d}$ at fixed $n_{Q}$: $S_{Q} = -3\zeta_{\gamma}$ and $S_{m} = -\tfrac94\zeta_{\gamma}$. (b) $\varepsilon$ alone: $\zeta_{\gamma} = \zeta_{Q} = 0$ and $S_{m} = \tfrac34\delta\ln\varepsilon$; the photons, the baryons and every charge carrier have no curvature perturbation of their own outside the Hubble length, and the mode is a pure isocurvature mode of the mirror's radiation (which perturbs the photons only gravitationally, after re-entry), which is below $0.0388$ of the radiation at the deposit under the dark-radiation cap $\xi < 0.448$ and below $1.7 \times 10^{-7}$ of it for a helium mirror. (c) $n_{Q}$ alone: $\zeta_{\gamma} = 0$ and $S_{Q} = \delta\ln n_{Q}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Consequence for the two descent problems.)} If the measured primordial spectrum is carried by a classical modulation of the deposit, it is carried by the time-shift direction of (i): the deposit per unit charge $\varepsilon$ and the charge per unit entropy must be spatially uniform up to the isocurvature the record allows, so the charge face of the deposit cannot carry the spectrum, and the spectrum's carrier is a field of local delays of the one descent, whose two-point function is still subject to the finite-range bound of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-cannot-seed-cmb}.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Large-scale estimate, argued.)} For (a), the matter carrying the deposited charge is at least the baryons and the mirror's baryons, a fraction $f_{Q} \ge 2\Omega_{b}/\Omega_{m} > 0.31$ of the matter; in the large-scale Sachs-Wolfe combination $\zeta + 2S_{\mathrm{eff}}$, $S_{\mathrm{eff}} = f_{Q}S_{Q}$, the non-adiabatic part is $6f_{Q}|\zeta| > 1.88|\zeta|$, and for either relative sign the non-adiabatic share of the large-scale temperature variance exceeds $0.27$ in magnitude, more than twenty times the bound of $0.013$ from Planck 2018 (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-isocurvature-and-isotropy-bounds}). For (b) and (c) the photons carry no curvature perturbation of their own, so neither can be the measured adiabatic spectrum.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.adiabatic-deposit-modulation-i.technical: Quasi-free deposits add only shot noise to the vacuum (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-is-vacuum-plus-shot-noise}), so if the descent's deposit carries the primordial spectrum it does so as a classical modulation of its local data, the separate-universe form of the curvature perturbation. The stored deposit has three local data: the reheating temperature, the deposited charge (the same for this tower and the mirror under the charge reading) and the energy per unit charge that, under Premise (R), alone sets the mirror's temperature. Treating each patch as its own descended universe, and each decoupled population's curvature perturbation as conserved outside the Hubble length, the entropy perturbations of the charge carriers and of the mirror's radiation against the photons are linear in the three modulations with a one-dimensional kernel: the charge must scale as the cube of the temperature and the energy per unit charge must not vary, which is a local shift of the time of the descent. A modulation of the energy per unit charge alone gives the photons and the charge carriers no curvature perturbation of their own: it is a pure isocurvature mode of the mirror's radiation, a few percent of the radiation at most; a modulation of the temperature at fixed charge gives the baryons and the mirror's baryons an isocurvature of minus three times the curvature perturbation, which on large scales would dominate the temperature anisotropy against Planck's bound of about one percent on non-adiabatic power. So the charge face of the deposit, the entries of the pre-descent theory, must be spatially uniform, and the spectrum face is narrowed to a field of local delays of the descent, which the finite-range bound still constrains and nothing stored supplies.
synthesis.adiabatic-deposit-modulation-i.lay: In this framework the universe's earliest state is laid down in one event, which also sets how much matter each family of worlds holds and how much energy the mirror world received. The ripples seen in the cosmic microwave background are of one particular kind, called adiabatic: everything, light and matter alike, was disturbed together, as if some regions simply started a little later than others. This result asks which of the event's settings could vary from place to place to make such ripples, under the framework's reading of matter as a stored charge. Only one kind of variation works: the event happening at slightly different times in different places, with the amount of matter per unit of light and the energy given to the mirror world the same everywhere. Varying the energy given to the mirror world gives ordinary light and matter no ripple of their own, only a mismatch between the mirror world's light and ours; varying the event's temperature while the matter stays fixed gives the wrong kind of ripple, which the measurements rule out. So the numbers the framework still has to supply about the event must be the same everywhere, and the ripples still need a source the framework does not have.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-is-vacuum-plus-shot-noise} a quasi-free deposit on the boundary-mode algebra exceeds the vacuum by shot noise only, below $10^{-77}$ at the pivot for dense deposits; a deposit that carries the measured amplitude must therefore contain a classical (non-quasi-free) component, and the one considered here is a modulation of the deposit's local data on scales far outside the descent's Hubble length (by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-cannot-seed-cmb}(iii), the pivot lay outside it by more than $2 \times 10^{5}$). On such scales each patch evolves as an unperturbed descended universe with its own data (the separate-universe reading; standard, cited from memory). The stored deposit has three local data. The visible bath's temperature $T_{d}$ at the deposit. The charge density $n_{Q}$: under the charge reading of Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.stored-asymmetry-charge-not-number}(i) the stored asymmetry is a charge fixed by the descent's data and independent of the tower's temperature, and the mirror carries the same baryon charge as this tower, so one $n_{Q}$ serves both. The deposit per unit charge $\varepsilon$ (not the asymmetry $\epsilon$ of $Q = \epsilon N$ in the charge reading): by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.mirror-temperature-measures-deposit-under-r}(ii), under (R), the mirror receives $\varepsilon T_{d}$ per unit charge, thermalised at once, so its radiation density at the deposit is $\rho_{m} = \varepsilon T_{d}n_{Q}$ up to the floor, which (i) of the same proposition puts below $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ in $\xi$ and which is neglected here. The towers exchange no energy afterwards (the same proposition's hypothesis that neither tower receives entropy beyond its copied history).

\emph{Curvature perturbations.} For a population that is decoupled and has a definite equation of state, the curvature perturbation on its own uniform-density slices, $\zeta_{i} = -\psi + \delta\rho_{i}/(3(\rho_{i} + p_{i}))$, is conserved outside the Hubble length (Wands, Malik, Lyth and Liddle 2000; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-superhorizon-zeta-conservation}). On the slice of uniform time at the deposit, taken flat ($\psi = 0$) in the separate-universe gauge, radiation has $\zeta = \tfrac14\delta\ln\rho$ and a conserved number $\zeta = \tfrac13\delta\ln n$. So $\zeta_{\gamma} = \tfrac14\delta\ln T_{d}^{4} = \delta\ln T_{d}$, $\zeta_{Q} = \tfrac13\delta\ln n_{Q}$ for every population whose number is fixed by the deposited charge, and $\zeta_{m} = \tfrac14(\delta\ln\varepsilon + \delta\ln T_{d} + \delta\ln n_{Q})$. The entropy perturbation of population $i$ against the photons is $S_{i} = 3(\zeta_{i} - \zeta_{\gamma})$, conserved with them.

\emph{(i)} For the three local data listed (further deposited populations not fixed by the charge would add entropy directions), substituting, $S_{Q} = \delta\ln n_{Q} - 3\delta\ln T_{d}$ and $S_{m} = \tfrac34(\delta\ln\varepsilon + \delta\ln n_{Q} - 3\delta\ln T_{d}) = \tfrac34(\delta\ln\varepsilon + S_{Q})$. The matrix of $v \mapsto (S_{Q}, S_{m})$ is
\[
\begin{pmatrix} -3 & 1 & 0 \\ -\tfrac94 & \tfrac34 & \tfrac34 \end{pmatrix},
\]
of rank $2$, with kernel spanned by $(1, 3, 0)$. With the entropy density $s \propto T_{d}^{3}$, $Y_{B} \propto n_{Q}/T_{d}^{3}$, so $\delta\ln Y_{B} = S_{Q}$; and with equal numbers of light species at the deposit, $\xi^{4} = \rho_{m}/\rho_{\gamma} \propto \varepsilon n_{Q}T_{d}^{-3}$, so $\delta\ln\xi^{4} = \delta\ln Y_{B} + \delta\ln\varepsilon = \tfrac43 S_{m}$, the differentiated form of the stored law $\xi^{4} = \tfrac43 Y_{B}\varepsilon$. Along $(1, 3, 0)$ every $\zeta_{i}$ equals $\delta\ln T_{d}$. A patch whose descent happens later by $\delta t$ and is otherwise identical has, on a common slice of uniform time after both deposits, expanded less and so has a higher temperature, $\delta\ln T = H\delta t$, with the same charge per unit entropy and the same $\varepsilon$: that is the direction $(1, 3, 0)$, the adiabatic mode. The check computes the matrix from the definitions, its rank and kernel with the store's exact linear algebra, a control grid on which every other direction is non-adiabatic, and the consistency with the deposit law.

\emph{(ii)} Reading the matrix: (a) $v = (1, 0, 0)\,\delta\ln T_{d}$ gives $S_{Q} = -3\zeta_{\gamma}$, $S_{m} = -\tfrac94\zeta_{\gamma}$; (b) $v = (0, 0, 1)\,\delta\ln\varepsilon$ gives $\zeta_{\gamma} = \zeta_{Q} = 0$ and $S_{m} = \tfrac34\delta\ln\varepsilon$, a pure isocurvature mode of the mirror's radiation, which perturbs the photons only gravitationally after re-entry; (c) $v = (0, 1, 0)\,\delta\ln n_{Q}$ gives $\zeta_{\gamma} = 0$, $S_{Q} = \delta\ln n_{Q}$. The mirror's share of the radiation at the deposit, with equal numbers of light species ($g' = g$, the proposition's assumption), is $\xi^{4}/(1 + \xi^{4})$, below $0.0388$ at the dark-radiation cap $\xi < 0.448$ of the same proposition (iii) and below $1.7 \times 10^{-7}$ at the upper edge $\xi = 2 \times 10^{-2}$ of the helium interval.

\emph{(iii)} The measured perturbation, of amplitude $A_{s} = (2.100 \pm 0.030) \times 10^{-9}$ at the pivot (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}), so $|\zeta_{\gamma}|$ of order $4.6 \times 10^{-5}$, is carried by the photons and the matter together: Planck 2018 (results X; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-isocurvature-and-isotropy-bounds}) bounds the non-adiabatic contribution to the observed temperature variance by $1.3$ percent for matter isocurvature and $1.7$ percent for neutrino density isocurvature at $95$ percent confidence. In (b) and (c) the photons carry no curvature perturbation of their own, and in (a) the charge carriers carry an isocurvature three times the curvature perturbation; a general modulation decomposes as a multiple of $(1, 3, 0)$ plus a part on which $(S_{Q}, S_{m})$ is injective, and that part must be small against $\zeta_{\gamma}$. So the deposit per unit charge and the charge per unit entropy are uniform up to the allowed isocurvature, and the carrier of the spectrum, if it is a modulation of the deposit, is the time-shift field $\delta t(\vec x)$. Its two-point function is a slice correlator of $\zeta = H\delta t$ (the sign of the time shift above), to which Theorem \claimref{synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-cannot-seed-cmb} applies unchanged: a delay field of finite range gives index $3$, and the amplitude needs correlations over one comoving length; nothing stored fixes such a field.

\emph{(iv) (Argued: large-scale estimate.)} On large angular scales the temperature anisotropy of mixed adiabatic and matter-isocurvature modes is proportional to $\zeta + 2S_{\mathrm{eff}}$, with $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ the matter-weighted entropy perturbation of the matter species (Langlois and Riazuelo 2000; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-large-scale-potential-and-sachs-wolfe-relations}; the relative sign depends on conventions and both signs are treated). In (a), every population fixed by the deposited charge has $S_{Q} = -3\zeta$; the baryons and the mirror's baryons (the same charge in the same number of baryons, the copied content giving the same mass per baryon) make up at least $f_{Q} = 2\Omega_{b}h^{2}/(\Omega_{b}h^{2} + \Omega_{c}h^{2})$ of the matter, with $\Omega_{b}h^{2} = 0.02237$ and $\Omega_{c}h^{2} = 0.1200$ (Planck 2018 VI; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}), so $f_{Q} > 0.314$ and the non-adiabatic amplitude $6f_{Q}|\zeta| = \tfrac{26844}{14237}|\zeta| > 1.88|\zeta|$. For a fully correlated mode the non-adiabatic share of the variance is $1 - (1 \pm 6f_{Q})^{-2}$, which is above $0.88$ or below $-0.27$, in magnitude more than twenty times $0.013$. Any further dark matter fixed by the deposited charge raises $f_{Q}$. The full-spectrum bound is the Planck one; the estimate here is the Sachs-Wolfe limit only.

synthesis.bott-shifted-model-leaves-the-.formal:
Call a signature $(p,q)$ causal if $\min(p,q) = 1$, and let $\beta$ add eight directions of the majority sign: $\beta(p,q) = (p+8,q)$ if $p > q$, $(p,q+8)$ if $q > p$. Let $M_{L}$ represent residues $6, 2, 1, 7, 3, 5$ by $(1,3), (3,1), (2,1), (1,2), (4,1), (1,4)$, the lowest causal member of each (the representatives Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives} gives these residues), and let $M_{8}$ agree with $M_{L}$ except at residues $3$ and $5$, where it takes $(12,1)$ and $(1,12)$; residues $0$ and $4$ are treated alike in both, by the costed single-ideal clause of Observation \claimref{dark-matter.status-rule}(vi).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The shift splits off a real matrix factor; proved, exact.)} For a causal $s = (p,q)$ of dimension $n$ let $\omega_{8}$ be the product of the eight added vectors of $\beta s$. Then $\omega_{8}^{2} = 1$, the elements $a_{i} = e_{i}\omega_{8}$ ($i \le n$) obey the relations of $\Cl(p,q)$, are fixed by reversion and commute with the eight added vectors, and $\Cl(\beta s) = A \otimes B$ with $A = \langle a_{i}\rangle \cong \Cl(p,q)$ and $B$ the algebra of the added vectors, $B \cong \Mat(16,\R)$, reversion acting factor by factor; $B$ has a primitive idempotent $f$ with $\widetilde{f} = f$ and $fBf = \R f$, so its reversion pairing on $Bf$ is symmetric. Hence $\Cl(\beta s) \cong \Mat(16, \Cl(s))$ with its reversion, and $s$, $\beta s$ have the same residue, causality, dimension mod $8$, pseudoscalar square and centrality, Clifford type, constituent field and reversion-pairing type. Not invariant: the complex Witt index $\lfloor(n+2)/2\rfloor$ of the conformal space $\hatV$, the stored number of ladder pairs, rises by $4$, and with it the content the gauge-algebra rule computes.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Residues $3$ and $5$: both are models of the descent's premises; proved.)} $M_{L}$ and $M_{8}$ each satisfy every premise of the window-sensitive results other than P3: F1 to F4, the eight-tower clock, the single-clock filter, Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p1-single-frozen-point} (one frozen point and one metric; its orientation clause acts on residues $2$ and $6$, shared by the models, and no odd tower is oriented in either), Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p2-indifference} (each model is closed under reversal), the costed clause, H1, H2 and Hypothesis (S) (stated for every signature), Premise \claimref{dark-tower-matter.u-transposition-rule} (U) (at $(12,1)$ and $(1,12)$ the field is $\HH$, which supplies the unit for the five pairs beyond the two real ones), the anomaly import (odd dimensions carry no local anomaly), the inverse-square law (no tower's unshared direction carries the one metric), R1 and R3 in their dimension-generic form, and R2 in its dimension-generic reading (its stated list of dimensions $2$, $3$, $4$ is P3's window, which $M_{8}$ leaves); the remaining postulates of the cone do not mention a tower's dimension beyond $n \bmod 4$, which $\beta$ preserves. So nothing in the descent, P3 aside, fixes the five-dimensional towers' dimension; $\beta$ can be iterated, giving a model with those towers at dimension $5 + 8k$ for every $k \ge 0$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Residues $1$ and $7$: Premise U fixes the window; proved, given U.)} Along residues $1$ and $7$ the constituent field is $\R$ in every causal member (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}, invariant under $\beta$ by (i)), the real Witt index of $\hatV$ is $2$ and the stored pair count is $\lfloor(n+2)/2\rfloor$ (\claimref{synthesis.gauge-algebra-by-tower}), which exceeds $2$ for $n > 3$. U3 requires the unit that builds each further pair to lie in the field, which $\R$ cannot supply; the conformal pseudoscalar along residue $7$ is central of square $-1$ but odd and does not act on the constituent ideal (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.residue-seven-unit}). So U admits only $(2,1)$ and $(1,2)$: at residues $1$ and $7$ the lowest-causal clause of P3 follows from Premise U, and P3 is not needed there.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The stored selector that separates the models.)} Premise (W) of \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-complement-window-lowest-causal} admits every representative of $M_{L}$ and neither shifted representative of $M_{8}$; up to dimension sixteen the lowest causal member is the only admitted causal member of each odd residue. (W) is not in the premise set; it was found with the fit known and is not adopted.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Cost.)} With R1 to R3 read in their dimension-generic form (share $V_{3}/V_{D}$ for a space of dimension $D$, one cell radius per unshared direction), the dark-to-baryon ratio is $(11\pi + 16)/3\pi \in (5.36, 5.37)$ in $M_{L}$ and $1 + 8/3 + 1920/\pi^{5} \in (9.9, 10.0)$ in $M_{8}$. The five-dimensional towers' dimension is therefore a recorded input of the unit-ball relation, selected among the models by the observed ratio, and P3 stays a costed premise for residues $3$ and $5$; the results stored under P3 about the five-dimensional towers' content hold given P3.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.bott-shifted-model-leaves-the-.technical: Every residue mod 8 has infinitely many causal signatures, spaced by eight dimensions along each sign. Multiplying each old generator by the product of eight new ones of the majority sign gives a copy of the old algebra that commutes with the new eight, which generate a sixteen by sixteen real matrix algebra; so the shifted algebra is the old one tensored with real matrices, reversion included, and residue, causality, flag bit, real chirality, anomaly parity, pairing type and the constituents' field are unchanged. The number of ladder pairs, the complex Witt index of the conformal space, is not unchanged: it grows by four. At residues 3 and 5 that does no harm, since the constituents' field is the quaternions, which supply the unit each extra pair needs; a second model of every premise other than P3 puts the five-dimensional towers at dimension thirteen, keeping everything else, and the dark-to-baryon ratio becomes about 9.94 instead of 5.364. At residues 1 and 7 the field is real in every causal member, so Premise U, which forbids an outside imaginary unit, admits only the three-dimensional member: there the window follows from U. The one stored hypothesis that would fix the five-dimensional window, premise (W), is not periodic and is not adopted.
synthesis.bott-shifted-model-leaves-the-.lay: The series sorts possible hidden worlds into eight families, each containing worlds of many different dimensions with a single time direction, and to predict the amount of dark matter it picks the smallest world in each family by an assumption. For the two families whose smallest worlds are three-dimensional, another assumption of the theory, that no imaginary unit may be brought in from outside, already rules out every larger world: there the choice is derived. For the two families whose smallest worlds are five-dimensional it is not: adding eight dimensions changes nothing that any other assumption looks at, and gives a different amount of dark matter (about 9.9 instead of 5.4 times the ordinary matter). So for those families the choice of the smallest world is an input that the observed amount selects, not a prediction.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} A tower representative is a signature $(p,q)$; its residue is $p - q \bmod 8$, which the $(1,1)$ ascent preserves (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-eight-towers-mod-8-clock}). The check builds each algebra with \texttt{GA.py}, the representative's own generators first and the eight added ones last.

(i) Let $s = (p,q)$ be causal of dimension $n$, with majority sign $\sigma$ ($\sigma = +1$ if $p > q$), and let $g_{1}, \dots, g_{8}$ be the added vectors of $\beta s$, all of square $\sigma$. Their product $\omega_{8}$ has $\omega_{8}^{2} = (-1)^{28}\sigma^{8} = 1$. Each old generator $e_{i}$ anticommutes with every $g_{j}$, hence commutes with $\omega_{8}$ (eight sign changes), while each $g_{j}$ anticommutes with $\omega_{8}$ (it meets seven others). So $a_{i} = e_{i}\omega_{8}$ has $a_{i}^{2} = e_{i}^{2}\omega_{8}^{2} = e_{i}^{2}$, $a_{i}a_{k} = e_{i}e_{k}$ for $i \ne k$ (so the $a_{i}$ anticommute), and $a_{i}g_{j} = e_{i}\omega_{8}g_{j} = -e_{i}g_{j}\omega_{8} = g_{j}e_{i}\omega_{8} = g_{j}a_{i}$. Reversion fixes $a_{i}$, a blade of grade $9$ ($(-1)^{36} = 1$), and each $g_{j}$. By the universal property the relations give an algebra map $\Cl(p,q) \to A = \langle a_{i}\rangle$; the products $a_{S}$ over subsets $S$ are $\pm e_{S}$ or $\pm e_{S}\omega_{8}$, distinct blades, so it is injective. The products $a_{S}g_{T}$ over all subsets are $2^{n+8}$ distinct blades up to sign (computed for $(2,1)$ and $(4,1)$; the mirror cases differ only in the signs of the squares), so $A \otimes B \to \Cl(\beta s)$ is onto, and by dimension an isomorphism; reversion of $\Cl(\beta s)$ restricts to the reversion of $A$ (it fixes the generators $a_{i}$ and reverses products) and of $B$. $B$ is $\Cl(8,0)$ or $\Cl(0,8)$, of residue $0$, a matrix algebra over $\R$ by the imported classification (Fact \claimref{dark-tower-matter.imported-clifford-structure}), of dimension $256$, so $B \cong \Mat(16,\R)$. \emph{Computed:} with $h = g_{1234}, g_{5678}, g_{1256}, g_{1357}$ (pairwise overlaps even, so they commute; each squares to $1$ for either sign), $f = \prod\tfrac12(1 + h)$ has $f^{2} = f$, $\widetilde{f} = f$, scalar part $\tfrac1{16}$, and $fxf \in \R f$ for all $256$ blades $x$, nonzero for exactly sixteen; so $fBf = \R f$ and $f$ is primitive. For $\psi, \varphi \in Bf$, $\widetilde{\psi}\varphi = c(\psi,\varphi)f$, and reversing gives $c(\varphi,\psi)f = c(\psi,\varphi)\widetilde{f} = c(\psi,\varphi)f$: the reversion pairing on $Bf \cong \R^{16}$ is symmetric. Therefore $\Cl(\beta s) \cong A \otimes \Mat(16,\R) \cong \Mat(16, \Cl(s))$, Morita equivalent to $\Cl(s)$ (Fact \claimref{tower.morita-equivalence-algebra-amplification}); its minimal left ideals are $S \otimes Bf$ with $S$ one of $A$, and its reversion pairing is that of $S$ tensored with a symmetric form, of the same symmetry type. The type data: $\beta$ adds $8$ to $p - q$ or subtracts it, so the residue is unchanged; $\min$ stays $1$; $n$ changes by $8$; the pseudoscalar square $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^{q}$ is multiplied by $(-1)^{8n + 28}$, and by $(-1)^{8}$ when $q$ grows, both equal to $1$ (computed for the four odd representatives); for odd $n$ the pseudoscalar is central in both (computed). Reversal $(p,q) \mapsto (q,p)$ commutes with $\beta$, since it exchanges the majority sign. The constituent field, the division ring of $\Cl^{0}(\hatV) \cong \Cl(p+1,q)$ (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}), is unchanged, since (i) applied to $(p+1,q)$ splits off the same $\Mat(16,\R)$. \emph{Not invariant:} $\hatV$ has dimension $n + 2$, so its complex Witt index $\lfloor(n+2)/2\rfloor$, the stored number of ladder pairs (\claimref{synthesis.gauge-algebra-by-tower}), rises by $4$ ($2 \to 6$ at residues $1$, $7$, $3 \to 7$ at residues $3$, $5$; computed), while its real Witt index stays $2$; a Witt index of $\hatV$ over $\C$ is not a Morita invariant of $\Cl(s)$, and the gauge-algebra rule, which reads it, gives different content at $s$ and $\beta s$.

(ii) Premise by premise, at the pinned versions, for $M_{L}$ and $M_{8}$, which differ only at residues $3$ and $5$. \emph{F1 to F4.} The foundation's directions with sign bits generate $\Cl(p,q)$ for every signature; the check confirms the Clifford relations of every representative of both models. \emph{The clock.} Every representative of both models has the residue it represents (computed). \emph{The single-clock filter.} All populated representatives are causal in both (computed). \emph{P1} (\claimref{dark-matter.p1-single-frozen-point}). It freezes one $I$ and couples every tower to one metric; it places no condition on a tower's signature (as \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-complement-window-lowest-causal} records, nothing in the series says the towers' spacetimes lie in the frozen point's complement). Its orientation clause acts on the reversal orbit $\{2, 6\}$, whose representatives $(3,1)$, $(1,3)$ are the same in both models and have dimension $0 \bmod 4$, so both carry the flag (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.oriented-causal-towers-mirror-pair-every-window}: oriented exactly when $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$); the odd representatives have odd dimension in both, so no odd tower is oriented in either. \emph{P2} (\claimref{dark-matter.p2-indifference}). It equates towers only along $r \mapsto -r$ and reaches labels; each model assigns to $-r$ the reversal of its signature for $r$ (computed), and the labels (residues and tower charges) are the same in both. \emph{The costed clause.} Residues $0$ and $4$ are treated alike in both models. \emph{H1, H2, (S).} H1 defines momentum on a spinor ideal of any signature; H2 identifies a tower's gauge algebra with the automorphisms of its hierarchy, and (S) makes the slots fermionic; all three are stated for every tower, so they hold at $(12,1)$ and $(1,12)$, where the content they produce differs (seven pairs, by (i)); the stored computations of that content (\claimref{synthesis.gauge-algebra-by-tower}) are made in dimensions three to five and do not apply at thirteen. \emph{Premise U} (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.u-transposition-rule}). (U1) and (U2) are definitions valid in every tower. (U3) asks that every complex unit building a ladder pair lie in the constituent field. At $(12,1)$ and $(1,12)$ the field is $\HH$, as at $(4,1)$, $(1,4)$ (by (i)); the real Witt index $2$ gives two real pairs and the other five need a unit, which $\HH$ supplies (a unit $u \in \HH$, with pair scalars $\mathrm{span}\{1, u\}$ as in the stored rule at dimension five), so U3 holds. \emph{Anomaly import.} Local gauge and gravitational anomaly forms have degree $n + 2$ and exist only in even dimension (and the gravitational one only for $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.residues-zero-four-real-chirality-anomaly}(i), (ii)); the odd representatives have odd $n$ in both models. The anomaly obstruction of that theorem's clause (iii) concerns residue $0$ at $(1,1)$, which the costed clause treats alike in both. \emph{Inverse-square law.} It bounds an extra direction carrying the one metric; in both models the towers' unshared directions are their own (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.thickness-not-gravitational-quantity}), so it is met alike. \emph{R1 to R3.} R1 and R3 are dimension-generic and hold in both. R2 as stated lists the dimensions $2$, $3$, $4$, the window P3 supplies; $M_{8}$ meets R2 only in its dimension-generic reading (one quantum per unit ball of a tower's own space, of any dimension), which is the reading used here and in (v). \emph{The remaining postulates of the cone.} T14's (U) on the rank-one eigenvalues at the ceiling, P4 (the same asymmetry on every oriented tower), P5 (what boundary modes return), CPT covariance, the flag as datum, the interface premise (I), (P), (Q), (R), the rate inputs (L, U), the slot-module hypothesis (this tower's composites), the common-ceiling premise (the reversal pair), tameness, the indifference premise and the frozen-point, tractor and field-theory imports: none mentions a tower's dimension beyond $n \bmod 4$, which $\beta$ preserves, or concerns the five-dimensional towers' signature, so each is met or not alike in both models. \emph{Selectors.} The flag bit reads $n \bmod 4$, real chirality reads $n \bmod 4$ and the pseudoscalar, the anomaly degree reads $n$'s parity and $n \bmod 4$, the pairing type reads the reversion form, the field reads $\Cl^{0}(\hatV)$: all unchanged by (i); the pair count changes but no premise bounds it at residues $3$, $5$. So no premise other than P3 separates the models; iterating $\beta$ at residues $3$ and $5$ gives a model for every $k \ge 0$ with the five-dimensional towers at dimension $5 + 8k$ (the check confirms U3 at all five causal members of each up to dimension $21$, of dimensions $5$, $7$, $13$, $15$, $21$).

(iii) Along residues $1$ and $7$ the causal members are $(2 + 8k, 1)$, $(1, 8 + 8k)$ at residue $1$ and their reversals at residue $7$. The check computes, for every causal member of an odd residue up to dimension $21$, the real Witt index of $\hatV = (p+1, q+1)$ from the Gram matrix of its generators (it is $2$, $\min(p+1, q+1)$ with $\min(p,q) = 1$) and the field by the stored rule (division ring of $\Cl(p+1, q)$ by its residue, which reproduces the table of \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field} at the lowest members: $\C$, $\C$, $\R$, $\R$, $\HH$, $\HH$ at residues $6, 2, 1, 7, 3, 5$). At residues $1$ and $7$ the field is $\R$ in every member, and the pair count $\lfloor(n+2)/2\rfloor$ equals the real Witt index $2$ only at $n = 3$; for $n > 3$ at least one pair needs a complex unit, $\R$ supplies none, and U3 forbids adjoining one. The conformal pseudoscalar along residue $7$ is central of square $-1$ (computed at $(1,10)$, $\Cl(2,11)$), but it has odd grade $n + 2$ and carries the even ideal to the odd one (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.residue-seven-unit}(ii)), so it does not act on the constituent ideal and is not an element of the field. Hence U3 admits exactly $(2,1)$ at residue $1$ and $(1,2)$ at residue $7$ among causal members (computed up to dimension $21$; for every $n > 3$ by the argument), and at residues $3$ and $5$ it admits every causal member. The lowest-causal clause at residues $1$ and $7$ thus follows from Premise U with the stored pair count; it is not independent of the premises.

(iv) Under (W) with $\Lambda > 0$ a causal signature is admitted exactly when $\max(p,q) \le 4$ (\claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-complement-window-lowest-causal}(ii), (iii)). Every representative of $M_{L}$ passes; $(12,1)$ and $(1,12)$ fail. An enumeration of all causal signatures of odd residue up to dimension sixteen finds exactly one admitted member per residue, the lowest. (W) is a selector that is not periodic along a residue, which (ii) shows the descent lacks at residues $3$ and $5$.

(v) With $V_{2k} = \pi^{k}/k!$ and $V_{2k+1} = 2^{k+1}\pi^{k}/(2k+1)!!$, the shares $V_{3}/V_{D}$ are $4/3$ ($D = 2$), $8/3\pi$ ($D = 4$) and $960/\pi^{5}$ ($D = 12$), with the mirror's share $1$ in both models. So the ratio is $1 + 8/3 + 16/3\pi = (11\pi + 16)/3\pi$ in $M_{L}$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.unit-ball-rule}) and $1 + 8/3 + 1920/\pi^{5}$ in $M_{8}$. The check brackets both with $\tfrac{333}{106} < \pi < \tfrac{355}{113}$: $(5.36, 5.37)$ and $(9.9, 10.0)$, disjoint. Since the observed ratio is the only datum separating the models, the five-dimensional towers' dimension is an input that the fit selects, which is the status Observation \claimref{dark-matter.status-rule} records for the relation; P3 remains a premise for residues $3$ and $5$, with its lowest-causal clause there shown independent of the descent, while at residues $1$ and $7$ it is a consequence of Premise U by (iii).

synthesis.cold-mirror-needs-non-equilibr.formal:
\emph{Hypotheses.} (B) Each tower of the reversal orbit carries a boundary-mode algebra in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.hawking.boundary-mode-algebra-windows-boost-dynamics}, $\mathfrak{A}$ for this tower and $\mathfrak{A}'$ for the mirror, with boost dynamics $\tau$, $\tau'$ generated by one-particle Hamiltonians $h$ and $h' = u h u^{*}$, where $u$ is a unitary carrying this tower's modes to the mirror's; that the reversal carries the mode set and its frequencies across in this way is assumed here, not derived. The joint dynamics is $\tau_{t} \otimes \tau'_{t}$ with no cross term, which is what the superselection of the tower charge gives (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.superselected-hence-dark-exactly-stable}, itself holding given P1 to P3 and tameness). Write $\xi$ for the ratio of the two towers' KMS temperatures where it is defined.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(One clock gives one temperature.)} Any state of the joint algebra that is KMS at $\beta$ for $\tau \otimes \tau'$ restricts on every window to the product of the two towers' Gibbs states at the same $\beta$, and is the product of the two I-states at $\beta$ (Theorem \claimref{hawking.i-state}); so $\xi = 1$. P2 is not applied to the energy the descent deposited per unit charge.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Two clocks persist.)} For $\beta \neq \beta'$ the product $\omega_{\beta} \otimes \omega'_{\beta'}$ of the I-states is invariant under $\tau \otimes \tau'$, is KMS for $\tau \otimes \tau'$ at no inverse temperature, and is KMS at $\beta$ for the flow $\tau_{t} \otimes \tau'_{(\beta'/\beta)t}$. So $\xi \neq 1$ requires a joint state that is not KMS for the shared flow, and under the decoupled dynamics such a state is stationary.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Symmetric law, asymmetric realisation.)} The mixture $\tfrac12(\omega_{\beta} \otimes \omega'_{\beta'} + \omega_{\beta'} \otimes \omega'_{\beta})$ is invariant under the exchange of the towers and under $\tau \otimes \tau'$, is not quasi-free, and is KMS for $\tau \otimes \tau'$ at no $\beta$; each of its two components has $\xi \neq 1$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading, conditional on a modelling hypothesis.} (M) If the descent's deposited state on the reversal pair is a state on two such algebras and T14's cosmological temperature ratio $\xi = T'/T$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-temperature-p2}) is the ratio of their KMS temperatures, then by (i) a descent in equilibrium for the shared clock gives $\xi = 1$ and $\Delta\Neff = 7.45$ without applying P2 to the deposit, and the cold mirror allowed by the $\Neff$ cap $\xi < 0.448$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.open-channels-their-costs}) requires, besides a scope of P2 that excludes the deposit, a descent state out of joint equilibrium, which (ii) then keeps. (M) is not proved here; the result proper is (i) to (iii) under (B).
synthesis.cold-mirror-needs-non-equilibr.technical: Suppose each tower of the reversal pair carries an algebra of boundary modes with its boost clock, the mirror's clock being the reversal's copy of ours, and the two evolve independently, as superselection gives (which itself holds given the dark-matter premises P1 to P3). If the joint state is in equilibrium for the shared clock, uniqueness of KMS states on windows puts both towers at one temperature, without applying P2 to the deposited energy. A product of the towers' equilibrium states at two temperatures is stationary under the decoupled dynamics but is an equilibrium only for a flow that runs the mirror's modes at another rate. A half-and-half mixture of the two assignments is invariant under the exchange of the towers and stationary but is neither quasi-free nor in equilibrium. If T14's mirror temperature ratio is read as this ratio of KMS temperatures, a modelling step not proved here, the cold mirror of the no-dark-radiation stance needs a descent that leaves the pair out of joint equilibrium, in addition to a narrowed P2.
synthesis.cold-mirror-needs-non-equilibr.lay: The framework's prediction of no extra dark radiation needs the mirror copy of our matter to be much colder than ours. This result works in a simplified model in which each copy carries the boundary modes the framework uses for black holes, each with its own copy of one shared clock. In that model, if the two copies are in thermal equilibrium for the shared clock, they have the same temperature, whatever is assumed about how the birth of the universe shared out its energy. A temperature difference is possible only if the two copies started out of equilibrium, and since they never interact afterwards except through gravity, it would then last. Whether the model's temperatures are the cosmological ones is an assumption, not a result.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} Under hypothesis (B) the joint algebra is the CAR algebra over $\ell^{2}(J) \oplus \ell^{2}(J')$ (Fact \claimref{hawking.imported-quasi-free-states-car-algebra}), its windows are $\mathfrak{A}_{F} \otimes \mathfrak{A}'_{F'}$, and the joint boost dynamics is the quasi-free flow of $h \oplus h'$ with $h' = u h u^{*}$. The absence of a cross term is what Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.superselected-hence-dark-exactly-stable} supplies (the towers interact only through the shared metric); that Proposition holds given P1 to P3 and tameness, so the result below holds given them too, and what it avoids is only the application of P2 to the deposited energy per charge. On a window the generator is $H_{F} + H'_{F'}$ with $[H_{F}, H'_{F'}] = 0$, and each window is invariant under the dynamics (Definition \claimref{obj.hawking.boundary-mode-algebra-windows-boost-dynamics}).

(i) Let $\omega$ be any state that is KMS at $\beta$ for the joint flow. Since windows are invariant under the dynamics, the restriction of $\omega$ to a window is KMS there, and by Lemma \claimref{hawking.gibbs-states-are-kms-conversely-finite} it is the unique such state, the Gibbs state $e^{-\beta(H_{F} + H'_{F'})}/\tr$, which factorises as $e^{-\beta H_{F}} \otimes e^{-\beta H'_{F'}}$ up to normalisation. So both towers' window states are Gibbs at the same $\beta$, every mode of the mirror has the Fermi-Dirac occupation of its partner, $n'_{j} = n_{j} = (e^{\beta\omega_{j}} + 1)^{-1}$, and $\xi = 1$. A state is fixed by its window restrictions, so $\omega$ is the quasi-free state with symbol $(1 + e^{\beta(h \oplus h')})^{-1} = A_{I} \oplus u A_{I} u^{*}$, the product of the two I-states at one $\beta$ (Theorem \claimref{hawking.i-state}; no quasi-free assumption is needed, since quasi-freeness follows); that it is KMS on the full algebra is Fact \claimref{hawking.imported-kms-passes-inductive-limits}. P2 is not applied to the deposit at any step.

(ii) The product of the two Gibbs factors at $\beta$ and $\beta'$ commutes with $H_{F} + H'_{F'}$, each factor commuting with its own tower's generator and, by the absence of a cross term, with the other's; so the state is invariant under the joint flow on every window and hence on the full algebra. (A cross term, for instance a hopping $a^{*}_{j}a'_{j} + a'^{*}_{j}a_{j}$ between partner modes, would break this invariance whenever $\beta \neq \beta'$; the check verifies that too.) If it were KMS at some $\beta''$ for the joint flow, uniqueness on windows would make it the Gibbs state at $\beta''$, forcing $\beta = \beta'' = \beta'$ on any mode of nonzero frequency. It is the Gibbs state at $\beta$ of $H_{F} + (\beta'/\beta)H'_{F'}$, that is, KMS at $\beta$ for the flow that runs the mirror's modes at rate $\beta'/\beta$.

(iii) The exchange of the towers through $u$ maps $\omega_{\beta} \otimes \omega'_{\beta'}$ to $\omega_{\beta'} \otimes \omega'_{\beta}$, so the half-sum is invariant, and it is invariant under the joint flow by (ii). For one mode $a$ of this tower and its partner $a'$, the half-sum gives $\omega(N N') = n_{\beta}n_{\beta'}$ while $\omega(N)\omega(N') = \bigl(\tfrac12(n_{\beta} + n_{\beta'})\bigr)^{2}$, unequal when $\beta \neq \beta'$; every cross two-point function, anomalous ones included, vanishes, so a quasi-free state would factorise these by Wick's theorem, and the half-sum is not quasi-free. By uniqueness on windows it is KMS for the joint flow at no $\beta$, the Gibbs state at any $\beta''$ being a product. Each component has temperature ratio $\beta/\beta' \neq 1$.

\emph{The reading under (M).} If T14's $\xi$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-temperature-p2}) is the ratio of these KMS temperatures and the descent's deposited state lives on the two algebras, then (i) gives $\xi = 1$ and $\Delta\Neff = 7.45$ for a descent in equilibrium for the shared clock, without applying P2 to the deposit, and the cap $\xi < 0.448$ of Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.open-channels-their-costs} can be met only by a joint state outside equilibrium, which (ii) keeps stationary. This paragraph is conditional on (M), which the store does not supply.

The checks verify (i) to (iii) exactly on a window of two modes per tower (frequencies $\omega$ and $2\omega$, Gibbs parameters as exact rationals), realising the modes in $\Cl(4,4)$ with the scalar part as normalised trace and the KMS identity tested as $\rho A = \tau_{\beta e_{2}e_{3}}(A)\rho$, $\tau_{\beta e_{2}e_{3}}(A) = e^{-\beta H}Ae^{\beta H}$, on the generators ($e_{2}e_{3}$ the complex unit of the boundary modes of the radial plane, called $J$ in \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom} and written out here because $J$ names the mode set), and verify that a cross term between the towers destroys the stationarity used in (ii), the obstruction being exactly the occupation gap $n_{\beta} - n_{\beta'}$ of the two partner modes. A separate check confirms the exact content of the numbers quoted under (M): $7.447$ rounds to $7.45$, exceeds the cap $0.3$ by more than a factor $24$, and $7.447\,\xi^{4} \le 0.3$ holds at $\xi = 0.448$ and fails at $0.449$.

synthesis.common-ceiling-coupling-premis.formal:
\emph{Premise (common ceiling coupling).} The two towers of the reversal orbit, this one ($r = 6$) and the mirror ($r = 2$), share one ceiling $M$, and the parameters of their deposited dynamics at that ceiling are equal: the gauge coupling of each factor of the copied gauge algebra, $\alpha_{2}(M) = \alpha_{6}(M)$, and every other coupling of the copied theory at $M$. With the copy of content (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}(i)), which gives the two towers the same $\beta$-functions in every scheme, the two theories at $M$ are then isomorphic, so $\Lambda_{2} = \Lambda_{6}$ and $c_{2} = c_{6}$ (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}(iii)).

\emph{Scope.} The premise equates parameters of the dynamics, which are neither the sector labels Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p2-indifference} equates at its version 2 (labels, not states) nor states: P2 so scoped reaches the stored charge and not the ceiling coupling (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.tower-charge-sector-label-temperature-not}, Reading). It equates no state and no deposited energy, so it leaves the mirror temperature ratio $\xi$ free and does not give the $\xi = 1$ of Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirrors-temperature-p2}. It acts along the reversal orbit $2 \leftrightarrow 6$ only: it says nothing of the odd towers or of the two-time fork, for which no coupling rule follows (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.no-coupling-rule-odd-towers-follows}).

\emph{What it costs.} One equality between two continuous parameters of two sectors (one per coupling of the copied theory), taken as given and derived by no result of the series; since no coupling value is derived either (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.no-coupling-rule-odd-towers-follows}(b)), it ties two undetermined numbers together without fixing either. On it rest the mass factor $m_{2}/m_{6} = 1$ up to the two sectors' composition, and with it the mirror's share $f_{2} = 1$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{mirror}} = \Omega_{b}$, one of the observed $5.364$ units. Without it the share is a free function of the coupling difference: with identical content a difference $\delta = \alpha_{2}(M)^{-1} - \alpha_{6}(M)^{-1}$ moves $\Lambda_{2}/\Lambda_{6}$ by $e^{-2\pi\delta/b}$, and the share stays within ten percent of one only for $|\delta| < 0.106$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-share-one-how-fragile}(ii)). It adds one premise to the register: the share of one holds given P1, P2 (for the asymmetry ratio), this premise (for the mass ratio) and the copy.

\emph{Refutation condition.} The premise is false if the series' dynamics, or another premise of the register, gives the two towers different ceilings or different couplings at the ceiling. It becomes a theorem, and is retired as a premise, if the equality is derived, for example from a symmetry of the descent that acts on the parameters of the dynamics along the reversal orbit.
synthesis.common-ceiling-coupling-premis.technical:
The mirror tower copies this tower's content, so the two have the same beta-functions; that alone does not make their coupling values equal. The share of one needs more: a common ceiling $M$ and equal couplings there, which with equal running give equal confinement scales and composite spectra, $\Lambda_{2} = \Lambda_{6}$ and $c_{2} = c_{6}$. Indifference, scoped to sector labels, does not supply that equality, since a coupling is neither a label nor a state. This premise supplies it: the two members of the reversal orbit share one ceiling and every coupling of the copied theory at it.

It equates no state, so the mirror's temperature ratio stays free, and it acts along the reversal orbit only, saying nothing about the odd towers or the two-time fork. What it costs is one posited equality between undetermined parameters of two sectors; it fixes no coupling value. On it rests the mass factor of the mirror share and so the share of one; without it a coupling difference $\delta$ in $\alpha^{-1}$ at the ceiling moves the share by $e^{-2\pi\delta/b}$, within ten percent of one only for $|\delta| < 0.106$. It is refuted if the series gives the two towers different ceilings or couplings, and it becomes a theorem if a symmetry of the descent acting on parameters of the dynamics derives it.
synthesis.common-ceiling-coupling-premis.lay: The mirror world has exactly the same kinds of particles and forces as ours, but that does not by itself make its forces equally strong. For the mirror's matter to weigh exactly as much as ours, its forces must start out with the same strengths as ours at the highest energy the theory reaches. The series' indifference assumption, as now worded, only matches fixed labels such as a stored charge, not force strengths, so this assumption is added to say the two worlds start with equal strengths. It says nothing about how hot the mirror is, and nothing about the other hidden worlds. Its cost is plain: one of the 5.4 units of dark matter rests on it, and a small difference in starting strengths would change the mirror's share a great deal.
