synthesis.frozen-point-complement-window.formal:
Let $I$ be the frozen point of Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p1-single-frozen-point}, a vector of the tractor space $\R^{2,4}$ with $Q(I) = \Lambda/3$, and $I^{\perp}$ its orthogonal complement (Theorem \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-makes-stelle-west-vector}(i)). Call a tower's spacetime, a quadratic space of signature $(p,q)$, \emph{admitted} if it or its negative is isometric to a nondegenerate subspace of $I^{\perp}$; write (W) for the hypothesis that every populated tower's spacetime is admitted, and (W$_{T}$) for the same with the whole tractor space in place of $I^{\perp}$. A signature is causal if $\min(p,q) = 1$, and (C) is the single-clock filter of Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.towers-are-residues-single-clock-filter}: towers hold matter only at causal signatures. (W) is a candidate premise that restates the window of P3; it was found knowing the window the unit-ball fit needs and is a costed alternative to Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives}, not a derivation of it.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The complement; computed, exact.)} $I^{\perp}$ has signature $(1,4)$ if $\Lambda > 0$, $(2,3)$ if $\Lambda < 0$, and is $(1,3)$ plus the radical spanned by $I$ if $\Lambda = 0$. For $\Lambda > 0$ it has residue $1 - 4 \equiv 5 \pmod 8$: the frozen point's complement has the signature of the residue-$5$ tower.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Admission; proved.)} A nondegenerate $(a,b)$ is isometric to a subspace of a space whose nondegenerate part is $(P,Q)$ if and only if $a \le P$ and $b \le Q$ (Sylvester inertia, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii)); it is admitted if and only if this holds for $(a,b)$ or for $(b,a)$. The sign freedom is what Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p2-indifference} requires: it equates residues $r$ and $-r$, and $(p,q) \mapsto (q,p)$ maps the admitted set onto itself.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The window; proved, exact census.)} For $\Lambda > 0$ the admitted causal signatures are exactly
\[
(1,1),\ (2,1),\ (1,2),\ (3,1),\ (1,3),\ (4,1),\ (1,4),
\]
of residues $0, 1, 7, 2, 6, 3, 5$: one for each residue other than $4$, and that one is the residue's lowest causal member, of dimension $\min(r, 8-r) + 2$. No causal member of residue $4$ is admitted: its lowest, $(1,5)$ and $(5,1)$, has five directions of one sign. Under (W$_{T}$) the admitted causal set is the same for every sign of $\Lambda$. Under (W) and (C) no choice of representative remains, and the lowest-causal clause and the emptiness of residue $4$ both follow, the latter without the pairing reading of mass and without (G6). (W) alone admits the definite $(0,4)$ and $(4,0)$ of residue $4$ (and $(0,2)$, $(2,0)$ and other definite signatures), sterile by (C). Since (W$_{T}$) admits the same causal set, this clause does not need the frozen point.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(A cosmological constant that is not positive.)} For $\Lambda < 0$ and for $\Lambda = 0$ the admitted causal signatures under (W) are $(1,1)$, $(2,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(3,1)$, $(1,3)$: residues $3$ and $5$, the five-dimensional towers, are not admitted. Under (W) the five-dimensional towers exist because $\Lambda > 0$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Residue $0$.)} The admitted representative of residue $0$ is the causal $(1,1)$, where Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives} has the two-time $(2,2)$. Given the imported anomaly theorems of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.residues-zero-four-real-chirality-anomaly}(iii), single-ideal matter there has no conserved stress in the one metric's field and cannot source it; with one spinor ideal residue $0$ is therefore empty under (W) as well. What (W) leaves of the costed clause is the choice of a single chiral ideal at $(1,1)$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.frozen-point-complement-window.technical: The frozen point of the descent reduces the six-dimensional tractor space of the one metric to its five-dimensional complement, which for a positive cosmological constant has one time and four space directions, the signature of a five-dimensional tower. Suppose every tower's spacetime fits inside that complement as a nondegenerate subspace, up to an overall sign of the metric, which is the freedom the indifference premise needs to treat a tower and its mirror alike. By the inertia theorem a space fits exactly when it has at most one direction of one sign and at most four of the other. Among signatures with a single time this leaves seven: one for each residue except 4, always the residue's lowest causal member, and none of residue 4, whose lowest member needs five directions of one sign. The whole tractor space gives the same seven, so this census does not need the frozen point; it enters only in the statement for a cosmological constant that is not positive. Definite signatures such as $(0,4)$ also fit, and they are excluded by the single-clock filter, which the result uses alongside the hypothesis. So the window premise P3 and the emptiness of residue 4 would follow from one geometric hypothesis with the single-clock filter; the hypothesis restates the window of dimensions up to five, found knowing that the fit needs it, and is a costed alternative to P3, not a derivation; residue 0 is represented by the plane $(1,1)$, where the store's anomaly result already rules out single-ideal matter. With a negative or zero cosmological constant the complement is smaller and the five-dimensional towers would not exist.
synthesis.frozen-point-complement-window.lay: The series sorts its hidden worlds into eight families and has to say how many dimensions each one has; so far it simply picked, for each family, the option closest to our four. This result offers a single geometric reason instead. The moment that froze the universe's structure singles out a five-dimensional space, the same shape as one of the hidden worlds. If every hidden world must fit inside that space, then each family has exactly one possible shape with a single time, the smallest one, except one family, which cannot fit at all, and that is the family the dark-matter count needs to be empty. The reason is new and has to be adopted as an assumption; it was found while knowing which answer the count needs, so it explains the choice rather than predicting the number.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i).} By Theorem \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-makes-stelle-west-vector}(i) the frozen point is a vector $I$ of the tractor space, of signature $(2,4)$, with $Q(I) = \Lambda/3$. If $Q(I) \neq 0$ the space is the orthogonal sum of the line of $I$ and $I^{\perp}$, so by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii) the signature of $I^{\perp}$ is $(2,4)$ minus that of the line: $(1,4)$ for $Q(I) > 0$ and $(2,3)$ for $Q(I) < 0$. If $Q(I) = 0$, $I \in I^{\perp}$ spans its radical, and $I^{\perp}/\langle I\rangle$ is nondegenerate of signature $(1,3)$. The check builds the Gram matrix of an exact basis of $I^{\perp}$ from geometric products in $\Cl(2,4)$ and diagonalises it by congruence, for basis and non-basis $I$ of each sign of $Q(I)$, and confirms the three signatures and the residue $1 - 4 \equiv 5$.

\emph{(ii).} Let $W$ be a nondegenerate subspace of signature $(a,b)$ of a quadratic space $U$ with nondegenerate part $(P,Q)$ and radical $R$. Choose an orthogonal basis of $U$ as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii) and let $N$ be the span of its $Q$ negative and its radical vectors, on which the form is negative semidefinite. A positive-definite subspace $W_{+} \subset W$ of dimension $a$ meets $N$ only in zero, so $a + Q + \dim R \le P + Q + \dim R$, that is $a \le P$; likewise $b \le Q$. Conversely the span of $a$ positive and $b$ negative basis vectors realises $(a,b)$. A spacetime is admitted when $(a,b)$ or $(b,a)$ passes; the two conditions are exchanged by $(p,q) \mapsto (q,p)$, which is the reversal $r \mapsto -r$ along which Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p2-indifference} equates towers, so the admitted set is a union of reversal orbits, as P2 requires (a hypothesis without the sign freedom would admit this world $(1,3)$ and exclude its mirror $(3,1)$, which P2 populates). The check confirms exhaustively that no plane spanned by two vectors with entries in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ of $\R^{1,4}$ is positive definite, and that coordinate subspaces realise every allowed $(a,b)$.

\emph{(iii).} For $\Lambda > 0$, by (i) and (ii) a causal $(p,q)$ is admitted if and only if $\max(p,q) \le 4$, that is $p + q \le 5$. The causal signatures of dimension two to five are $(1,1)$; $(2,1)$, $(1,2)$; $(3,1)$, $(1,3)$; $(4,1)$, $(1,4)$, with residues $0$; $1$, $7$; $2$, $6$; $3$, $5$: seven signatures, seven distinct residues, residue $4$ absent. A causal signature of residue $r$ has dimension $m + 2$ with $m \equiv \pm r \pmod 8$, so the least is $\min(r, 8-r) + 2$, which is the dimension of the admitted one in each of the seven residues; residue $4$'s least is $6$, $(1,5)$ or $(5,1)$, with $\max(p,q) = 5$. The restriction to causal signatures is the filter (C): without it (W) also admits definite signatures, $(0,4)$ and $(4,0)$ among them, which (C) leaves sterile. For the whole tractor space, $(a,b)$ is admitted if and only if $\min(a,b) \le 2$ and $\max(a,b) \le 4$, which for causal signatures is again $\max(p,q) \le 4$: the same seven, for every $\Lambda$. The check enumerates all causal signatures up to dimension sixteen, compares with an independent enumeration of each residue's lowest causal members, and confirms the sets for $(1,4)$ and $(2,4)$ and their closure under reversal.

\emph{(iv).} For $\Lambda < 0$ the complement is $(2,3)$ and for $\Lambda = 0$ its nondegenerate part is $(1,3)$; in both, by (ii), a causal signature is admitted if and only if $\max(p,q) \le 3$, which removes $(4,1)$ and $(1,4)$, residues $3$ and $5$, and keeps the other five. Checked by the same enumeration.

\emph{(v).} The admitted member of residue $0$ is $(1,1)$ by (iii); there the pseudoscalar $e_{0}e_{1}$ squares to $+1$ and is central in the even algebra (checked), the really chiral case. Theorem \claimref{synthesis.residues-zero-four-real-chirality-anomaly}(iii), conditional on the imported anomaly theorems it names, shows that single-ideal matter at $(1,1)$, massive or massless, has no conserved rotation-covariant stress in the one metric's field and cannot source its field equations. Under (W) residue $0$ has no other admitted member, so with one ideal it holds no tower matter. With both chiral ideals admitted at $(1,1)$ that content is vector-like and anomaly-free (the same theorem's closing remark), so the single-ideal choice there is what remains of the costed clause; residue $4$ needs no clause at all.

\emph{Readings (argued; not part of the check).} (W) is a premise, not a consequence of P1: P1 freezes one $I$, and nothing in the series says that the towers' spacetimes live in its complement. Its support is that the complement is the frozen event's own space, the space whose bivectors are the gauge algebra of the series' MacDowell-Mansouri action (Theorem \claimref{dark-energy.frozen-point-makes-stelle-west-vector}(i): the reduced connection is a connection on $I^{\perp}$), so that (W) reads: every tower's spacetime is a nondegenerate subspace of the space on which gravity's action is a gauge theory; and that Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.nesting} already places this world's algebra inside the residue-$5$ tower's, the tower whose signature the complement has. It was looked for knowing that the window of dimensions up to five gives the unit-ball fit (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.towers-are-residues-single-clock-filter}(iii) lists that window), so it does not turn $5.364$ into a prediction; it replaces Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives}, its tie-break included, and the residue-$4$ half of the costed clause by one geometric hypothesis together with the single-clock filter (C); it is recorded as a costed alternative to P3, not adopted. Clause (iv) concerns universes with $\Lambda \le 0$, not a test of this one, since $\Lambda > 0$ was known when (W) was chosen: if (W) were adopted, the five-dimensional towers' share is tied to the sign of $\Lambda$, and a universe with $\Lambda \le 0$ would carry the unit-ball total $1 + 8/3 = 11/3$ under R1 to R3.

This result shows that when there is any ordinary matter anywhere in a connected region, that direction is the only one the field carries unchanged, up to an overall factor. The overall factor is not fixed by the argument and remains an assumption of the series.

abla$ is a constant multiple of $I$, $I' = c\, I$. Consequently, for $c

eq 0$ has the no-kernel property. The no-kernel property fails at points of Petrov type N (the null propagation vector is a kernel vector) and on regions where the Weyl part of the field strength vanishes (conformally flat derived metric); on the latter uniqueness itself fails, the tractor connection being flat with a six-dimensional space of parallel tractors.

abla$ here is the normal tractor connection, for which a tractor is parallel in the physical scale only on Einstein regions, so the application to towers above concerns frozen points parallel for that connection, that is Einstein regions. synthesis.frozen-point-unique-where-weyl.technical:
A parallel tractor is annihilated by the curvature of the tractor connection, which for a gravitational field on flat spacetime is the field strength of its $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field. In an Einstein scale that curvature acts as the Weyl tensor on the middle slot of a tractor and kills the other two, the Cotton terms vanishing because the Schouten tensor is a constant multiple of the metric. So where the Weyl tensor has no kernel vector the middle slot of every parallel tractor vanishes; by continuity this holds on an open set, where the parallel transport equations then force the top slot to be constant and the bottom slot to equal $\Lambda/6$ times it. A parallel tractor that is a constant multiple of $I$ on an open set is that multiple everywhere on a connected manifold. Hence the gravitational field admits one frozen point up to a constant factor.

For the towers this reduces the metric clause of P1 to a shared conformal structure, one point where the Weyl tensor has no kernel vector (any point near a black hole qualifies), and a common normalisation of the frozen points; the normalisation is the residue. Some hypothesis on the Weyl tensor is needed: where the Weyl part of the field strength vanishes uniqueness fails, a universe with vanishing Weyl part admitting two frozen points with different Einstein metrics (filed alongside, synthesis.two-frozen-points-conformally-flat); whether points of type N or III also allow several parallel tractors is not decided here. The argument holds for every value of $\Lambda$, zero included. The orientation clause of P1 is a separate matter not treated here.
synthesis.frozen-point-unique-where-weyl.lay: The series assumes that every hidden sector of the universe feels the same gravity, because they all share one special frozen point fixed at the universe's origin. This result shows that much of that assumption follows from the presence of genuine tidal gravity somewhere, such as around any black hole. Where gravity stretches and squeezes in the way it does near a star, the geometry permits only one frozen point, up to an overall scale. So if every sector's frozen point is compatible with the same shape of spacetime, they must all be the same point, apart from a single number per sector setting its scale. In a universe with no tidal gravity at all, by contrast, there would be room for several different frozen points.

synthesis.gauge-algebra-by-tower.technical:
T12 and T14c compute a gauge algebra the same way: take the smallest composite that can have mass, write it as a two-level hierarchy $K^{a} \otimes K^{b}$ (constituent slots tensor pair slots), and take the Lie algebra of the maps $A \otimes B$ that preserve both levels and the positive norm, modulo the common scalars. Assuming, as T14c does, that this algebra is the gauge algebra (premise H2) and that the construction transposes by its rule U (with the momentum premise H1 in dimensions three and five), the three inputs are where mass begins ($a$), how many ladder pairs a constituent carries ($b$, the complex Witt index of the conformal space) and which scalars the pairs carry ($K$: the reals when the real ladder pairs already suffice, otherwise the circle that the pair unit generates inside the constituents' field). With T14c's inputs the rule gives, in the six causal towers: $\C^{2} \otimes \C^{3}$ and $\su(2) \oplus \su(3) \oplus \uu(1)$ (dimension $12$) in this tower and its mirror; $\R^{2} \otimes \R^{2}$ and $\so(2) \oplus \so(2)$ (dimension $2$) in the three-dimensional towers; $\C^{1} \otimes \C^{3}$ and $\uu(3)$ (dimension $9$) in the five-dimensional towers.

In four dimensions T14c's inputs coincide with T12's (two constituents from T11's mass formula, three complex pairs, the unitary ladder), so the rule reproduces T12's theorem, including its seventeen-dimensional control at three constituents. The mirror's row is the same, as the mirror copy theorem requires; this agreement depends on taking the constituents' field from the even conformal ideal (where it is $\C$ in both signatures), not from the full Clifford module (quaternionic for ours, real for the mirror's). In five dimensions the constituents' field is the quaternions but the hierarchy's scalars are complex: the rule's $K$ is not the field. The check recomputes the onset count, the field, the real pairs and every automorphism algebra in exact arithmetic, and confirms that a different onset count, pair count or field gives a different algebra.
synthesis.gauge-algebra-by-tower.lay: The Standard-Model paper found our forces as the symmetries of the smallest composite that can have mass: two constituents, each with three internal slots, with complex numbers as scalars. The dark-matter note applied the same recipe to the other worlds of the series. This result writes the recipe down once and runs it in all six worlds that can hold matter, under the note's premises that the recipe gives the forces and that it carries over to other worlds in one stated way. In our world it gives back exactly the Standard Model's forces, as it must. In the mirror world it gives the same forces, as the series' mirror theorem says, but only because the recipe reads the scalars from the right part of the algebra. In the three-dimensional worlds it gives two independent forces like electromagnetism; in the five-dimensional worlds a colour force and one charge.

proofs.main:
\textit{The premises.}\enspace The identification of a tower's gauge algebra with the automorphism algebra of its minimal massive hierarchy is H2 (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.h2-identification}); the definition of a constituent, its field and the two factors' groups is Premise U (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.u-transposition-rule}), clauses U1 to U3; in dimensions three and five the constituent's momentum is H1 (\claimref{dark-tower-matter.h1-momentum}), which in dimension four is T12's own setting. Nothing else is assumed. The six causal towers and their signatures are those of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}.

\emph{The inputs, tower by tower.}  The field $F$ is read from Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}: $\C$ at $r = 6, 2$, $\R$ at $r = 1, 7$, $\HH$ at $r = 3, 5$. The check recomputes it as $f\Cl^{0}(V)f$ with $f = \tfrac12(1 + e_{i}e_{j})$, $Q(e_{i}) = 1$, $Q(e_{j}) = -1$, the field acting on the right of $S = \Cl^{0}(V)f$ as in Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.ladder}: it has real dimension $1$, $2$ (commutative) and $4$ (not commutative) in the three pairs of towers.

The onset count $a$ is Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins}: in dimensions three and four the reversion pairing on $S$ is alternating, a single constituent is massless and mass begins at two; in dimension five it is not alternating and mass begins at one. The check recomputes the criterion: the symmetrised pairing $\rev{\psi}_{1}\psi_{2} + \rev{\psi}_{2}\psi_{1}$ vanishes on every pair of basis elements of $S$ exactly when $n \le 4$.

The pair count $b$ and the pairs' scalars are Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.pairs}: the real Witt index of $\hatV$ is $2$ in every causal tower and the complex one is $\lfloor (n+2)/2 \rfloor$, so $b = 2$ with real pairs for $n = 3$ and $b = 3$, the third pair needing a complex unit, for $n = 4, 5$. By U3 that unit lies in $F$. For $F = \C$ (this tower and the mirror) it is fixed up to sign and its centraliser in $F$ is $F$ itself, so $K = \C$. For $F = \HH$ Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.third-pairs-unit-five-dimensions}(i) and (iii) give the centraliser of the pair algebra in $\HH$ as $\mathrm{span}\{1, u\}$, so again $K = \C$; the check confirms in $f\Cl^{0}(V)f$ that the centraliser of a unit $u$ is two-dimensional, and that in the commutator space $[F, F] = \mathfrak{sp}(1)$, the slot algebra of one quaternionic constituent, it is one-dimensional, the circle of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.gauge-algebras}(ii). For $F = \R$ no unit is needed, and none would be available: the case in which the pairs need a unit and $F$ supplies none does not occur among the causal towers.

The slot group is the momentum-preserving group of $a$ constituents, $O(a)$, $U(a)$ or $Sp(a)$ as $F = \R, \C, \HH$ (Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.ladder}), cut in the quaternionic case to the subgroup commuting with $u$, which for $a = 1$ is $U(1)$; the pair group is, by U2, the unitary group over $K$ of the $b$ pairs, $O(b)$ or $U(b)$.

\emph{The automorphism algebras.}  An automorphism of $K^{a} \otimes_{K} K^{b}$ is $A \otimes B$; $A \otimes B = 1$ forces $A = \lambda 1$, $B = \lambda^{-1}1$ with $\lambda$ a unit scalar of $K$ (the argument of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}, a linear map fixing every line being a scalar). Over $\C$ the kernel is a circle and $\mathfrak{g}_{r} = (\uu(a) \oplus \uu(b))/\uu(1) = \su(a) \oplus \su(b) \oplus \uu(1)$, of dimension $a^{2} + b^{2} - 1$, as in Proposition \claimref{standard-model.four-dimensions-forces-converse}(2); over $\R$ it is $\{\pm 1\}$, discrete, and $\mathfrak{g}_{r} = \so(a) \oplus \so(b)$, of dimension $\tfrac12 a(a-1) + \tfrac12 b(b-1)$. The check computes each $\mathfrak{g}_{r}$ as the image of $\mathfrak{g}(a, K) \oplus \mathfrak{g}(b, K)$ acting by $X \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes Y$ on the real form of $K^{a} \otimes K^{b}$, as an exact rank, for all $a, b \le 3$ over both fields; it confirms that every image element is antisymmetric (it preserves the norm) and, over $\C$, commutes with the complex structure, and it computes the centre and the derived algebra: for $\C^{2} \otimes \C^{3}$ dimension $12$, centre $1$, derived algebra $11 = 3 + 8$, the images of $\su(2)$ and $\su(3)$; for $\C^{3} \otimes \C^{3}$, $17$, $1$, $16$; for $\C^{1} \otimes \C^{3}$, $9$, $1$, $8$; for $\R^{2} \otimes \R^{2}$, $2$, abelian. Substituting the inputs gives the table.

\emph{(i) The four-dimensional row.}  At $r = 6$ the inputs are T12's. Two constituents: Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins}(i) in dimension four is T11's two-constituent formula (Proposition \claimref{mass.mass-symplectic-area-two-twistor-formula}) written in the even algebra, the pairing $\rev{\psi}_{1}\psi_{2}$ in a copy of $\C$ playing the bracket (Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.four-dimensional-case-t11s-formula}). Three pairs: the complex Witt index $3$ of Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.pairs}(ii) is Lemma \claimref{standard-model.pair-count-dimension} at $n = 4$. The field and the groups: $F = \C$, and by T14c's Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.why-u} any complex unit commuting with the spin action, the complexification's included, acts on the constituent ideal as $\pm I_{6}$, so T14c's real construction and T12's complexified one give the same $\C$; the slot group $U(2)$ of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.ladder} is T12's $U(2)$ (Proposition \claimref{standard-model.internal-symmetry-ladder}), and U2 takes the pair group $U(3)$ as T12 does. So the rule's hierarchy is $\C^{2} \otimes \C^{3}$, with automorphism algebra $\su(2) \oplus \su(3) \oplus \uu(1)$ of dimension $12$: Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}. At $a = 3$ the same computation gives its seventeen-dimensional control. The rows $r = 1, 7$ (dimension $2$) and $r = 3, 5$ (dimension $9$) are not the Standard Model algebra, by Proposition \claimref{standard-model.four-dimensions-forces-converse}(2) for the complex rows and by dimension for the real ones.

\emph{(ii) The mirror row.}  At $r = 2$, signature $(3,1)$ and conformal signature $(4,2)$, every input is the same as at $r = 6$. The field is $\C$ by Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}; the check confirms that the centre of $\Cl^{0}(4,2)$, like that of $\Cl^{0}(2,4)$, is $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{6}\}$ with $I_{6}^{2} = -1$, and that $e_{K} \mapsto (-1)^{|K|/2}e_{K}$ is an algebra isomorphism of the even algebras in both the tower and the conformal signatures (Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirror-algebra}(i)). The onset count is two (dimension four), the pairs are three and complex (Proposition \claimref{dark-tower-matter.pairs}(ii) names the mirror), and the ladder is $U(n)$ (Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.ladder} names the mirror). So the mirror's row is this tower's, $\su(2) \oplus \su(3) \oplus \uu(1)$, which is the gauge algebra of the mirror copy theorem, Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}(i). The two derivations are independent: T14 runs T12's chain on the reversed data over $V_{\C}$, T14c's rule reads the real even algebras. The agreement uses U1. The commutant of the full Clifford module, computed in the check with a primitive idempotent, is $\HH$ for $\Cl(1,3)$ and $\R$ for $\Cl(3,1)$: with that reading the mirror's pairs would need a complex unit that $\R$ does not supply, and the two rows would not agree, which is T14c's reason (Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.why-u}) for rejecting it; that commutant is T14's ground type, a different object from the constituent field (Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.t14s-types-are-different-commutant}). Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.mirror-algebra}(ii) sends the mirror's conformal unit to $-I_{6}$: the mirror's $\C$ is ours with the opposite orientation, which conjugates the representations and leaves the algebra unchanged.

\emph{(iii) The odd rows}  are Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.gauge-algebras}: (i) for $r = 1, 7$ and (ii) for $r = 3, 5$.

\emph{(iv) $F$ and $K$.}  In the five-dimensional towers $F = \HH$ and $K = \C$, by the centraliser computation above. A rule that took $K = F$ there would keep the quaternionic slot group: that is the external-unit branch of T14c's Remark \claimref{note.dark-tower-matter.branches-break-u-what-they-give}, which breaks U3 and is not this rule.

\emph{What fails with wrong inputs.}  The table is sensitive to each input: three constituents in dimension four give $17$, two pairs give $7$, real pairs ($\R^{2} \otimes \R^{3}$) give $4$, one constituent gives $9$; none is $12$. In the check, replacing the onset count, the pair count, the field column or the scalars rule by another value makes it fail.

synthesis.imported-alvarez-gaume-witten-.formal:
Let $\psi$ be a chiral (Weyl) spin-$\tfrac12$ field in even dimension $n$, coupled to a gravitational field (the rotation-gauge field, with field strength $\mathcal{R}$, the curvature) and to a gauge field with field strength $F$ acting in a representation $\rho$, whose matrices, like all numbers here, have entries in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, the scalar field of an abstract complex matrix algebra. Its local anomalies, the failure of the effective action to be invariant under infinitesimal rotation-gauge (local Lorentz and coordinate) and gauge transformations, are given by descent from the anomaly polynomial
\[
I_{n+2} \;=\; \Bigl[\hat{A}(\mathcal{R})\,\mathrm{tr}_{\rho}\,e^{I_4F/2\pi}\Bigr]_{n+2},
\qquad
\hat{A} \;=\; \prod_{i}\frac{x_{i}/2}{\sinh(x_{i}/2)} \;=\; 1 - \frac{p_{1}}{24} + \frac{7p_{1}^{2} - 4p_{2}}{5760} - \dots,
\]
the degree-$(n+2)$ part of the $\hat{A}$ genus (in the Chern roots $x_{i}$ of the curvature, Pontryagin classes $p_{j}$) times the Chern character, which is the index density of the Dirac operator in dimension $n+2$; the opposite chirality contributes with the opposite sign. The pure-gauge part is $\mathrm{tr}_{\rho}(I_4F/2\pi)^{(n+2)/2}/((n+2)/2)!$ and the purely gravitational part is $\dim\rho$ times the degree-$(n+2)$ part of $\hat{A}$, which is nonzero only when $n + 2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. So purely gravitational anomalies occur only in dimensions $n = 4k + 2$, where Weyl fields of spin $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac32$ and self-dual antisymmetric tensor fields carry them, and such fields cannot be coupled to gravity in those dimensions unless the contributions of the different fields cancel. A chiral content is free of local anomalies when the sum of its anomaly polynomials vanishes. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{AGW1984}; the polynomial's normalisation as remembered.
synthesis.imported-alvarez-gaume-witten-.technical: The theorem says which field contents can be consistently coupled to gravity and to gauge fields at the quantum level. Each chiral fermion contributes a characteristic polynomial in the curvature and the gauge field strength, of total degree two more than the dimension, read from the index theorem for the Dirac operator in that higher dimension. The theory is consistent only if the contributions of all its fields add to zero. Because the curvature enters only through Pontryagin classes, of degree a multiple of four, a purely gravitational anomaly needs the dimension plus two to be a multiple of four: dimensions two, six, ten and so on. In Gauge Theory Gravity the gravitational part is the anomaly of the rotation-gauge field. The series uses it to ask whether the matter of a tower of dimension two or six can be of one chirality.
synthesis.imported-alvarez-gaume-witten-.lay: Some quantum theories that look consistent turn out to break their own symmetries once quantum effects are included; these breakdowns are called anomalies. Alvarez-Gaume and Witten worked out exactly when a particle with a handedness spoils the consistency of its coupling to gravity: it can happen only in two, six, ten and so on dimensions, and a theory is safe only if the contributions of its particles cancel.

imported_from.citation: L. Alvarez-Gaum'e and E. Witten, Gravitational anomalies, Nucl. Phys. B 234 (1984), 269--330.

synthesis.imported-bardeen-zumino-consis.formal: For a chiral field coupled to a gauge field $A$ and to a gravitational field (the rotation-gauge field), the anomaly appears in two forms. The \emph{consistent} anomaly is the variation of the effective action under the infinitesimal symmetry; it satisfies the Wess-Zumino consistency condition and is in general not covariant. The \emph{covariant} anomaly is the covariant divergence of a current (or stress tensor) that transforms covariantly. The covariant current is the consistent current plus a local polynomial $X(A)$ in the potentials (the Bardeen-Zumino polynomial), so both forms are correct, for the covariant divergences of different currents; the covariant anomaly is read from the anomaly polynomial $I_{n+2}$ directly and vanishes exactly when the consistent one does. For gravitational anomalies the two forms correspond to two different energy-momentum tensors, the covariant one being the stress that enters a covariantly conserved source. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{BardeenZumino1984}.
synthesis.imported-bardeen-zumino-consis.technical: An anomaly can be written in two ways that look different. The consistent form comes from how the quantum effective action changes under a symmetry and obeys an integrability condition but is not covariant; the covariant form is the divergence of a current or stress that transforms properly. Bardeen and Zumino showed that the two currents differ by a local polynomial in the potentials, so the two forms describe the same obstruction, and that for gravity they belong to different stress tensors. A field theory's matter can source covariant field equations only through a covariantly conserved stress, so the covariant form is the one that decides whether it can.
synthesis.imported-bardeen-zumino-consis.lay: When a quantum symmetry breaks down, physicists can describe the breakdown in two ways. Bardeen and Zumino showed how the two descriptions are related, and which one matters when asking whether a kind of matter can act as a source of gravity.

imported_from.citation: W. A. Bardeen and B. Zumino, Consistent and covariant anomalies in gauge and gravitational theories, Nucl. Phys. B 244 (1984), 421--453.

synthesis.imported-high-temperature-symm.formal: In a gauge theory with scalar fields $\phi_{a}$ at temperature $T$ well above the masses, the one-loop thermal correction to the effective potential adds $\tfrac12 c_{ab}T^{2}\phi_{a}\phi_{b}$, with $c_{ab}$ set by the gauge, Yukawa and quartic couplings. When every eigenvalue of $c$ is positive (as for a single scalar, or for positive cross-couplings) the broken symmetry is restored above a critical temperature of order its breaking scale. With several scalars, negative cross-couplings can make an eigenvalue of $c$ negative while the zero-temperature potential stays bounded below, and then a symmetry broken at $T = 0$ stays broken at high temperature, or a symmetric one breaks (symmetry non-restoration, inverse breaking). In minimal SU(5) a range of the Higgs potential's parameters keeps the grand-unified symmetry broken at high temperature, so the transition that would produce monopoles does not occur. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{KirzhnitsLinde1972}, \cite{DolanJackiw1974}, \cite{Weinberg1974} (restoration and its exceptions); \cite{DvaliMelfoSenjanovic1995} (the SU(5) range and the monopole problem).
synthesis.imported-high-temperature-symm.technical: Heating usually undoes symmetry breaking: the thermal bath gives the Higgs fields a positive mass squared proportional to the temperature squared, which wins over the negative one that breaks the symmetry, so above a critical temperature the symmetric phase returns and the broken phase forms again on cooling. Weinberg observed that this is not universal: with several scalar fields and negative cross-couplings the thermal mass can be negative in some direction, and the symmetry stays broken however hot the bath. Dvali, Melfo and Senjanovic found such a range in minimal SU(5) and noted that it removes the transition that would make monopoles. Whether the series' Pati-Salam breaking is restored at high temperature therefore depends on its scalar couplings.
synthesis.imported-high-temperature-symm.lay: A hot enough universe usually restores the symmetries that are broken today, so they must break again as it cools, making magnetic poles. In some theories, with the right kind of interactions between the Higgs fields, heat does not restore the symmetry, and the problem is avoided.

imported_from.citation: D. A. Kirzhnits and A. D. Linde, Macroscopic consequences of the Weinberg model, Phys. Lett. B 42 (1972), 471--474.
L. Dolan and R. Jackiw, Symmetry behavior at finite temperature, Phys. Rev. D 9 (1974), 3320--3341.
S. Weinberg, Gauge and global symmetries at high temperature, Phys. Rev. D 9 (1974), 3357--3378.
G. Dvali, A. Melfo and G. Senjanovic, Is there a monopole problem?, Phys. Rev. Lett. 75 (1995), 4559--4562; arXiv:hep-ph/9507230.

synthesis.imported-kibble-preskill-causa.formal: When a phase with topologically nontrivial vacuum manifold forms by a causal process (a thermal transition at $T_{c}$, or any formation in which the Higgs field's orientation is uncorrelated beyond a length $\xi$), the orientations in distinct correlation volumes are independent, and a defect forms at a meeting point with a probability fixed by the geometry of the vacuum manifold. Causality bounds the correlation length by the horizon distance, $\xi \lesssim H^{-1}$ at formation. For monopoles the probability is about $p \approx \tfrac{1}{10}$ per correlation volume, so the initial number density is at least about $p\,\xi^{-3} \ge p\,H^{3}$, and with entropy density $s$ the ratio $n_{M}/s$ is at least about $p\,H^{3}/s$ at formation. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Kibble1976} (the causal mechanism); \cite{Preskill1979} (the monopole estimate).
synthesis.imported-kibble-preskill-causa.technical: The Kibble mechanism: regions that have not been in causal contact cannot coordinate the direction in which a symmetry breaks, so where independent regions meet, topological defects are left. For monopoles Preskill estimated about one per ten correlation volumes, and the correlation length is at most the horizon distance. So a causal transition leaves at least about $p H^{3}$ monopoles per unit volume, a lower bound that depends only on the temperature at which the broken phase forms. It is the estimate that makes the monopole problem of grand unification: in a universe that is not diluted afterwards, the predicted abundance far exceeds what is observed.
synthesis.imported-kibble-preskill-causa.lay: As the early universe cooled and a unified force split apart, distant regions could not agree on how to split it, and magnetic poles were left where they met. This estimate says how many: about one for every ten regions the size of the horizon, or more.

imported_from.citation: T. W. B. Kibble, Topology of cosmic domains and strings, J. Phys. A 9 (1976), 1387--1398.
J. P. Preskill, Cosmological production of superheavy magnetic monopoles, Phys. Rev. Lett. 43 (1979), 1365--1368.

synthesis.imported-macro-monopole-flux-l.formal:
The MACRO experiment at Gran Sasso, using its scintillation counters, limited streamer tubes and nuclear track detectors separately and in combination, found no magnetic monopole candidate and set the 90\% confidence upper limit
\[
\mathcal{F} \;<\; 1.4 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}
\]
on the local flux of magnetic monopoles over the velocity range $4 \times 10^{-5} < \beta < 1$, below the Parker bound over the whole range where grand-unified monopoles are expected (read for magnetic charge of one Dirac unit or more, as remembered). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{MACRO2002}.
synthesis.imported-macro-monopole-flux-l.technical: MACRO was a large underground detector built in part to look for magnetic monopoles from the early universe. Its final analysis found none and limited their flux through the Earth to below $1.4 \times 10^{-16}$ per square centimetre per second per steradian, for any speed from a few times $10^{-5}$ of light speed upwards. Converted to a number density with the monopoles' speed, at least the halo's virial speed for galactic monopoles, this bounds the monopole-to-entropy ratio today, the bound a causal grand-unified transition must meet.
synthesis.imported-macro-monopole-flux-l.lay: A large underground experiment looked for magnetic poles left over from the early universe and found none. Its result limits how many can be passing through the Earth, and so how many the early universe can have made.

imported_from.citation: M. Ambrosio et al. (MACRO Collaboration), Final results of magnetic monopole searches with the MACRO experiment, Eur. Phys. J. C 25 (2002), 511--522; arXiv:hep-ex/0207020.

synthesis.imported-monopoles-second-homo.formal: Let a gauge theory with connected, simply connected compact group $G$ be broken by a Higgs field to a closed subgroup $H$ at scale $v$. The exact homotopy sequence of $H \to G \to G/H$, with $\pi_{2}(G) = 0$ and $\pi_{1}(G) = 0$, gives $\pi_{2}(G/H) \cong \pi_{1}(H)$, and every nontrivial class is carried by a finite-energy ('t Hooft-Polyakov) monopole, of mass of order $4\pi v/g$ for gauge coupling $g$; the monopoles of the classes that generate the group are stable. For $G = SU(4) \times SU(2)_{L} \times SU(2)_{R}$ broken to the Standard Model group (the unbroken $U(1)$ of electromagnetism lying inside $H$), $\pi_{1}(H)$ contains $\mathbb{Z}$, and the lightest monopole carries two Dirac units of magnetic charge, $4\pi/e$, together with a colour magnetic field. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Preskill1984} (the homotopy classification, as remembered); \cite{LazaridesMaggShafi1980} (the Pati-Salam monopole).
synthesis.imported-monopoles-second-homo.technical: Whether a symmetry breaking leaves magnetic monopoles is a topological question: with a simply connected unbroken-phase group, the monopole charges are the closed loops of the residual group $H$ that cannot be shrunk, $\pi_{1}(H)$. Every grand-unified breaking to the Standard Model group has $\pi_{1}(H) \supseteq \mathbb{Z}$, because electromagnetism's circle cannot be unwound, so it leaves stable superheavy monopoles. For the Pati-Salam group the lightest carries twice the Dirac charge. This is a topological result, stated for the gauge groups; the series uses it for its own Pati-Salam chain.
synthesis.imported-monopoles-second-homo.lay: When the forces of a unified theory separate as the universe cools, knots in the fields can be left behind that behave as isolated magnetic poles. Topology says when this must happen; for the unification scheme the series uses, it must, and each pole carries twice the smallest magnetic charge Dirac allowed.

imported_from.citation: J. Preskill, Magnetic monopoles, Ann. Rev. Nucl. Part. Sci. 34 (1984), 461--530.
G. Lazarides, M. Magg and Q. Shafi, Phase transitions and magnetic monopoles in SO(10), Phys. Lett. B 97 (1980), 87--92.

synthesis.imported-preskill-monopole-ann.formal: In a radiation-dominated plasma, monopoles and antimonopoles annihilate by diffusing towards one another through the charged particles of the bath and capturing into bound states. The annihilation rate per monopole is proportional to $n_{M}$ and falls faster than the expansion rate once $n_{M}/s$ is below a value of order $10^{-10}$ (for grand-unified monopole masses; Preskill's estimate grows with the monopole mass, a dependence cited here from memory). So annihilation reduces an initial $n_{M}/s$ above that value to about that value, and does not change one below it. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Preskill1979}.
synthesis.imported-preskill-monopole-ann.technical: Monopoles and antimonopoles left by a transition can find each other and annihilate, but only while they are dense: the rate of encounters drops with the density, and below a monopole-to-entropy ratio of order $10^{-10}$ for grand-unified masses it is slower than the expansion. So annihilation can cure an overabundance only down to that value, which is still far above what observation allows; it cannot lower an abundance that starts below it.
synthesis.imported-preskill-monopole-ann.lay: Magnetic poles and their opposites can destroy each other, but only while they are crowded together. Preskill showed that this stops long before their number is small enough to agree with observation.

imported_from.citation: J. P. Preskill, Cosmological production of superheavy magnetic monopoles, Phys. Rev. Lett. 43 (1979), 1365--1368.

synthesis.imported-two-dimensional-covar.formal:
Let a chiral field live on a two-dimensional gravitational field with derived metric $g$, scalar curvature $R$ and Christoffel symbols $\Gamma$. For right-handed (one-chirality) fields the consistent gravitational anomaly is
\[
\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu}{}_{\nu} \;=\; \frac{1}{96\pi\sqrt{-g}}\,\epsilon^{\beta\delta}\partial_{\delta}\partial_{\alpha}\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\nu\beta},
\]
and the covariant anomaly, the covariant divergence of the covariant stress tensor $\tilde{T}$, is
\[
\nabla_{\mu}\tilde{T}^{\mu}{}_{\nu} \;=\; -\frac{1}{96\pi\sqrt{-g}}\,\epsilon_{\mu\nu}\,\partial^{\mu}R
\]
(in the paper's conventions for $\epsilon$ and $R$). In Gauge Theory Gravity on the flat plane $\R^{1,1}$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}, $d = 2$), with $I_{2}$ the unit bivector of the plane, the covariant form says that the covariant divergence $\dot{\tilde{T}}(\dot{D})$ of the covariant stress-energy map is $\pm\frac{1}{96\pi}$ times the $I_{2}$-dual of the physical gradient $\hb^{T}(\nabla R)$ of the scalar curvature, the sign fixed by the source's conventions. For a content with central charges $c_{L}$ and $c_{R}$ of left- and right-moving fields the coefficient is proportional to $c_{R} - c_{L}$, so the covariant stress is conserved wherever $c_{L} = c_{R}$ or $R$ is constant, and not conserved where $c_{L} \neq c_{R}$ and $R$ varies. The store's scalar curvature has the source's sign (de Sitter positive, conventions C6 and C7), so $R$ carries over unchanged; whether the divergence vanishes does not depend on any sign. The covariant form is the one used to derive the Hawking flux from the anomaly near a horizon; Robinson and Wilczek's original derivation used the consistent form. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{IsoUmetsuWilczek2006} (equations (13) and (14)); \cite{RobinsonWilczek2005}.
synthesis.imported-two-dimensional-covar.technical: In two dimensions a field that moves only one way (one chirality) cannot have a conserved stress tensor on a gravitational field whose scalar curvature varies: the covariant divergence of its stress is proportional to the gradient of the curvature, with coefficient $1/96\pi$ in the paper's normalisation, and to the difference of the left- and right-moving central charges. Iso, Umetsu and Wilczek wrote this covariant form and used it to derive the Hawking flux from the anomaly in the near-horizon two-dimensional sections of a black hole, extending Robinson and Wilczek's derivation, which used the consistent form. The series uses it to ask whether one-chirality matter on the planes of the one metric can source the field equations.
synthesis.imported-two-dimensional-covar.lay: In a world with one space and one time dimension, particles that move only in one direction cannot carry a conserved energy and momentum if gravity bends that world unevenly. This result gives the precise formula. It is also a known route to Hawking radiation from black holes.

imported_from.citation: S. Iso, H. Umetsu and F. Wilczek, Hawking radiation from charged black holes via gauge and gravitational anomalies, Phys. Rev. Lett. 96 (2006), 151302; arXiv:hep-th/0602146.
S. P. Robinson and F. Wilczek, A relationship between Hawking radiation and gravitational anomalies, Phys. Rev. Lett. 95 (2005), 011303; arXiv:gr-qc/0502074.

synthesis.invariant-forms-on-spinor-idea.formal:
Let $V$ have nondegenerate signature $(p,q)$, $n = p + q$, and let $f$, $f'$ be idempotents of $\Cl^{0}(V)$ with left ideals $S = \Cl^{0}(V)f$ and $S' = \Cl^{0}(V)f'$, on which the spin Lie algebra acts by left multiplication by bivectors. Call a real bilinear form $B : S \times S' \to \R$ \emph{invariant} if $B(b\psi, \phi) + B(\psi, b\phi) = 0$ for every bivector $b$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Every dimension and every nondegenerate signature $(p,q)$; proved.)} $B$ is invariant if and only if
\[
B(\psi, \phi) \;=\; B\bigl(f, \rev{\psi}\phi\bigr) \qquad \text{for all } \psi \in S,\ \phi \in S',
\]
that is, if and only if $B$ is a linear functional of the reversion pairing $\rev{\psi}\phi \in S'$; and every linear functional of the reversion pairing is invariant. So the invariant forms on $S \times S'$ vanish identically exactly when $\rev{\psi}\phi = 0$ for all $\psi \in S$, $\phi \in S'$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Every dimension; proved.)} At a causal signature of residue $0$ or $4$ ($n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, $\omega^{2} = +1$), every invariant form on an ideal of one chirality vanishes identically, and so does every invariant form between any number of copies of that ideal; between the two chiralities invariant forms exist. At every other causal residue the spinor ideal of Definition \claimref{obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-momentum} carries a nonzero invariant form. Hence with one spinor ideal per tower no mass term exists at residues $0$ and $4$ in any dimension: no derivative-free spin-invariant bilinear in the field, of Dirac or Majorana type, real or complex.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Computed, exact.)} At the nine causal signatures of dimensions two to six (both chiralities in dimensions two and six) the invariant forms on $S \times S$ have dimension $0$ at $(1,1)$, $(1,5)$, $(5,1)$, $1$ at $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $2$ at $(1,3)$, $(3,1)$ and $4$ at $(1,4)$, $(4,1)$, and in each case they are spanned by the blade components of $\rev{\psi}\phi$; on $S_{+} \times S_{-}$ the dimension is $1$ at $(1,1)$ and $4$ at $(1,5)$, $(5,1)$. At $n = 3, 4$ every invariant form is alternating; at $n = 5$ the space has a basis of one symmetric and three alternating forms.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Computed, exact.)} The least number of constituents of one ideal carrying a nonzero invariant pairing is one when some invariant form is not alternating, two when all are alternating and some is nonzero, and none when there is no invariant form. By (iii) it is two, two and one at $n = 3, 4, 5$, the thresholds of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins}, and none at $n = 2$ and $6$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the pairing reading of mass in dimensions $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ (the costed clause of Observation \claimref{dark-matter.status-rule}(vi), resting on Proposition \claimref{synthesis.reversion-pairing-vanishes-residues-zero-four}) is not a choice among pairings: it is the reading that mass is carried by an invariant pairing of constituents, as in T14c's mass laws and in a field mass term, and under it one ideal at residues $0$ and $4$ carries no mass in any dimension. The only alternative left is the momentum reading, which assigns an invariant mass to pairs of quanta that individually have no mass term. Which of the two readings of mass the series takes remains the clause; which pairing is no longer open.
synthesis.invariant-forms-on-spinor-idea.technical: A mass term for a field is a quadratic expression in the field, without derivatives, that every rotation and boost leaves unchanged: a spin-invariant bilinear form on the spinor ideal. Invariance under the bivectors propagates to the whole even subalgebra, since products of bivectors span it, in the form $B(a\psi, \phi) = B(\psi, \rev{a}\phi)$. Writing $\psi = af$ and using the idempotent twice gives $B(\psi, \phi) = B(f, \rev{\psi}\phi)$: every invariant form is read off the reversion pairing, and the reversion pairing is the only one there is. At residues $0$ and $4$ the reversion pairing vanishes on one chirality in every dimension, so no invariant form survives there, and a single chiral ideal, or any number of copies of it, has no mass term of any kind; the two chiralities together do pair. Exact computation at the nine lowest causal signatures confirms the factorisation and shows that the symmetry type of the invariant forms (alternating in dimensions three and four, with a symmetric member in five) reproduces the series' thresholds for where mass begins.
synthesis.invariant-forms-on-spinor-idea.lay: For a particle to have mass, the equations describing it need a term that pairs the particle's field with itself in a way that looks the same to every observer. This result shows that for the building blocks the dark-matter papers use, all such pairings are versions of a single one, the pairing the series already uses for mass. In the two families of hidden worlds that the dark-matter count needs to be empty, that pairing is identically zero in every dimension, so a world built from one kind of building block can have no mass term at all there. What remained a choice of pairing is now no choice; what remains open is only whether mass must come from a pairing at all.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} Let $B$ be invariant. For a bivector $b$, $\rev{b} = -b$, so invariance reads $B(b\psi, \phi) = B(\psi, \rev{b}\phi)$. If the identity $B(a\psi, \phi) = B(\psi, \rev{a}\phi)$ holds for $a$ and for $a'$, it holds for $aa'$: $B(aa'\psi, \phi) = B(a'\psi, \rev{a}\phi) = B(\psi, \rev{a'}\rev{a}\phi) = B(\psi, \rev{(aa')}\phi)$; it holds for scalars and is linear in $a$. Every even blade is a product of bivector blades, $e_{i_{1}}e_{i_{2}}\cdots e_{i_{2k-1}}e_{i_{2k}} = (e_{i_{1}}e_{i_{2}})\cdots(e_{i_{2k-1}}e_{i_{2k}})$, so the identity holds for every $a \in \Cl^{0}(V)$ (the check confirms for $2 \le n \le 7$, all signatures, that products of bivector blades reach every even blade). Every element of $S$ is $\psi = af$ for some $a \in \Cl^{0}(V)$, and $f = ff$. Hence, for $\phi \in S'$,
\[
B(af, \phi) = B(f, \rev{a}\phi) = B(ff, \rev{a}\phi) = B\bigl(f, \rev{f}\rev{a}\phi\bigr) = B\bigl(f, \rev{(af)}\phi\bigr) = B(f, \rev{\psi}\phi),
\]
where $\rev{\psi}\phi = \rev{f}\rev{a}\phi$ lies in $\Cl^{0}(V)f' = S'$, the domain of $B(f, \cdot)$. Conversely, for any linear $\lambda$ on $\Cl^{0}(V)$ and bivector $b$, $\lambda(\rev{(b\psi)}\phi + \rev{\psi}b\phi) = \lambda(\rev{\psi}(\rev{b} + b)\phi) = 0$. So the invariant forms are exactly the linear functionals of the reversion pairing, and they all vanish if and only if the pairing does.

\emph{(ii)} By Proposition \claimref{synthesis.reversion-pairing-vanishes-residues-zero-four}(i), at a causal signature the conditions $n$ even, $\omega^{2} = +1$, $\rev{\omega} = -\omega$ hold exactly at residues $0$ and $4$, where $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$; there $P_{\pm} = \tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$ are central idempotents of $\Cl^{0}(V)$ with $\rev{P_{+}} = P_{-}$. For $\psi, \phi$ in ideals of chirality $+$ (in $\Cl^{0}(V)P_{+}$, any number of copies), $\rev{\psi}\phi = \rev{\psi}P_{+}\phi$ and $\rev{\psi} = \rev{(\psi P_{+})} = P_{-}\rev{\psi}$ with $P_{-}$ central, so $\rev{\psi}\phi = \rev{\psi}P_{-}P_{+}\phi = 0$; by (i) every invariant form vanishes. Between the chiralities $\rev{P_{+}}P_{-} = P_{-} \neq 0$ and the cross forms exist (computed in (iii)). At the other causal residues the reversion pairing on $S$ is not identically zero (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.reversion-pairing-vanishes-residues-zero-four}(ii)), and each of its blade components is an invariant form by the converse in (i). A mass term of a field valued in $S$ (or in several copies of $S$, or a complex combination, read as a real form on the underlying real space) is a derivative-free bilinear expression invariant under the connected spin group, hence under its Lie algebra; for anticommuting fields it uses an alternating form, for a pair of fields any form. Every such form is invariant in the sense above, so none is nonzero at residues $0$ and $4$ for one ideal. The dimension-six ideal is that of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.lowest-causal-residues-zero-four-content}, with the chiral factor in $f$.

\emph{(iii)} The check builds $S$ at each signature as in Definition \claimref{obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-momentum}, writes the left action of each basis bivector as an exact matrix on a basis of $S$, and solves the linear conditions $B(b\psi, \phi) + B(\psi, b\phi) = 0$ for the matrix of $B$; the kernel dimensions are those stated. It then forms, for every blade $C$, the bilinear form $\psi, \phi \mapsto$ (coefficient of $C$ in $\rev{\psi}\phi$), and verifies that these forms span a space of the same dimension and that adjoining the kernel does not raise the rank, which is (i) in coordinates. At $(1,4)$ and $(4,1)$ it also verifies $B(a\psi, \phi) = B(\psi, \rev{a}\phi)$ for every even blade $a$ and every invariant form. The symmetry types are read off the kernel bases.

\emph{(iv)} For one constituent the pairing in question is $B(\psi, \psi)$; over a field of characteristic zero it vanishes for every $\psi$ exactly when $B$ is alternating. So some invariant form is nonzero on a single constituent exactly when some invariant form is not alternating; otherwise a nonzero pairing needs two constituents, $B(\psi_{1}, \psi_{2})$, which exists when some form is nonzero. With (iii): two at $n = 3, 4$, one at $n = 5$, none at $n = 2, 6$. Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins} proves mass begins at two constituents for $n = 3, 4$ (the reversion pairing is alternating there) and at one for $n = 5$; the thresholds agree. The agreement concerns where an invariant pairing first exists, not the mass formulas themselves, which are the theorem's.

\emph{Scope.} The result is Clifford structure, transport-absent. It does not decide between the pairing and momentum readings of mass in dimensions $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$; it shows that the pairing reading has no internal freedom (every invariant pairing is the reversion pairing read through a functional), and that it coincides with the field-theoretic notion of a mass term. The standard field-theory statement that a single chirality has no mass term in dimensions $2 \bmod 4$ (cited from memory, for comparison only) is recovered here with an own proof and is not used. The factorisation (i) is in substance the classical description of spin-invariant bilinear forms on spinors through the reversion and conjugation anti-involutions (Harvey, \emph{Spinors and Calibrations}; Alekseevsky and Cort\'es; both cited from memory, for comparison only); the proof given here is self-contained and uses neither. The argument of (i) does not use nondegeneracy of the quadratic form beyond the existence of the bivector action, so it also covers degenerate signatures, which are not claimed here.

synthesis.lowest-causal-residues-zero-fo.formal:
Use the constituent definitions of Definition \claimref{obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-momentum}, with the momentum of Premise \claimref{dark-tower-matter.h1-momentum} read in dimensions two and six as it is read in dimensions three and five, and in dimension six take $f = \tfrac{1}{4}(1 + e_{t}e_{a})(1 \pm I)$, $I$ the pseudoscalar of $V$, a primitive idempotent of $\Cl^{0}(V)$ for either sign.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Floors; proved.)} Along a tower of $(1,1)$ ascents over a definite ground $(m,0)$ or $(0,m)$, $\min(p,q)$ rises by one per floor, so the tower has exactly one causal floor, $(m+1,1)$ or $(1,m+1)$, while residue and Morita class are constant along it (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-eight-towers-mod-8-clock}). The causal signatures of residue $r$ are therefore one per tower, of dimension $m + 2$ with $m \equiv r$ or $m \equiv -r \pmod 8$, and the lowest has dimension $\min(r, 8-r) + 2$. A rule reading only data constant along towers cannot choose among them; the causal filter chooses the floor, and the remaining choice is the tower.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Residue 0; computed, exact.)} At $(1,1)$, the lowest causal signature of residue $0$, $\Cl^{0}(V) \cong \R \oplus \R$, the spinor ideal $S$ is one-dimensional with field $\R$, and $j(\lambda f) = \lambda^{2} j(f)$ with $j(f)$ null. Every total momentum of constituents from $S$ is null: no number of constituents is massive. The single ideal is one of two chiralities: $\Cl^{0}(V)$ has two non-isomorphic simple modules, and $f = \tfrac12(1 + e_{t}e_{a})$ picks one by the orientation of $e_{a}$, a choice that is not canonical in dimension two (in dimensions three to five all such ideals are isomorphic). The complementary ideal $\Cl^{0}(V)(1-f)$ carries the opposite null ray, and one constituent from each ideal has $m^{2} = 1$: with both chiralities admitted, mass begins at two constituents at $(1,1)$ as well. The emptiness of residue $0$ is therefore a consequence of the single-ideal definition, not of the algebra alone.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Residue 4; computed, exact.)} At $(1,5)$ and at $(5,1)$, for either sign of the chiral factor, $S$ has real dimension $8$ and field $\HH$, $Q(j(\psi)) = 0$ identically on $S$, and two constituents are massive ($m^{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$ on two basis elements): mass begins at two constituents, as in dimensions three and four (Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins}(i)).
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The window; computed.)} Under the lowest-causal choice and the single-ideal definition, the absence of massive matter in residue $0$ follows from (ii); in residue $4$ it does not follow from content. Under R1 to R3 (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.unit-ball-rule}) a populated tower of space dimension five adds $V_{3}/V_{5} = 5/(2\pi)$, giving $\tfrac{11}{3} + \tfrac{47}{6\pi}$, between $6.160$ and $6.161$, about $12$ standard errors above the observed $5.364 \pm 0.065$. The unit-ball value is a fit (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.status-rule}: the relation was found by solving for the observed value, and its clauses were chosen with it known), and the emptiness of residue $4$ is one of the clauses that fit needs. Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives} secures this by representing residue $4$ by the definite $(4,0)$ or $(0,4)$, a non-causal signature; no content result secures it at the causal $(1,5)$ or $(5,1)$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.lowest-causal-residues-zero-fo.technical: Apply T14c's own definitions of constituents, spinor ideal and momentum, under Premise H1 extended to dimensions two and six, at the lowest causal signatures of the two residues where Premise P3 departs from the lowest causal choice. Along a tower of $(1,1)$ ascents exactly one floor is causal, so within a residue the causal signatures are one per tower and the open choice is which tower. At $(1,1)$ (residue $0$) the even algebra splits as $\R \oplus \R$, the spinor ideal is one-dimensional and every momentum lies on one null ray, so constituents of one ideal never combine to a massive composite; the ideal is one of two chiralities, fixed by the orientation of a space direction, and one constituent of each chirality is massive. At $(1,5)$ and $(5,1)$ (residue $4$) the ideal is eight-dimensional over $\HH$, single momenta are null and pairs are massive: mass begins at two, as in this world. So under the lowest-causal choice residue $0$'s emptiness follows from the single-chirality definition and residue $4$'s does not follow from content. If R1 to R3 hold and residue $4$ were populated at dimension six, the unit-ball ratio would be between $6.160$ and $6.161$, about $12$ standard errors above the observed $5.364 \pm 0.065$; the unit-ball value is a fit, and it needs residue $4$ empty, which P3 supplies by choosing the non-causal $(4,0)$.
synthesis.lowest-causal-residues-zero-fo.lay: The dark-matter paper assigns each of eight families of possible worlds one representative signature, and its premise P3 makes two of those choices differently from the simplest rule (take the smallest signature with exactly one time direction). This result tests the two disputed families with the series' own description of matter, under the series' assumption about how a constituent's momentum is defined. In the two-dimensional world of one family, the paper's definition admits constituents of one handedness only; these can only move at light speed in one direction, so they never bind into anything with mass. Constituents of both handednesses together would bind, so this family is empty of massive matter because of that one-handedness choice, not by the algebra alone. In the six-dimensional world of the other family, constituents bind into massive pairs just as in ours. So content does not empty that second family; if it held matter in the proportions the paper uses, the predicted dark-to-visible ratio would be about 6.16 instead of the observed 5.36. The paper's match therefore depends on a premise that keeps the second family empty.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} A tower of $(1,1)$ ascents is the sequence $(p+k, q+k)$, $k \geq 0$, over a ground with $\min(p,q) = 0$, that is a definite $(m,0)$ or $(0,m)$. Then $\min(p+k,q+k) = k$, which equals $1$ at $k = 1$ only, so the unique causal floor is $(m+1,1)$ or $(1,m+1)$, of dimension $m+2$. The residue $p - q$ is unchanged by the ascent, and $\Cl(p+k,q+k) \cong \Mat(2^{k}, \Cl(p,q))$ (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-eight-towers-mod-8-clock}), so residue, Morita class and division-ring type are constant along each tower. The ground $(m,0)$ has residue $m \bmod 8$ and $(0,m)$ has residue $-m \bmod 8$; so the causal signatures of residue $r$ are the causal floors of the towers with $m \equiv r$, respectively $m \equiv -r$, modulo $8$, the least $m$ being $\min(r, 8-r)$ (with $0$ for $r = 0$). This reproduces the census of Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.towers-are-residues-single-clock-filter}(i), and adds that the causal filter picks exactly one floor in each tower. The check enumerates every ground of dimension at most twelve.

\emph{(ii)} The objects are those of Definition \claimref{obj.dark-tower-matter.ideals-fields-momentum}, and the momentum is that of Premise \claimref{dark-tower-matter.h1-momentum}, read at dimensions two and six as at three and five; this extension is a hypothesis of the statement. At $(1,1)$ the even algebra is spanned by $1$ and $b = e_{t}e_{a}$ with $b^{2} = -Q(e_{t})Q(e_{a}) = 1$, so $\Cl^{0}(V) = \R f \oplus \R(1-f)$ with $f = \tfrac12(1+b)$, and $S = \Cl^{0}(V)f = \R f$. For $\psi = \lambda f$, $j(\psi) = \lambda^{2} j(f)$. Since $e_{t}$ anticommutes with $b$, $e_{t}f = (1-f)e_{t}$ and $\rev{f} = 1 - f$, so $f e_{t}\rev{f} = f e_{t}(1-f) = f e_{t}$ and $j(f) = \tfrac12(e_{t} - Q(e_{t})e_{a})$, a null vector. Every total momentum $\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2} j(f)$ is a nonnegative multiple of $j(f)$, hence null, and $m^{2} = 0$ for every finite set of constituents from $S$. The same computation for $1 - f$ gives $\tfrac12(e_{t} + Q(e_{t})e_{a})$, the other null ray, and the sum of the two has $m^{2} = Q(e_{t})Q(e_{t}) = 1$. The two ideals are not isomorphic as $\Cl^{0}(V)$-modules, $f$ and $1 - f$ being distinct central idempotents. The definition's $f = \tfrac12(1 + e_{t}e_{a})$ selects one of them by the orientation of $e_{a}$ (replacing $e_{a}$ by $-e_{a}$ exchanges $f$ and $1 - f$), so the single spinor ideal is a chirality choice; the conclusion of (ii) is relative to it.

\emph{(iii)} At $(1,5)$ and $(5,1)$ the pseudoscalar $I$ of $V$ is even, central in $\Cl^{0}(V)$ and satisfies $I^{2} = 1$; it commutes with $b$ and is invariant under the adjoint, so $f = \tfrac14(1+b)(1 \pm I)$ is an adjoint-invariant idempotent. The check finds $\dim_{\R} S = 8$ and $\dim_{\R} f\Cl^{0}(V)f = 4$, and it exhibits two anticommuting elements of the corner with square a negative multiple of $f$, so the corner is $\HH$, a division algebra, $f$ is primitive, and the field is $\HH$, the division algebra of residue $5$ as in Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field}. Writing $\psi = \sum_{i} x_{i}s_{i}$ on a basis $s_{1}, \ldots, s_{8}$ of $S$, $j(\psi)$ is a quadratic form in $x$ with vector coefficients $J_{il}$, and $Q(j(\psi)) = \sum Q(J_{il}, J_{km})\,x_{i}x_{l}x_{k}x_{m}$; the check collects the coefficient of every quartic monomial and finds each zero, so $Q(j(\psi)) = 0$ as a polynomial identity over $\Q$, not on samples. Two basis constituents have total momentum with $m^{2} = \tfrac14 \neq 0$. Hence mass begins at two constituents. The same routine reproduces Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.where-mass-begins} at $(1,3)$ and $(2,1)$ (single momenta null, pairs massive) and at $(1,4)$ (single momenta not all null), and the fields of Theorem \claimref{dark-tower-matter.constituents-field} at those signatures.

\emph{(iv)} Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.unit-ball-rule} gives each populated dark tower the share $V_{3}/V_{D}$ with $D$ its space dimension; $V_{3} = \tfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $V_{5} = \tfrac{8\pi^{2}}{15}$, so $V_{3}/V_{5} = \tfrac{5}{2\pi}$, and $1 + \tfrac83 + \tfrac{16}{3\pi} + \tfrac{5}{2\pi} = \tfrac{11}{3} + \tfrac{47}{6\pi}$. With $\tfrac{333}{106} < \pi < \tfrac{355}{113}$ the check shows that $\tfrac{11}{3} + \tfrac{16}{3\pi}$ lies inside $5.364 \pm 0.065$ and that $6.160 < \tfrac{11}{3} + \tfrac{47}{6\pi} < 6.161$, between $12$ and $13$ standard errors above $5.364$. Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.status-rule} records that the unit-ball relation was found by solving for the observed value and that its clauses were chosen with it known, so the agreement is a fit; the emptiness of residue $4$ is among those clauses. Which towers are populated is observation-level (Observation \claimref{dark-matter.which-towers-are-populated}); the statement is only that residue $4$'s emptiness, on which the match depends, is not a consequence of the content in (iii). The lowest-causal choice itself is the minimality reading that Premise \claimref{dark-matter.p3-nearest-dimension-representatives} cites as its support, applied inside the causal filter; it is not derived here.

synthesis.matter-asymmetry-registered-fr.formal:
\emph{Premise ($\epsilon$), the matter asymmetry as a registered input.} Let $\epsilon$ be the asymmetry per mode of the oriented towers, the strength at which the flag acts on an oriented tower's modes, equal in this tower and the mirror (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}(v)), so that the asymmetry stored in an oriented tower is the charge $Q = \epsilon N$ (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.stored-asymmetry-charge-not-number}(i)); the asymmetry lives only in this tower and the mirror (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.asymmetry-arrow-counted-fifteenth-refutation}(iii)). The premise: \emph{$\epsilon$ is a free number of the series}, inherited, not generated: it is not computed from the transport structure, from another premise of the register, or from a dynamics of the series, and it is not a function of $N$ (Premise \claimref{synthesis.number-n-registered-free-input}) or of $\xi G$ (Premise \claimref{synthesis.rung-unit-second-free-number}). It is initial data of the descent, the stance of Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.asymmetry-arrow-counted-fifteenth-refutation}(iv), registered here as a premise. Its value is taken from the record: in this tower it is fixed by the measured baryon density, $\Omega_{b}h^{2} = 0.02237 \pm 0.00015$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}), equivalently the $8.7 \times 10^{-11}$ baryons per unit entropy that the stored results use.

\emph{Scope.} The premise registers the value. Its equality across this tower and the mirror is Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}(v), not this premise (the former Premise P4, democracy of the asymmetry over the oriented towers, is retired as a postulate: nothing stored used it beyond the mirror). The first route of that clause takes the stance registered here, that $\epsilon$ is a datum of the descent and not of a tower's state, as a stated hypothesis; no assumes edge is drawn for it. That it is one number across space, rather than a field, agrees with Theorem \claimref{synthesis.adiabatic-deposit-modulation-is-a-time-shift}: under the charge reading and the mirror's deposit law the charge per unit entropy must be uniform up to the isocurvature the record allows. It is not the deposit energy per unit charge $\varepsilon$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.mirror-temperature-measures-deposit-under-r}, which this premise does not register.

\emph{What it is for.} The charge reading of the stored asymmetry, with the mirror's equal baryon charge, takes $\epsilon$ as initial data of the descent (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.stored-asymmetry-charge-not-number}); the dark-to-baryon count uses only its equality across the reversal orbit, not its provenance; on that stance the unexplained numbers of the event are $N$ and $\epsilon$, with the orientation bit a third datum (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.asymmetry-arrow-counted-fifteenth-refutation}(iv)). Registering it makes it a counted input of the register, exchanged for the baryon density of the standard cosmological model. No assumes edge to it is drawn here.

\emph{What it does not give.} It does not explain the value or its sign; it does not say how the descent deposits the charge, nor with what energy per unit charge (the open entries of the pre-descent theory); and it does not decide the trichotomy's classification of $\epsilon$, whose kinematic clause runs for it at observation level and whose dynamical clause does not (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-trichotomy-descents-data}).

\emph{Refutation condition.} The premise is false if $\epsilon$ is produced dynamically by any in-framework calculation (the refutation condition of the stance in Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.asymmetry-arrow-counted-fifteenth-refutation}(iv)); if it is computed from the transport structure or from another premise of the register; or if it is shown to be a function of $N$ or of another registered number.

\emph{Note (the unit of $\epsilon$, 2026-11-11).} The words ``per mode'' and the formula $Q = \epsilon N$ are the charge reading's own (Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.stored-asymmetry-charge-not-number}; Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.mirror-tower-copy-one}(v)), whose argument uses only that $N$ is common to the two towers. They do not give $\epsilon$ a number: with $N = M_{P}/H$, about $10^{61}$, no count of modes makes $8.7 \times 10^{-11}$ the factor (the baryon number inside the de Sitter radius is about $5 \times 10^{78}$ today, and it is not constant, the radius being fixed while the density dilutes). The figure $8.7 \times 10^{-11}$ is this tower's yield $n_{B}/s$ today: the conserved charge per comoving volume, measured with this tower's entropy as the unit of comoving volume. It is the descent's datum only if no entropy is produced in this tower after the descent. The equality along the reversal orbit is an equality of charge per comoving volume, $n_{B}' = n_{B}$; it is not $n_{B}'/s' = n_{B}/s$, which is the thermal reading that clause (iv) of the Proposition rejects (the mirror's own ratio is larger by $\xi^{-3}$, the stored $\eta' = \eta/\xi^{3}$). What the premise registers is unchanged.
synthesis.matter-asymmetry-registered-fr.technical: The series inherits its matter asymmetry rather than generating it: the descent creates the tower charges and makes one orientation choice, and the size of the asymmetry, $\epsilon$ per mode, so that each oriented tower stores the charge $\epsilon N$, was until now held as a flagged stance inside a proved result: initial data of the descent, refuted by any in-framework calculation that produces it. This premise registers that number as a free input, as the D-term level and $N$ are registered: $\epsilon$ is not derived and is not a function of the other registered numbers, and its value comes from the measured baryon density, about $8.7 \times 10^{-11}$ baryons per unit entropy. Its equality across this tower and the mirror is a clause of the copy theorem, and its uniformity across space agrees with the stored result that only a time shift of the descent is an adiabatic modulation of the deposit. It is not the deposit energy per unit charge that the mirror's temperature measures, which stays unregistered. It would be refuted by any in-framework dynamical calculation of $\epsilon$, by a derivation from the structure or another premise, or by showing it is a function of another registered number.
synthesis.matter-asymmetry-registered-fr.lay: There is more matter than antimatter in the universe. Most theories try to explain how a process in the early universe produced that excess; this framework does not. It takes the size of the excess to have been set when the universe began, as a starting condition, and reads its value off the measured amount of ordinary matter. This entry records that size as one of the basic numbers put in by hand, beside the huge number N and the number that sets the weak scale. It would be overturned if a calculation within the framework produced the excess.
